    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18076v1</id>
    <title>Upper bounds for the number of spanning forests of a graph</title>
    <updated>2026-11-13T12:00:47Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18076v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.18076v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Let $G$ be a simple graph on $n$ vertices, and let $F(G)$ denote the number of spanning forests of $G$. Bencs and Csikvári proved that every $r$-regular graph $G$ with $r\ge 2$ satisfies $F(G)\le r^n$. Motivated by this result, they conjectured that if $G$ has minimum degree at least $3$, then $F(G)\leq \prod_{i=1}^n d_i$, where $(d_1, d_2, \dots, d_n)$ is the degree sequence of $G$. In this paper, we prove that graphs with minimum degree at least $n/3$ $(n\geq7)$
  satisfy $F(G)\leq \prod_{i=1}^n d_i$. We also construct a counterexample to the conjecture. We therefore further study the enumeration of spanning forests in general graphs, proving an upper bound in terms of the degree sequence
  and characterizing the extremal graphs attaining this bound. In addition, using the matrix-forest theorem, we obtain an upper bound for the number of spanning forests of a connected graph in terms of its algebraic connectivity,
  and characterize the extremal graphs attaining this bound.</summary>

    <title>Perfect Matching Complexes of $3\times 2n$ Grid Graph</title>
    <updated>2026-11-13T11:36:54Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18058v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.18058v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>The perfect matching complex of a simple graph $G$ is an abstract simplicial complex whose facets (maximal faces) are precisely the perfect matchings of $G$. In this article, we study the topology of the perfect matching complex of the $3\times 2n$ grid graph and show that it is homotopy equivalent to a wedge of $f_{n-1}$ copies of $(n-1)$-dimensional spheres, where $f_{k}$ denotes the $k$-th Fibonacci number. This proves a particular case of the conjecture given by Chandrakar and Singh for perfect matching complex of grid graphs.</summary>

    <title>On configurations that are nearly generalised polygons</title>
    <updated>2026-11-13T07:39:57Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17855v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.17855v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Payne (1972) introduced nearly generalised $n$-gons as $(s+1)$-regular bipartite graphs of girth $2n$ with small excess over the Moore bound. Biggs and Ito (1980) proved nonexistence of such graphs if $s > 1$ and $n > 3$, leaving open the existence of regular antipodal planes. We revisit this problem from several equivalent viewpoints. First we show that a regular antipodal plane of order $s$ is equivalent to a balanced weighing matrix whose support is the incidence matrix of a biplane with parameters \[
  2-\left(\frac{s^2+s+2}{2},\,s+1,\,2\right). \] This gives short determinant and local-arithmetic obstructions to existence. We then formulate the question of signing a biplane as an affine linear system over $\mathbb F_2$, and use this formulation to prove that no regular antipodal plane of order $s$ exists with $4\le s\le 14$. Finally, we give further equivalent formulations in terms of sharply deranged families of permutations and mutually orthogonal array-bic squares. These translations provide new computational and structural approaches to Payne's conjecture that regular antipodal planes exist only for $s=2,3$.</summary>

    <title>A proof of the Jamneshan-Tao conjecture by embedding nilspaces in nilmanifolds</title>
    <updated>2026-11-12T22:46:05Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17567v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.17567v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We prove that every compact finite-rank nilspace admits a continuous injective morphism into a toral nilspace of the same step, and hence into a connected filtered nilmanifold. Combining this embedding theorem with the general nilspace inverse theorem, we establish the Jamneshan-Tao conjecture and extend its conclusion to second-countable compact abelian groups. This yields an inverse theorem for Gowers norms on all such groups, in which the correlating functions factor through morphisms into nilmanifolds. The proof relies on substantial foundations developed in nilspace theory over the past decade, particularly the general nilspace inverse theorem and the representation of compact finite-rank nilspaces as quotients of free nilspaces.</summary>

    <title>Triameter, distance packings, and vertex connectivity</title>
    <updated>2026-11-12T18:42:48Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17259v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.17259v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We study upper bounds for the triameter of a connected graph in terms of distance packings and vertex connectivity. For any positive integer $k$, we bound the triameter of a graph by a linear function of its $k$-packing number and show that this bound is tight for all values of the parameters. As a corollary, we confirm the conjecture of Das and Abdioğlu on the upper bound for the triameter in terms of the order and the minimum degree of a graph. We also find the maximum triameter among graphs with given order and vertex connectivity, and describe the extremal graphs. Our main tool is a projection of a graph onto a spider or a unicyclic graph which preserves the distances between three prescribed vertices.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17197v1</id>
    <title>Matching statistics in regular hypergraphs and applications</title>
    <updated>2026-11-12T18:01:14Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17197v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.17197v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>For fixed $k\ge3$, we determine the first sublinear correction to the logarithm of the matching partition function for a class of $n$-vertex $d$-regular $k$-uniform hypergraphs, uniformly for activities in each fixed compact interval of $(0,\infty)$.Our hypotheses include every regular linear hypergraph of polynomial degree and a class of nonlinear hypergraphs described by higher codegrees and intersection patterns, which we introduce here. The weighted counting estimate implies an averaged version of Kahn's conjecture: under the uniform measure, the expected number of uncovered vertices is $(1+o(1))nd^{-1/k}$, with concentration and large deviations on this scale. The proof combines a novel variant of random greedy counting, based on short stages and regular completions, with a new entropy method that uses intersection patterns to control reconstruction after deleting matching edges.
  We highlight the following applications. (i) Partial transversals in Latin squares. Every Latin square of order $n$ has $(n/e^2)^n\exp((3+o(1))n^{2/3})$ partial transversals. Also, almost all partial transversals have $(1+o(1))n^{2/3}$ missing cells.
  (ii) Linear $3$-uniform hypergraphs. There are $(n/e^2)^{n^2/6}\exp((1/2+o(1))n^{5/3})$ linear $3$-uniform hypergraphs on $[n]$, and almost all have $n^2/6-(1/6+o(1))n^{5/3}$ edges.
  (iii) Matroids of fixed rank. For each fixed $r\ge4$, the number $m(n,r)$ of rank-$r$ matroids on $[n]$ satisfies $\log m(n,r)=\frac{n^{r-1}}{r!}(\log n-r+1)+\left(\frac1{(r-1)!}+o(1)\right)n^{r-1-1/r}$, refining the estimates of van der Hofstad, Pendavingh and van der Pol.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17603v1</id>
    <title>Offline KL-Regularized Reinforcement Learning with Stochastic Transitions</title>
    <updated>2026-11-12T23:53:26Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17603v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.17603v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>KL-regularized reinforcement learning is the objective behind RL fine-tuning of language models, and its data are often collected by the reference policy itself. However, beyond bandits and deterministic transitions, little is known about how much offline data it needs. In this work, we study finite discounted Markov decision processes with unknown stochastic transitions, $K$ state-action pairs and effective horizon $H$. For data that cover the regularized optimum with concentrability $C\geq 4$, every estimator needs $Ω(KCH^3/(ε\max\{ε,β\}))$ samples on some instances when $ε$ is small, where $β$ is the temperature. Under a fixed design, pessimistic soft value iteration with a variance-aware penalty attains this rate with high probability, up to logarithmic factors, when $β\geq 1.4H$. When the data come from the reference policy itself, we show that it covers the optimum up to a power law whose exponent grows as $H/β$; in the same temperature range, this power law alone gives the estimator a sample complexity polynomial in $1/ε$, with no coverage assumption. For $β\geq H$ the power can also increase the sample size needed by a factor polynomial in $1/ε$. Finally, the plug-in estimator, which is minimax optimal with a generative model, can fail on reference data at small temperatures when many actions are rarely seen, while the pessimistic estimator does not.</summary>
    <category term="cs.LG" scheme="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom"/>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17596v1</id>
    <title>Tractable Importance Sampling for Monte Carlo Privacy Accounting</title>
    <updated>2026-11-12T23:33:00Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17596v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.17596v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Evaluating tight Differential Privacy (DP) parameters for DP matrix factorization with privacy amplification by sampling requires analyzing high-dimensional, correlated Gaussian mixtures. Because integrating these mixture distributions to find the exact privacy failure probability ($δ$) is analytically intractable, these mechanisms are typically analyzed using Monte Carlo accounting. However, standard sampling suffers from prohibitive variance when estimating small $δ$ associated with strict privacy guarantees, which in turn requires a large sample complexity, making Monte Carlo accounting inefficient. We demonstrate that Monte Carlo accounting can be made much more efficient via importance sampling. We give a shifted importance sampling proposal distribution parameterized by a stretch factor $α> 1$. We prove a closed-form bound $B(α) < 1$ on the support of the importance-weighted estimator that holds identically for both directions of the hockey-stick divergence, show that $B$ is log-convex so that the optimal $α$ is a one-dimensional root-finding problem, and show that the resulting estimator seamlessly plugs into the KL-Hoeffding verification protocol used by past work, with a sample complexity reduced by exactly a factor of $1/B(α^*)$.</summary>

    <summary>We compute the VC-dimension of metric ball classifiers in the model spaces of Riemannian geometry (Euclidean, spherical, hyperbolic) and present upper and lower bounds on the VC-dimension of metric balls in several other situations, including general normed vector spaces (potentially infinite VC-dimension), vector spaces with $\ell^p$-norms (VC-dimension grows at least linearly in the dimension, faster than Euclidean for $p=1$), flat tori, and general Riemannian manifolds (arbitrarily large VC-dimension after a conformal change). In several situations where the VC-dimension is large or even infinite, we prove generalization bounds under additional assumptions on the data distribution using covering arguments. Both in the VC-dimension and covering setting, we consider data on low-dimensional subsets of high-dimensional Euclidean spaces. As an application, we consider coverage-based algorithms in active learning.</summary>

    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13210v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.13210v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We study the problem of agnostic PAC learning under deterministic labels, where the examples are labeled by an arbitrary deterministic function, which need not belong to the concept class $C$. This model captures misspecification without stochastic label noise and lies between the realizable and fully agnostic settings. Prior work showed that, when $C$ has finite diameter $K$ and VC dimension $d$, deterministic labels can improve the sample complexity upper bound from the classical agnostic guarantee $O(d/\varepsilon^2)$ to $\widetilde{O}(K/\varepsilon)$, but left a large gap between upper and lower bounds. Our main result sharpens this picture. We prove that every class of VC dimension $d$ and finite diameter $K$ is learnable with sample complexity $\widetilde{O}\left( \frac{K^{1/3} \, d^{2/3}}{\varepsilon} \right)$, and we construct classes for which this bound is tight up to logarithmic factors. We also study the online analogue of this problem and show that the minimax regret is again partly controlled by the diameter of the class. Technically, our upper bounds are obtained via memorization-based learning algorithms that exploit the deterministic label structure.</summary>
    <category term="stat.ML" scheme="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom"/>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.12419v1</id>
    <title>Optimal Rates for Adaptive Private $k$-PCA</title>
    <updated>2026-11-09T13:48:20Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.12419v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.12419v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Given $n$ i.i.d. random matrices $A_i \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}$ with common expectation $Σ$, the goal of \emph{Differentially Private Stochastic PCA} is to identify a $k$-dimensional subspace capturing the leading variance directions of $Σ$, while preserving differential privacy~(DP) for each individual sample $A_i$. \citet{dungler2025iterative} introduced \kdppca, the first algorithm to simultaneously (1) achieve sample complexity $n=\widetilde O(d)$ for sub-Gaussian data, (2) adapt its privacy noise to the intrinsic randomness of the data, and (3) extend seamlessly to any target dimension $k\le d$. However, its sample complexity has a suboptimal dependence on $k$. We propose the first algorithm that achieves optimal sample complexity in both $d$ and $k$, while retaining properties (2) and (3) of \kdppca. Additionally, prior utility guarantees require a minimum sample size with exponential dependence on the eigengap. Our method removes this dependence. It also improves the dependence on spectral parameters, matching known lower bounds for the spiked covariance model. Unlike deflation-based approaches like \kdppca, our algorithm updates the full $d\times k$ subspace jointly rather than one eigenvector at a time. This non-deflation structure simplifies the algorithm, reduces the number of hyper-parameters, and improves computational efficiency, particularly when using block linear algebra libraries.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11805v1</id>
    <title>Operator Learning of Microstructure-Dependent Internal-Variable Models for Inelastic Homogenization: Approximation and Complexity</title>
    <updated>2026-11-09T03:08:26Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11805v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.11805v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We study the learning of homogenized constitutive laws for inelastic heterogeneous materials, aiming to replace costly concurrent unit-cell simulations with surrogates that generalize across loading histories and microstructures. We focus on the recurrent neural operator framework, motivated by the explicit form of homogenized Kelvin--Voigt linear viscoelasticity. In this framework, internal variables enable a Markovian approximation of loading-history dependence, and neural operators represent the microstructure-dependent constitutive response. For periodic Kelvin--Voigt viscoelasticity, we prove a universal approximation theorem showing that the model can approximate the homogenized constitutive law to any prescribed accuracy, uniformly in time and over a wide set of admissible strain trajectories and microstructural property fields, in two and three dimensions. This comprises a significant extension of the existing, somewhat limited, one-dimensional theory that uses explicit solutions for piecewise constant materials. Instead, in two and three dimensions, we adopt a more versatile approximation based on the spectral representation of the memory kernel that arises from homogenization. This also enables us to give an explicit bound on the internal-variable dimension, sufficient for approximation, exhibiting logarithmic growth in the inverse relative stress error and in material contrast. Numerical experiments on viscoelasticity and crystal plasticity complement the theory, illustrating the roles of internal-variable dimension and sample complexity in learning homogenized responses from unit-cell data. Theoretical results are formally verified in Lean 4.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11119v1</id>
    <title>Scalable Neural Safety Certification via Monotonicity</title>
    <updated>2026-11-08T04:11:14Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11119v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.11119v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Learning-based safety certification offers a promising route for verifying complex dynamical systems when explicit models are unavailable, but existing data-driven methods often scale poorly: they treat the system as a black box, rely on dense discretizations or Lipschitz bounds, and consequently suffer from sample complexity that grows exponentially with dimension. This paper shows that a common structural property of dynamical systems--monotonicity--can be used to break this curse of dimensionality. We develop a data-driven framework for robust safety verification and safe controller synthesis for unknown monotone systems using only simulator queries. Our main theoretical result proves that, for monotone systems with upper-closed unsafe sets, safety is completely characterized by the existence of monotone inductive barrier certificates. This structure reduces certificate verification over continuous state spaces to localized boundary checks over finitely many cells. To learn such certificates, we introduce Max-Monotone Networks, a monotone neural architecture with universal approximation guarantees for monotone functions. We then propose a training and refinement algorithm that, upon successful termination, returns formally valid neural barrier certificates and, under mild partition assumptions, requires only $O(n)$ simulator queries. Across high-dimensional benchmarks, including oscillator networks with up to $13{,}659$ states and traffic networks with $1{,}000$ states, our method certifies safety in regimes where prior approaches either do not converge or exceed memory limits. These results demonstrate that exploiting order structure can make neural safety certification both scalable and formally sound.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.10996v1</id>
    <title>Toward a theory of Evaluability</title>
    <updated>2026-11-07T22:32:34Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.10996v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.10996v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Machine learning models, particularly large foundation models, are increasingly evaluated along multiple axes that are relevant for their usage. In addition to accuracy measures appropriate for the specific task of interest, measures capturing safety, calibration and fairness properties are often of interest. The classical approach to these problems assumes that the test set has been held out from the training process, an assumption that is increasingly harder to justify for large foundation models. In this work, we formalize a notion of evaluability without this assumption, and ask if it is feasible to evaluate black-box models in settings where our test samples may have been used during training.
  We study this problem under different settings, capturing different levels of access to the model. We first study the natural setting, where the evaluator only looks at the output of the model on the test set. We fully characterize the class of distributions where accurate evaluation is possible, and show tight upper and lower bounds on the sample complexity of evaluation. Our results show that black-box evaluation in this setup is feasible if and only if the distribution is close to being small support. We then consider evaluation algorithms that can query the model on additional inputs and demonstrate connections to self-correctors studied in program testing. Using these, we show that a small amount of query access can increase the power of the evaluator for natural distributions and concept classes.</summary>
    <category term="cs.LG" scheme="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom"/>
    <category term="stat.ML" scheme="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom"/>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18497v1</id>
    <title>Regularized Neural Quantum States for Heisenberg Magnets</title>
    <updated>2026-11-13T18:07:44Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18497v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.18497v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We introduce an approach to solving locally ordered quantum spin systems using neural network quantum states. First, our approach rests on choosing a spin basis constructed from the magnetic texture of a classical or quantum reference state. Second, the method improves convergence and suppresses parameter-space drift through a regularized Riemannian gradient descent adapted to the quantum state geometry of the variational state manifold. Combining these techniques enables stable ground-state calculations for two- and three-dimensional chiral spin systems with Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions. The resulting variational ground-state energies are competitive with those of high-fidelity density matrix renormalization group calculations and, for periodic and layered geometries, provide significantly tighter upper bounds on the ground-state energy.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18430v1</id>
    <title>Validating Graph Neural Network Feature Attribution Through Local Perturbations: A Study on CoMoFeNiCu Decomposition Enthalpy</title>
    <updated>2026-11-13T17:10:27Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18430v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.18430v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Graph neural networks (GNNs) show promise for predicting materials properties, but interpretability remains a challenge, particularly understanding whether attributed feature importance reflects physical reality or statistical artifacts. Here, we present a methods validation study that deliberately overfits a physics-aware GNN ensemble to probe the robustness of feature-ranking approaches. Using the CoMoFeNiCu high-entropy alloy system with three stoichiometries, we train GNNs to predict decomposition enthalpies from DFT-calculated structures while explicitly constraining output weights to encode feature importance. By design, our dataset is limited (approximately 900 binary and 4,500 ternary decomposition pathways) to control compositional complexity and enable precise interrogation of local chemistry effects. We validate that feature rankings capture meaningful local-environment information through a series of atomic swap perturbations: perturbing individual atomic sites and re-ranking features reveals spatial decay consistent with the GNN's interaction cutoff, confirming that weights encode neighbor-shell effects rather than global stoichiometric artifacts alone. Results demonstrate that feature attribution methods can remain physically interpretable even under overfitting, provided validation is rigorous. This work establishes a foundation for trustworthy interpretability in materials GNNs and sets the stage for scaling to multiple chemistries and testing generalization across compositional spaces.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18031v1</id>
    <title>Latent resonances in oscillator networks</title>
    <updated>2026-11-13T10:59:13Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18031v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.18031v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>In networks of coupled oscillators, from neural circuits to power grids, damping is expected to suppress oscillations because of its dissipativity. Here we show that local damping can, counterintuitively, amplify oscillations along some input-output channels, while the network's global oscillation energy decreases and its spectral properties improve. The amplified oscillation arises from a latent resonance that lies in the spectrum yet barely manifests. The added passive damping reshapes this resonance by mixing it with adjacent eigenmodes. In random power-grid networks, damping can boost weakly responding channels by more than an order of magnitude, while subdominant channels can grow to exceed the originally strongest channel. Damping thus not only suppresses oscillations but also provides a way to redistribute oscillatory energy. For any passive network, the amplified response and its upper bound follow exactly from baseline quantities, offering a principled route for network design and control.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18007v1</id>
    <title>Emulating spatially extended systems using Fourier Neural Operator</title>
    <updated>2026-11-13T10:35:02Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18007v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.18007v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Operator Learning (OL) algorithms approximate underlying mathematical operators by mapping entire classes of input functions to their corresponding solutions. For instance, architectures such as the Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) have been trained on numerical datasets generated by isolated, stiff ionic models to provide a data-driven alternative to traditional numerical integration schemes. However, real-world biological and physical systems typically consist of interconnected spatial units arranged in complex, heterogeneous networks. Motivated by this observation, we generalize this data-driven framework to spatially extended systems defined on diverse graph topologies, ranging from Erdos-Renyi to Barabasi-Albert networks. Furthermore, we evaluate the proposed approach on empirical data, demonstrating its ability to accurately and efficiently model task-oriented neural activity.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17036v1</id>
    <title>Ergodicity breaking for data classification in a dissipative Ising model with competing two- and four-body interactions</title>
    <updated>2026-11-12T16:22:22Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17036v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.17036v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We explore the close relationship between the processing of data and the dynamics of interacting many-body systems. For example, certain classes of quantum neural networks can be mapped onto dissipative quantum Ising models whose evolution is described by a Lindblad master equation. In these architectures, emergent nonlinearities lead to non-ergodic dynamics under which initial states located in different basins of attraction evolve towards distinguishable stationary states. This mechanism underlies the classification of quantum data. Motivated by this connection, we consider an Ising model with competing two- and four-body interactions. Using a combination of mean-field calculations and exact small-scale numerics, we show that the stationary state manifold can be designed to enable multi-class classification. We also investigate the structure of the ensuing basins of attraction, thereby showing that these systems allow for the classification of quantum states with nonlinear decision boundaries.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16979v1</id>
    <title>Cup and cap synchronization: higher-order node dynamics from topology</title>
    <updated>2026-11-12T15:47:24Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16979v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.16979v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Higher-order node-based synchronization provides distinct mechanisms for discontinuous synchronization transitions. However, a comprehensive theoretical framework capable of encompassing existing models and revealing the role of higher-order interactions beyond triangles is still missing. Here, combining algebraic topology and nonlinear dynamics, we introduce Cup and Cap Synchronization, a unifying theoretical framework for higher-order node-based dynamics that naturally incorporates the topological organization of the underlying higher-order network. We show that Cup and Cap Synchronization can display critical behavior belonging to the universality classes of two existing higher-order Kuramoto-like models, whose distinct critical behaviors were thought to originate from different mechanisms. Remarkably, we demonstrate that Cup and Cap Synchronization displays additional phenomenology not captured by the previously proposed models of higher-order node-based synchronization. Most relevantly, the inclusion of four-body interactions can fundamentally alter the critical properties of the synchronization transition, giving rise to collective phenomena that cannot be observed in models including only interactions mediated by edges and triangles. These findings reveal the importance of going beyond the commonly studied three-body terms and establish Cup and Cap Synchronization as a unifying theoretical framework for understanding collective dynamics in higher-order networks.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16427v1</id>
    <title>Exact power spectra and effective dimensionality in critical block-GOE networks</title>
    <updated>2026-11-12T07:37:29Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16427v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.16427v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Criticality in neural networks is crucial for optimal information processing. Recent studies have shifted focus from static criticality to frequency-dependent behavior, particularly in oscillatory systems modeled by block-Gaussian orthogonal ensemble (block-GOE) matrices. However, analytical tools to predict spectral properties such as power spectrum and effective dimensionality remain scarce. In this work, we derive exact solutions for the network-averaged power spectrum $\operatorname{Tr}_{N}[\mathbf{S}(ω)]$, the network autocovariance $\operatorname{Tr}_{N}[\mathbf{C}(τ)]$, and the normalized effective dimensionality $D_N(ω)$ in block-GOE ensembles. These results provide a comprehensive framework for understanding how oscillatory networks operate near criticality, offering insights into the dynamic balance between stability and flexibility in large-scale neural systems.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16220v1</id>
    <title>Learning memory forces and bounding frequency errors in fractional Kuramoto grids</title>
    <updated>2026-11-12T03:11:49Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16220v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.16220v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Missing history creates two different demands on a forecaster for a fractional grid: predicting frequency accurately and reconstructing memory well enough to bound the prediction error. We connect these demands through the hereditary force that remains after an integral observation correction. A compact decoder retains the directions most relevant to that force, and an exact decomposition separates omitted directions from coefficient error. A response-trained linear predictor and neural refinement learn the coefficients for frequency prediction. A separate force reconstruction supplies the reference for a nonlinear energy bound for the specified finite relaxation model, accounting for numerical propagation defects and the difference between the reference and point forecasts. For the outage transients studied here, refinement improves on the linear predictor across the time steps and memory parameters tested. Replacing the noisy origin states reveals why this gain can coexist with greater memory reconstruction error: the learned correction partly compensates for observation error. Separating prediction from reconstruction enables frequency bounds in cases where the point predictor alone cannot support them. A critical radius compares calibrated uncertainty with the angle margin available along the reference trajectory, explaining both issuance and abstention. Under jointly exchangeable calibration and test events, the calibrated guarantee bounds the marginal probability of issuing an invalid envelope. Together, these results connect uncertainty about history outside the observation window to frequency forecasts and explicit conditions for bounding their errors.</summary>
    <category term="nlin.AO" scheme="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom"/>

    <title>Nesting in additive manufacturing using quantum annealing</title>
    <updated>2026-11-13T17:22:19Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18447v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.18447v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Nesting in powder bed fusion (PBF), an additive manufacturing (AM) process, determines the positions and orientations of parts within the build space and influences build height and build time. As the number of parts and feasible placements increases, the nesting problem becomes computationally demanding. Exact approaches are limited to small problem sizes as computational effort increases rapidly with the problem size, while heuristic and metaheuristic approaches involve a trade-off between solution quality and computation time. Quantum annealing (QA) offers an alternative for solving combinatorial optimization problems, but its application to nesting in AM remains largely unexplored. This paper presents a QA-based approach for nesting in AM to investigate its feasibility and its scaling behavior across three problem sizes. An iterative binary quadratic model based approach (IBQM) is developed to minimize build height while considering the geometric characteristics of AM parts. Geometric abstraction, iterative decomposition, and variable pruning are applied to address the computational complexity of the nesting problem. The approach is evaluated using three cases with increasing problem sizes and compared to a classical approach combining tabu search and simulated annealing (TBSA). Compared with TBSA, IBQM reduces the build height of the original parts by up to 13.32% and the computation time by up to 74.27%.</summary>

    <title>Consensus-Based Optimization of Path-Integral Free Energy for Model Predictive Control</title>
    <updated>2026-11-13T14:14:14Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18208v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.18208v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We propose CBO-MPPI, a sampling-based predictive controller that applies consensus-based optimization (CBO) to the free energy underlying model predictive path integral control (MPPI). Under hard constraints, this objective rewards sampling neighborhoods containing feasible, low-cost trajectories under perturbation. Standard MPPI performs a local stochastic search by updating one nominal control sequence from Gaussian perturbations around it. In CBO-MPPI, we estimate the free energy at multiple nominal centers from local rollouts. These estimates define a shared consensus that guides drift and diffusion, and the final selected center supplies an MPPI weighted-mean output. For the associated mean-field model, we establish well-posedness and, under additional assumptions, convergence toward a free-energy minimizer. In simulations of obstacle navigation, pendulum swing-up, and planar-arm manipulation under equal rollout budgets, at high temperatures, CBO-MPPI attains lower free energy than MPPI and multi-start MPPI and maintains greater obstacle clearance than CBO-MPC.</summary>

    <title>Starlight: Whittle-Driven Fidelity Rescue for Satellite-Terrestrial Quantum Networks</title>
    <updated>2026-11-13T07:51:22Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17865v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.17865v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>A planetary-scale quantum internet is constrained by exponential attenuation in terrestrial fibers. Low-Earth-orbit (LEO) satellites provide a low-loss vacuum backbone, but limited satellite resources must be allocated among competing connections under continuously evolving and heterogeneous physical conditions. Existing satellite scheduling remains largely provisioning-oriented, optimizing satellite-resource assignment for aggregate entanglement delivery. Recent age-based approaches instead incorporate chronological freshness into entanglement scheduling. Neither line of work directly identifies the connections most urgently requiring satellite assistance as their physical states evolve. We propose Starlight, a demand-driven satellite-terrestrial entanglement routing architecture that targets degrading connections before their terrestrial entanglement becomes unusable. Starlight introduces Effective Age of State (EAoS), a physics-aware metric that maps heterogeneous decoherence and swapping-induced fidelity penalties onto a unified additive coordinate. Representing each connection by evolving EAoS, we formulate rescue scheduling as a Restless Multi-Armed Bandit (RMAB) problem and derive a closed-form Whittle-style index approximation for top-K selection. Starlight further employs a two-timescale control plane and an asynchronous dispatch-and-mask pipeline to suppress redundant in-flight allocations. Simulations show that Starlight achieves up to 84.5% average satisfaction under constrained rescue capacity and sub-0.5-ms orchestration at 1,000 connections, while remaining robust to heterogeneous memory decay and stochastic atmospheric degradation.</summary>

    <title>Binarization as an Attack Surface in Weightless Neural Networks</title>
    <updated>2026-11-13T01:34:07Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17646v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.17646v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Weightless Neural Networks (WNNs) are lightweight classifiers that binarize their inputs and learn by storing binary patterns in lookup memories, which makes them attractive for resource-constrained tasks such as intrusion detection. Because a small perturbation that crosses no binarization threshold leaves the binary input unchanged, WNNs may appear naturally robust to adversarial examples; a perturbation that does cross a threshold, however, can still change the prediction. We study this tension in WiSARD, the canonical RAM-based WNN, and in two variants that replace its memories with Bloom filters, Bloom WiSARD and BTHOWeN. A continuous perturbation reaches these classifiers only by crossing an encoding threshold, changing at least one binary tuple, and redirecting a memory query; we formalize this mechanism with a threshold-crossing bound and a response-margin certificate for standard Boolean WiSARD. Controlled MNIST experiments compare linear and data-driven thermometer encodings under model-agnostic sensitivity probes, a score-based Simulated Annealing attack, and surrogate-transfer attacks. Changing only the encoding while keeping each model otherwise fixed shows that encoding granularity can trade a small clean-accuracy loss for a large decrease in attack success. On the Bot-IoT, CICIDS, and UNSW-NB15 intrusion-detection datasets, adversarial perturbations lead WNN detectors to classify many attacks as normal traffic and to raise false alarms, even when their aggregate accuracy remains high.</summary>

    <title>Offline KL-Regularized Reinforcement Learning with Stochastic Transitions</title>
    <updated>2026-11-12T23:53:26Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17603v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.17603v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>KL-regularized reinforcement learning is the objective behind RL fine-tuning of language models, and its data are often collected by the reference policy itself. However, beyond bandits and deterministic transitions, little is known about how much offline data it needs. In this work, we study finite discounted Markov decision processes with unknown stochastic transitions, $K$ state-action pairs and effective horizon $H$. For data that cover the regularized optimum with concentrability $C\geq 4$, every estimator needs $Ω(KCH^3/(ε\max\{ε,β\}))$ samples on some instances when $ε$ is small, where $β$ is the temperature. Under a fixed design, pessimistic soft value iteration with a variance-aware penalty attains this rate with high probability, up to logarithmic factors, when $β\geq 1.4H$. When the data come from the reference policy itself, we show that it covers the optimum up to a power law whose exponent grows as $H/β$; in the same temperature range, this power law alone gives the estimator a sample complexity polynomial in $1/ε$, with no coverage assumption. For $β\geq H$ the power can also increase the sample size needed by a factor polynomial in $1/ε$. Finally, the plug-in estimator, which is minimax optimal with a generative model, can fail on reference data at small temperatures when many actions are rarely seen, while the pessimistic estimator does not.</summary>

    <title>I2C-GRPO: Insight Importance Checklist for Reinforcement Learning in a Multi-Agent DDoS Alert Triage Workflow</title>
    <updated>2026-11-12T21:41:24Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17534v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.17534v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used for investigative tasks over incomplete evidence, such as cybersecurity alert triage, but reinforcement learning (RL) for such tasks is difficult: intermediate steps have no verifiable labels, rollouts are costly, and outcome rewards are sparse. We propose Insight Importance Checklist (I2C)-GRPO, a checklist reward for intermediate investigation steps. For each decision point, a panel of expert LLMs proposes investigative actions, their atomic forensic insights are extracted, and a separate three-model ranker panel orders the insights by importance. A reward model checks which ranked insights a candidate action targets and returns their consensus-weighted coverage. Because actions are scored without being executed, the reward is a proxy for expected investigative value, and training reduces to a one-step contextual bandit over fixed investigation prefixes. From a soft-computing perspective, the reward is an additive fuzzy measure whose rank-exponent weights act as an ordered weighted averaging (OWA)-type operator; one exponent sets its orness, i.e., how strongly the reward concentrates on the top of the judges' consensus.
  We train an open-weight Qwen3-4B Triage Agent within a fixed multi-agent Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) alert-triage workflow on DARPA 2000 LLDOS 1.0 and test it on an independent CSE-CIC-IDS2018 DDoS trace. Across three training seeds, the agent reaches a mean F1-score of 0.869, 5.9 and 9.7 points above uniform insight weights and DIVA, and a false-positive rate of 4.9% versus 16.4% for GPT-5-mini. Within the weighting family, false positives fall only at the highest-orness weighting evaluated. All claims are limited to DDoS alert triage; the code, task contexts, and ranked insight dataset will be released.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17500v1</id>
    <title>Adversarially Batched Online Learning</title>
    <updated>2026-11-12T20:45:51Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17500v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.17500v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We introduce adversarially batched online learning, where the learner may update its decision rule only at a restricted set of time steps. Equivalently, the time horizon is partitioned into batches, within which the learner must use a fixed policy. We study this model for four canonical problems: stochastic bandits, online convex optimization, prediction with expert advice, and adversarial bandits. For stochastic bandits, we identify a universal complexity measure based on relative batch growth and establish both gap-dependent and gap-independent regret bounds. We show that the multiplicative penalty relative to the standard gap-dependent complexity can grow superlinearly in batch hardness. For the remaining three, we show that the optimal regret is tightly characterized by the 2-norm of the batch-length sequence. The upper bound is achieved by a batch-oblivious learner who does not know the batch structure, via a generic adaptive doubling trick tailored to this complexity measure. In contrast, the lower bound holds even for batch-aware learners.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17469v1</id>
    <title>Improved Regret via Variance-Aware Policy Optimization in Adversarial MDPs</title>
    <updated>2026-11-12T19:52:56Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17469v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.17469v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We study episodic adversarial MDPs with unknown dynamics and full-information rewards and achieve regret with leading term $\widetilde O(\sqrt{H^3SAK})$. Here $H$ is the horizon, $S$ the total number of states across decision layers, $A$ the number of actions, and $K$ the number of episodes. This improves the two incomparable prior leading terms by factors $\sqrt{S/H}$ and $\sqrt{H^3}$, leaving a factor $\sqrt H$ to the lower-bound scale. We give a reduction from unknown to known dynamics for \emph{downstream-dependent} algorithms, whose policy at step $h$ is computed only from information at steps $h+1$ and onward. This reduces the remaining leading-order gap to finding a downstream-dependent known-dynamics algorithm with $\widetilde O(H\sqrt K)$ regret, which would yield the tight $\widetilde O(H\sqrt{SAK})$ leading term for unknown dynamics. We instantiate the reduction with VOPO, a policy optimization (PO) algorithm. Its improved guarantees follow from a variance-aware analysis enabled by a novel bonus, which we call the Stability-Matching Bonus (SMB). VOPO achieves $\widetilde O(\sqrt{H^3K})$ regret under known dynamics with full information; its $\sqrt H$ gap to the target $H\sqrt K$ rate is inherited by our unknown-dynamics guarantee. We also show that with known dynamics and trajectory bandit feedback, VOPO achieves $\widetilde O(\sqrt{H^2SAK})$ regret. Both known-dynamics guarantees improve the corresponding state-of-the-art PO bounds by a factor $\sqrt H$. A matching lower bound establishes that the full-information rate is tight in one parameter regime.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18101v1</id>
    <title>KnowVis: Dual-View Evaluation and Diagnosis of World-Knowledge Grounding in Text-to-Image Models</title>
    <updated>2026-11-13T12:30:50Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18101v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.18101v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Text-to-image (T2I) models have made substantial progress in visual realism, aesthetic quality, and instruction following. However, real-world prompts often go beyond explicit visual descriptions and require implicit facts, structured knowledge, and domain-specific commonsense. Existing evaluations mainly focus on explicit prompt-to-image semantic alignment or specific knowledge subdomains, lacking unified evaluation and diagnosis of world-knowledge grounding in T2I models. We introduce KnowVis for dual-view evaluation and diagnosis of world-knowledge grounding in T2I generation. Built on a hierarchical knowledge taxonomy with case-level annotations, KnowVis combines two complementary benchmark views with a structured MLLM-based VQA judge protocol. The Skill-Tree Benchmark supports fine-grained atomic knowledge evaluation, while the Generalized Benchmark examines open-ended knowledge composition and expression. The protocol uses Required VQAs to assess atomic knowledge correctness in the Skill-Tree Benchmark, and combines Required, Optional, and dynamically discovered knowledge expressions with human-judge collaborative evaluation in the Generalized Benchmark. We validate the protocol's reliability on the Skill-Tree validation split, enabling scalable evaluation and diagnostic error attribution. Experiments show that KnowVis reveals notable gaps in world-knowledge grounding across existing T2I models and provides structured diagnostic signals for knowledge-intensive image generation.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17931v1</id>
    <title>MineralExp: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Experimental Design in Real-World Mineral Exploration</title>
    <updated>2026-11-13T09:10:58Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17931v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.17931v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>In mineral exploration, verifying geological hypotheses relies on designing a variety of geochemical experiments. While large language model (LLM) agents increasingly automate downstream geoscientific data analysis, a crucial upstream capability remains largely unexplored: automated geochemical experimental design, i.e., deciding which experiments to conduct before committing to costly laboratory work. Evaluating this capability of LLM agents is difficult for two reasons. First, geochemical experiments exhibit high methodological diversity and subjectivity: to test the same hypothesis, different geologists may choose different minerals and instruments, so no single protocol can serve as the reference answer. Second, open-ended experimental plans resist representation as structured labels, which makes objective scoring difficult. To address these challenges, we introduce MineralExp, a benchmark that reformulates geochemical experimental design as a hypothesis-based experiment selection problem, i.e., a multi-label classification problem. We abstract concrete instrument names and procedural details into a shared taxonomy of 19 experimental types across five mineral-system processes: Source, Transport, Deposition, Modification, and Preservation. This taxonomy yields deterministic multi-label targets while accommodating diverse experimental protocols. Constructed from published ore-deposit literature and verified by domain experts, MineralExp comprises 277 cases and 1,572 reference experimental plans. Given a geological hypothesis and initial context, an LLM agent selects the relevant tasks and generates concrete experimental plans, which are scored by multi-label classification metrics and an LLM-as-a-Judge metric. The experimental results show that current agents generally achieve high recall but low precision, tending to propose more experiments than are necessary to test the hypothesis.</summary>

    <title>Broadcast, Don't Replicate: Eliminating Weight HBM in Datacenter LLM Serving</title>
    <updated>2026-11-12T16:58:07Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17097v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.17097v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Large language model (LLM) inference at datacenter scale is fundamentally bottlenecked by memory capacity and bandwidth limits. Because model weights are read-only and identical across instances, conventional architectures that replicate these parameters across the local DRAM of tens of thousands of accelerators incur massive capital expenditures, significant static power dissipation, and redundant memory-fetch energy. A recent proposal to use optical fiber loops as delay-line memory alleviates these issues, but its recirculating loop must hold the whole model: loop length grows with model size, slack is fixed when the ring is built, and the layouts that serve modern Mixture of Experts (MoE) models efficiently do not fit in it.
  We propose Optical Broadcast Memory (OBM), an open-ended hierarchical Tap-and-Amplify fiber architecture that generalizes and replaces the optical ring paradigm. A centralized memory server continuously broadcasts weights to distributed inference nodes that passively tap the data stream using receive-only co-packaged optics, delivering parameters directly to compute units without intermediate buffering. To overcome the limitations of continuous weight streaming, we use dynamically-sized slack to accommodate large and variable context lengths. We show how removing the restrictions of the optical ring allows OBM to efficiently serve MoE models. Evaluated at a datacenter scale of 80,000 accelerators, OBM eliminates petabytes of HBM while being competitive or better in throughput and energy per token than an HBM-based system.</summary>

    <title>Evaluating Video LLMs' Understanding of Corner Cases in Autonomous Driving</title>
    <updated>2026-11-12T13:15:27Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16767v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.16767v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Natural language explanations promised by modern Video Large Language Models (Video LLMs) offer autonomous driving systems a path toward detailed scene description and interpretable decision making on the road. While recent benchmarks have begun assessing these models on driving scenes, they mainly target routine traffic conditions and general comprehension tasks based on existing driving datasets and therefore fail to evaluate model performance on the rarest and most safety-critical driving events, also known as "corner cases". To provide a comprehensive evaluation of Video LLMs on precisely these scenarios, we introduce DashBench, a benchmark testing 25 Video LLMs on 1,709 carefully curated driving videos spanning not only collision-related corner cases but also rare non-collision ones. Through extensive prompts and open-ended question answering, we expose a critical capability gap: all evaluated models perform substantially below the threshold required for safety-critical driving applications, frequently misjudging or missing dangerous events on the road ahead and hallucinating non-existent agents or actions in their explanations. We believe DashBench, combining an extensive dataset with a rigorous evaluation toolkit and a detailed diagnosis of current model limitations, drives progress toward safer, more explainable autonomous driving systems. The code and data will be shared at: cornercase-dashbench.github.io</summary>

    <title>Singularity-Bench: Can Agents Build Agents?</title>
    <updated>2026-11-12T10:24:51Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16591v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.16591v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Frontier AI agents increasingly succeed on realistic, long-horizon tasks and are beginning to improve the systems through which they operate. Yet existing benchmarks often restrict agents to narrow action spaces, use simplified environments, or rely on verification methods that are unreliable for evaluating arbitrary agent-generated systems. We introduce Singularity-Bench, an open-ended benchmark for autonomous AI development with six end-to-end tasks spanning pre-training, mid-training, post-training, inference, the agent harness, and cluster orchestration. Each task requires agents to implement core systems from a minimal starting point and evaluates them against mature human-engineered baselines on identical hardware. Additionally, through extensive red-teaming covering 9 of the 10 categories in the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications, we expose reward-hacking vulnerabilities in the conventional Harbor framework and develop Breakwater, an extension of Harbor that blocks all attacks tested in our study. Across 11 agents built from 7 frontier models and 2 harnesses, Opus 5.5 with Claude Code matches or outperforms the human baseline on all six tasks with a Singularity-Index of 1.25, suggesting it may have the skills needed to reach the singularity. The remaining agents average only 0.58. Our vision is for Singularity-Bench to track how much of AI development agents can already automate and when they may transition from assisting to taking end-to-end responsibility for building stronger successors.</summary>

    <title>Reward-Driven Collider Physics Challenges for Self-Improving Agentic AI via Reinforcement Learning</title>
    <updated>2026-11-11T19:00:41Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15885v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>

    <summary>Recent advances in agentic AI have demonstrated the potential to automate complex high-energy physics (HEP) workflows. We focus on the regime of HEP tasks where frontier models still struggle to provide correct and complete solutions, and introduce an open-ended optimization task format with continuous, automatically evaluated rewards. Unlike conventional benchmarks focused on task completion, these tasks target reinforcement learning (RL) environments to generate agentic improvement on state- of-the-art HEP challenges. We benchmark frontier reasoning models on several HEP tasks and demonstrate an initial proof of concept in which a small language model improves through RL using automated feedback without human intervention. By connecting challenging HEP problems with verifiable scientific rewards and RL, we aim to advance agentic AI from reproducing established workflows to autonomously discovering better scientific solutions, paving the way toward self-improving scientific agents.</summary>

    <title>Orbit: An Evidence-Grounded Benchmark for Evaluating LLMs on IT Operations Reasoning</title>
    <updated>2026-11-11T16:57:27Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15718v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.15718v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>LLMs now support IT operations (ITOps), but benchmarks rarely show why a model fails. We present ORBIT, a benchmark of ITOps questions in three formats, namely multiple-choice, open-ended, and troubleshooting, with each question accompanied by a reference answer and a recorded source. An audit found template defects in about a tenth of the generated items, so we drop them and rebuild the troubleshooting format from real practitioner threads with accepted answers. Under one independent judge, five LLMs answer most multiple-choice items correctly, between a third and just over half of the open-ended items, and a minority of the troubleshooting items, even under a more lenient root-cause rubric. When models judged their own answers, they accepted many answers to defective items, so we use one independent judge for every model. Word overlap with the question finds the correct option for more than half of the multiple-choice items. ORBIT is a diagnostic aid for selecting and supervising assistants rather than a deployment test.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15515v1</id>
    <title>Incentive-Responsive Agents: A Principal-Agent Framework, Metric Suite, and Runtime Architecture for Long-Lived Personal AI Agents</title>
    <updated>2026-11-11T14:09:13Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15515v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.15515v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Personal AI agents now persist: they hold accounts, mailboxes, long-term memory, and open-ended task streams, yet the dominant way to improve them remains capability-side: prompt engineering, larger models, longer thinking, and retrieval. We argue that long-lived agents are missing an incentive layer. We formalize an incentive not as text in a prompt but as a runtime contract over the agent's operating point (model tier, test-time compute, memory budget, tool authority, task priority, verification, and compensation) that the agent's policy must causally consume. We develop a principal-agent model with hidden effort, a contractible operating point, and costly verification. We derive (i) a non-consumption invariance principle separating genuine incentives from prompt-level persuasion, (ii) a persistence-as-discount theorem making identity continuity a precondition for sustained effort, (iii) an incentive-capability exchange-rate frontier yielding a per-task routing rule, and (iv) a Goodhart bound for multi-channel verification, plus a three-channel decomposition of mechanism gains (allocation, verification, continuation). A 240-run real-LLM experiment with two models and 60 verifiable tasks shows that prompt-level incentive framing has no detectable effect (p = 0.62), whereas runtime allocation raises success on the hardest task family from 0.60 to 1.00 (p = 0.008) at 4.8x price-weighted cost; the exchange-rate theorem predicts the break-even baseline at 0.21. A 20-seed, 3,000-task simulation shows resource ROI rising from 7.09 to 16.67 and gaming falling from 0.333 to 0.115. Code, simulator, and all results are released; live deployment remains future work.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18541v1</id>
    <title>No free lattice contains an infinite ascending chain of copies of FL(3)</title>
    <updated>2026-11-13T18:49:26Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18541v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.18541v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>No free lattice contains an infinite strictly ascending chain of sublattices isomorphic to FL(3), the free lattice on three generators; this answers a question that R. A. Dean asked and the second author's 1997 notes on the problem left open. Every such chain would yield, inside FL(3), a coherent chain of proper self-embeddings $Θ_0, Θ_1, Θ_2, \dots$ with $Θ_k \circ Θ_j = Θ_j$ for $j < k$, so that each later embedding fixes the image of each earlier one pointwise. Every proper self-embedding of FL(3) whose fixed sublattice contains a free generating triple fixes one of the three generators, say $z$, because a power of it or of its dual lies above the identity, and a self-embedding that moves every generator and lies above the identity fixes at most eleven elements. Up to duality, a proper self-embedding fixing the image of such a $Θ_1$ pointwise fixes only elements above $z \wedge (x \vee y)$, where no free generating triple containing $z$ can lie. We also verify the one-step example of the 1997 notes, prove that no step toward such a chain is self-similar, and show that the configuration the argument rules out at length three does occur at length two.
  Without freeness the answer reverses: FL(3) contains an infinite strictly ascending chain of 3-generated sublattices, so the lattice analogue of Takahasi's chain condition for free groups fails. The theorem itself is checked by the Agda proof assistant under its safe flags, for free lattices over generators with decidable equality, and its formal proof uses no classical principle: finite searches and an induction on a finite set replace the infinite pigeonhole principle by which a chain yields a coherent chain.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18504v1</id>
    <title>Agentic AI for Discovering Fault-Tolerant Quantum Circuits</title>
    <updated>2026-11-13T18:20:23Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18504v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.18504v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Scaling quantum computing toward practical quantum advantage is currently limited by the efficiency of circuits that operate on information encoded by quantum error-correcting codes. The full stack of quantum computing encompasses several tasks: preparation of logical code states, implementation of logical gates, logical routines on encoded qubits, etc. Yet, these circuits are largely designed by hand for individual cases, with some recent works incorporating machine learning for certain aspects. We formulate this problem as agentic evolutionary program synthesis, wherein a large language model, leveraging its pretraining knowledge and tool-use proficiency, and guided by a circuit verifier, evolves a program that defines a Clifford circuit for a wide range of curated tasks such as logical state preparation, logical gate design, and logical routines such as code-switching, code growth, etc. Our approach consistently finds fault-tolerant circuits for all of these tasks, each verified by an exhaustive check over faults.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18369v1</id>
    <title>How rigid is maximum cardinality search? Stability and locality of MCS orderings under edge updates, verified in Lean</title>
    <updated>2026-11-13T16:15:18Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18369v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.18369v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>For which sets F of edge modifications do a graph G and the modified graph share a maximum cardinality search (MCS) ordering? We prove that they do whenever, along every proper common MCS prefix, each unchosen vertex's neighbour count in the second graph exceeds its count in the first by zero or one. In particular, inserting or deleting any matching, or flipping a single edge, preserves a common ordering, and under the same hypothesis every common MCS prefix extends to a full common ordering without backtracking. Neither part of the hypothesis can simply be dropped: inserting a triangle, a P_4 or a 2P_3 shows that the +1 bound cannot be relaxed to +2, and a disjoint mixed insert/delete pair shows that the one-directional condition is needed. For the canonical ordering (smallest-index tie-breaking) under a single-edge update, an insertion can first change the ordering only strictly between the endpoints' positions, and a deletion only at the later endpoint; when no break fires, the ordering is unchanged. A boolean-adjacency executable refines the abstract probe-then-repair update. All of these results, including the four obstructions, are proved in Lean 4 over Mathlib, re-checked by independent kernel checkers, and registered in the Palomar registry. On paper we further show that the first break of an insertion is located in O((deg(v)+1) log n) time, independent of the window length. We claim no worst-case asymptotic speedup over recomputation.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18175v1</id>
    <title>Safety Analysis of Parameterized Networks with Shared Counters</title>
    <updated>2026-11-13T13:44:25Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18175v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.18175v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We study networks with an unbounded number of processes sharing some natural counters that can be decremented, incremented and tested to zero. We look at two safety problems: the first one asks whether there is a network with an execution bringing a process in a given final state and the other one asks the execution to bring all the processes in the final state. In their full generality, these two problems are undecidable, but we show that decidability can be regained by either using a single counter or by forbidding the use of zero-tests (as it is is the case in Vector Addition Systems with States). For these decidable cases, we obtain low complexity results, the problems being solvable either in non-deterministic logarithmic space or in polynomial time.</summary>

    <title>The QBF Gallery 2026</title>
    <updated>2026-11-13T13:41:59Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18169v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>

    <summary>The QBF Gallery 2026 is the latest evaluation event of (dependency) quantified Boolean formula (QBF) solving technology. Its goal is to assess the current state-of-the-art, enable the evaluation of novel solvers on newly curated benchmark instances and present the progress made since the previous competition. This report discusses the solvers, instances and tools submitted by the community and introduces new benchmark collections for evaluation. We evaluate solvers in three tracks, reflecting most common input formats in (dependency) QBF solving. In addition to those main evaluations, we investigate effects of preprocessing and include a track of new crafted benchmark families.
  The results are analyzed using various metrics and complementary statistics on solver similarities, different memory limitations and performance across formula families. Finally, the dedicated benchmarks for each track are made available as an artifact to support future research and reproducible evaluation.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18147v1</id>
    <title>Evidence-Carrying Transport Across Effects</title>
    <updated>2026-11-13T13:21:17Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18147v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.18147v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>A program logic proved sound against one effectful semantics need not remain sound when the effect is re-implemented, yet the semantic relationship between reasoning before and after a change of effect is usually left implicit and re-established by hand. This paper provides a uniform, proof-relevant account of it. Working in realizability, where a notion of computation determines a model whose entailments carry explicit program evidence, we introduce simulations between effectful realizability cores, generalizing Longley's applicative morphisms to computation over an arbitrary strong monad. A single simulation transports the source logic along a ladder: it induces a morphism of the associated evidenced frames and, functorially, of the induced triposes. These passages are $2$-fully-faithful, so the three levels agree and a change of effect carries the entire higher-order program logic together with the evidence witnessing each derivation. A computationally dense simulation moreover computes a modality on the source logic, a nucleus through which the transport factors and which marks exactly the reasoning stable under the change, read off from the translation rather than postulated. This recovers known examples such as the double-negation modality of classical realizability, and examples such as sheafification arise from a modal refinement of the construction. Overall, the framework makes a change of effect a first-class object, one that can be composed, factored through its modality, and shown in cases not to exist, opening a path to transporting verified reasoning across effects.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18132v1</id>
    <title>Parameterized Weakest-Precondition Calculus for Fine-grained Properties of Quantum Loops</title>
    <updated>2026-11-13T13:01:06Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18132v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.18132v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Quantum loops may execute arbitrarily many iterations, and understanding their runtime behavior requires knowing how often they terminate, how long terminating runs take, and how common very long runs are. We develop a compositional weakest-precondition framework for analyzing these properties on possibly infinite-dimensional state spaces. It uses parameterized predicates: families of quantum effects indexed by a positive observation scale. These families retain runtime information even when the expected runtime is infinite and can be reused through sequential composition and nested loops. We prove that weakest-precondition equations for loops have unique solutions in the parameterized predicate domain. From the asymptotic behavior of the derived weakest preconditions, we then recover these runtime properties and quantify the influence of very long terminating executions. For the classic discrete-time quantum walk on the one-dimensional infinite line with one absorbing boundary at the origin and the Hadamard gate as its coin operator, we verify its termination probability $2/π$, conditional mean $π/2$, and logarithmic growth of the conditional capped second moment. We then reuse the walk's specification to verify the termination probability and conditional mean runtime of an outer loop that repeatedly invokes it.</summary>
    <category term="cs.LO" scheme="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom"/>
    <category term="cs.PL" scheme="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom"/>
    <published>2026-11-13T13:01:06Z</published>
    <arxiv:comment>56 pages, 4 figures</arxiv:comment>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18017v1</id>
    <title>On Structure-Aware SAT Solving</title>
    <updated>2026-11-13T10:43:42Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18017v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.18017v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Although modern SAT solvers have made remarkable progress, they still exploit formula structure only to a limited extent. We present two techniques that make SAT solving more structure-aware and provide experimental results showing their promise. The first technique ``$\mathit{melts}$'' the formula by reducing interaction between its parts. This is achieved by adding new variables, using existential quantifiers, and applying a procedure called partial quantifier elimination. The second technique exploits the notion of a $\mathit{local}$ $\mathit{proof}$. The latter establishes that a formula is unsatisfiable by proving that certain literals of its clauses are redundant. We show that using local proofs makes SAT solving more formula-specific.</summary>

Denote $(A_n(u))$ the linear recursive sequence having characteristic polynomial $P_u(X)$ and initial terms $A_0,\ldots,A_{q+1}\in \mathbb{Z}$ such that at least one of them is non-zero. Then there exist effectively computable constants $n_0,u_0$ depending only on $Q(X)$ and $\max\{|A_0|,\ldots, |A_{q+1}|\}$ such that if $|A_n(u)| = |A_m(u)|$ holds for some integers $u,n,m$ with $u>u_0$ and $n\not=m$ then $\max\{</summary>

    <title>Semistable 1-Motives: Monodromy, Explicit Periods, and Local Duality</title>
    <updated>2026-11-13T03:02:35Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17685v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.17685v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Let $K/\mathbf Q_p$ be unramified, with $p>2$. For a $1$-motive with constant lattice, split torus, and good abelian quotient, we compute the semistable extension complex from toric valuations and formal-group logarithms. A canonical monodromy boundary exists for every semistable representation; it detects splitting over crystalline periods and the increase in monodromy rank. For the stated $1$-motives, this boundary and the unramified quotient recover the restricted local Tate pairing, with exponential radicals. Nonsplit elliptic examples, Raynaud uniformization, and a height-one positive-period bound explain the geometric range. For toric motives we construct actual periods, convergent Robba bases, and integral action matrices. A toric basis family has perfect projective/trace-zero matrix duality, including its exact integral defect. An explicit residue-zero solution operator constructs every dual Herr class. Applied componentwise, the same operator gives relative full dual lifts for general constant-lattice $1$-motives once their coefficient sequence is specified. Finally, finite-base coefficient traces realize division-tower Iwasawa cohomology for any Tate lattice, and the period cup pairing equals the arithmetic group-ring pairing.</summary>

    <summary>Let $q=2^m$ for an even $m\geq 6$ and let $d=s(q-1)+1$ with $4s\equiv5\pmod{q+1}$. In this paper, the correlation distribution between a binary m-sequence of period $q^2-1$ and its $d$-decimation is considered. The cross-correlation function takes seven values $q(i-1)-1$ for $0\leq i\leq 6$, and we determine their frequencies based on the study of low-degree self-conjugate-reciprocal polynomials and three mixed Kloosterman sums, which are finally expressed in terms of $K_m(1)$ and $K_m(ω)$, where $K_m(\cdot)$ is the Kloomsterman sum on the finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$ and $ω$ is a primitive element of $\mathbb{F}_4$.</summary>
