    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23890v1</id>
    <title>EVA-RSI: Recursive Self-Improvement of Video Evaluators for Judging Temporal Quality</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T05:41:49Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23890v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.23890v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Video evaluators play an important role in video generation, yet they miss motion defects, limiting the quality of generated videos. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) has made strong progress in mathematics and coding, where explicit verifiers provide reliable feedback on a single goal. Video evaluation poses two difficulties for RSI: it has no verifier, and it must judge many dimensions at once, such as physics, smoothness and dynamics, where a gain on one can cost another. We introduce EVA-RSI, a multi-agent framework for exploring RSI under these two constraints. We build a fixed proxy exam with construction-defined targets by applying controlled changes to videos, such as temporal reversal and frame dropping. These edits supply supervision without human annotation. A small set of human-labeled real videos anchors the exam to human judgment. Each dimension has an LLM agent that proposes improvements. A leader agent coordinates the proposals, and a Nash bargaining rule selects updates that balance progress across dimensions. Humans design the exam, review candidate changes and revise the curriculum between stages. Starting from Qwen3-VL-8B, EVA-RSI improves motion evaluation, with the largest gain on smoothness, and the gains carry over to defect types never seen during the run. On the dynamics subsets of public benchmarks, our evaluator achieves the highest observed scores among 21 tested models. As an RL reward, it increases generated motion and earns human preference. A data-selection pipeline incorporating it also increases motion.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23774v1</id>
    <title>Improve How You Improve: Recursive Policy Self-Improvement for Zero-Shot Open-Vocabulary Multi-Object Navigation</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T03:31:09Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23774v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.23774v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>To advance the development of embodied general navigation, zero-shot open-vocabulary multi-object navigation has attracted increasing attention, aiming to enable robots to efficiently search multiple objects in unseen environments without training. For this task, the key lies in improving navigation policies from earlier searches to locate subsequent goals more efficiently. Recent methods automate this process through trajectory reflection and rule revision, enabling policy self-improvement. However, the mechanisms for diagnosing problems and generating revisions are typically designed by humans and remain fixed across iterations. Consequently, the system's capacity for continued self-improvement remains constrained, even as its navigation policy evolves. To this end, we propose RPSI-Nav, a Recursive Policy Self-Improvement framework for zero-shot multi-object navigation that revises both the navigation program and its revision mechanism. RPSI-Nav diagnoses search behavior, requests diagnostic views when existing observations cannot distinguish competing causes, and generates targeted navigation revisions. Feedback from subsequent goal searches is linked to the rules that produced these revisions, guiding changes to diagnosis, observation acquisition, and revision planning. The updated improver governs subsequent navigation improvements, forming a recursive loop in which RPSI-Nav revises its own improvement process. Across goals, the robot conditionally inherits accepted program updates and spatial memory, enabling search experience to improve both future navigation and adaptation. Benchmark experiments and qualitative real-robot evaluations validate RPSI-Nav's effectiveness.</summary>

    <title>KnowMe Paper Radar: Lightweight Discovery of Promising Papers in the Age of Autoresearch</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T01:47:31Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23702v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.23702v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>The growing volume of topically similar papers makes it difficult to identify new work that can offer useful research insights or methodological guidance. We present KnowMe Paper Radar, a lightweight discovery tool that combines multiple sources of evidence into personalized reading priorities. Users specify topics, priorities, exclusions and dates; the system brings together topical relevance, recency, author research histories, collaboration paths and direction-specific institutional context. By exposing each score component and its supporting sources, KnowMe helps readers select promising papers for their current questions and discover relevant work beyond familiar authors. Automatic acquisition, version merging and graph-cache reuse keep this workflow convenient without large language model (LLM) inference during ordinary use. Experiments on 174,640 acquired records show more than threefold faster repeated context preparation, while cached abstracts improve normalized discounted cumulative gain at rank 10 (NDCG@10) from 0.412 to 0.598 on expert-judged retrieval tasks. Complementary analyses examine how the same accumulated records support semantic retrieval, research-history modeling and literature-grounded planning. A browser interface and a structured command-line interface (CLI) make these capabilities available to both researchers and research agents, positioning KnowMe as a practical upstream tool for literature-informed recursive self-improvement (RSI) workflows.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24876v1</id>
    <title>Learning to Interact in Multi-Agent Self-Play for Controllable Autonomous Driving Scenario Generation</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T18:23:29Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24876v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24876v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Large-scale, multi-agent self-play trains robust driving policies effectively in simulation, but controlling these models to generate specific, safety-critical edge cases remains a key challenge. Existing goal-conditioned self-play frameworks rely primarily on static map-location goals and fail to reliably produce complex agent interactions such as aggressive tailgating or adversarial cut-offs. These agent interactions are necessary for rigorous autonomous vehicle (AV) testing. To address this, we present an extended multi-agent self-play framework that introduces agent-relative dynamic goals. By conditioning policies on this extended goal representation, our framework enables targeted, controllable scenario synthesis. We demonstrate that our approach successfully generates interactive driving behaviors that static-goal baselines cannot simulate, providing a flexible tool for long-tail scenario generation in AV testing.</summary>

    <title>Reliable Tree Recruitment from Scarce Annotations for Forest Inventory Expansion</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T13:31:37Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24401v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24401v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Species-level inventories of individual tree crowns (ITCs) from UAV imagery are limited by annotation cost: in tropical forests, many species are represented by only a handful of field-validated crowns. We propose a reliable tree recruitment framework that expands a small annotated inventory by iteratively self-training a multi-task DeepLabV3 network, combining semantic segmentation with a crown-distance regression head, on RGB UAV orthomosaics. At each iteration, candidate crowns enter the training inventory only if they pass a confidence filter on class probability and distance map and a morphology filter on crown area and solidity, with at most five new crowns per species, keeping recruited samples consistent with the reference inventory. We evaluate the framework at two Brazilian sites: an Amazonian rainforest in Acre (17 species, 355 annotated crowns, 4 cm GSD) and a forest site in the Cerrado of Maranhão (4 species, 51 annotated crowns, 1.8 cm GSD). Over 20 iterations, the number of retained crowns grew from about 500 to 960 in Acre and from about 700 to over 3100 in Maranhão, while crown-level F1 exceeded single- and multi-task DeepLabV3 baselines (53.5% vs. 50.0% and 45.2%; 92.2% vs. 79.7% and 83.6%). The framework offers a low-cost route to expanding species inventories with consumer-grade UAVs and limited fieldwork.</summary>

    <title>Semi-Supervised GAN-Based Segmentation of CTPA Scans for Pulmonary Emboli Boundary Extraction</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T08:09:43Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24018v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24018v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Pulmonary embolism (PE) is a pulmonary vascular disease associated with high morbidity and mortality, where delayed diagnosis can be fatal. While computed tomography pulmonary angiography (CTPA) is the clinical gold standard for PE detection, interpreting these scans manually is time-consuming and error-prone. In this work, we propose a semi-supervised segmentation method, employing generative adversarial networks (GANs) to leverage large pools of unlabeled CTPA scans. The proposed method addresses more effectively the challenges of CTPA image segmentation than previous methods by employing the dice loss and the cross-entropy loss to tackle the highly imbalanced nature of CTPA scans, the feature matching loss to encourage the generator to produce anatomically plausible segmentation maps that are indistinguishable from ground truth, as well as the self-training loss to reinforce learning from highly-confident pseudo-labeled samples. The experimental evaluation on a publicly available dataset shows that the proposed method maintains accurate segmentation, despite a limited number of labeled CTPA scans. with a Dice coefficient of 88.75% and a 95th percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95) of 1.74, outperforming fully supervised baselines.</summary>

    <title>SWE-growth: Teacher-Guided Adaptive Self-Play for Software Engineering Agents</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T05:29:18Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23876v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.23876v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Self-play offers a scalable way to train software engineering agents by generating repository-level repair tasks. However, with binary repair rewards and finite rollout budgets, all-fail groups provide no reward-based group-relative advantage. Such tasks may still offer learning opportunities when a Teacher can provide verified repairs absent from the Student's own attempts. We introduce SWE-Growth, a teacher-guided adaptive self-play framework that uses verified Teacher outcomes to identify learning opportunities for the current Student. Tasks with all students failure but reliable Teacher success provide demonstrations for supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and post-SFT Student rollouts identify mixed-outcome tasks with a positive Teacher--Student gap for reinforcement learning. Task eligibility also guides Injector updates, connecting Student training with subsequent task generation. Starting from 101 seed issues, \textsc{SWE-Growth} improves Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct from 27.7% to 31.7% on SWE-bench Pro and from 11.0% to 17.2% on held-out TerminalBench 2.1 by Round~2. It exceeds Student-only self-play by 2.6 and 4.1 percentage points, respectively, and Teacher-augmented self-play by 1.8 and 2.5 points under approximately matched budgets. These results support adapting both supervision and task selection to the Student's evolving repair capability.</summary>

    <title>A Comparison of Heuristic, Human-Sensitive, and Self-Play DRL Policies in Human-Agent Teaming</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T02:59:54Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23747v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.23747v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Dynamical Perceptual-Motor Primitives (DPMPs) offer a tractable framework for generating human-like movement dynamics in artificial agents (AAs) and have been used to support coordination in human-AI teaming tasks. Traditionally, DPMP controllers rely on heuristic (rule-based) decision policies derived from human behavior to guide goal selection and action sequencing. Although effective in structured tasks, such heuristics can be difficult to generalize to more complex settings, motivating interest in deep reinforcement learning (DRL) approaches for learning decision policies for human-AI interaction. A key challenge, however, is ensuring that DRL policies remain aligned with human strategies, particularly when agents are trained through self-play. To examine this issue, we compared three target-selection policies governing DPMP-based AAs in a first-person herding task: (1) a human-derived heuristic policy, (2) a self-play DRL policy (SP-DRL), and (3) a human-sensitive DRL policy (HS-DRL) trained alongside a heuristic agent. Results showed that heuristic agents most closely matched typical human-human coordination patterns, followed by HS-DRL agents, whereas SP-DRL agents deviated most. These findings highlight the importance of human-informed training when developing DRL-based teammates and suggest that simple heuristic policies may remain an effective approach for designing human-aligned AAs capable of human-AI collaboration.</summary>

    <title>FairPGT: Partitioned Graph Transformers for Dual-Level Fair Graph Clustering</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T23:41:54Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23631v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.23631v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Clustering on attributed graphs can produce demographically biased clusters, particularly when communities align with protected groups. Graph transformers can amplify this bias through same-group attention, while global attention limits scalability. We propose FairPGT, a partitioned graph transformer for fair graph clustering. FairPGT restricts attention to METIS partitions and connects them through routing tokens, which divides the quadratic cost of attention by the number of partitions. A graph-aware self-training target guides clustering, with a provably bounded deviation from the standard DEC target. Fairness is imposed at two levels: a mutual-information term promotes demographic parity in cluster assignments, while a normalized cross-group attention ratio (nCGAR) guides attention toward group neutrality through self-distillation. We prove that the nCGAR correction moves attention toward neutrality and establish a condition preventing overshooting. Across seven benchmarks, FairPGT achieves the best clustering performance and statistical parity on the three largest graphs (Credit, Pokec-n, Pokec-z), with a statistical-parity gap approximately ten times lower than DMoN, and is Pareto-dominated on only one dataset. On controlled stochastic block models, FairPGT attains 97% of the derived upper bound on NMI for exactly fair clustering when communities and protected groups coincide. These graphs further show that, under strong alignment, assignment-level fairness alone makes the attention group-heterophilous, whereas attention-level fairness alone improves neutrality without ensuring fair clusters. Code for reproducibility is available at https://github.com/SiamakGhodsi/FairPGT.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23581v1</id>
    <title>ExiST: Existence-Aware Self-Training for Semi-Supervised Multi-Organ Segmentation</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T22:27:46Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23581v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.23581v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Semi-supervised multi-organ segmentation should learn more than a dozen organs from a handful of labeled scans, and the smallest organs occupy less than one percent of the foreground. We identify a failure mode of self-training that is specific to this regime. When a teacher misses a small organ in a scan, every voxel of that organ receives the confident pseudo-label background, and the student is trained toward the organ absence. Repeated over many scans, this loop extinguishes tail organs. In a pilot study, removing the gallbladder from the pseudo-labels reduced its Dice on AMOS from 36.5 to 1.0. We argue that a missing organ should be treated as unresolved rather than absent and propose Existence-aware Self-Training (ExiST). It builds pseudo-labels by leave-one-out consensus of independently trained networks, screens them with a quality gate on validation scans, and infers, per scan and per organ, whether the organ was found. For every unresolved organ, the background voxels of that scan receive the set-valued target, trained with a marginal cross-entropy that accepts either answer and a Dice term that skips uncertain voxels. We show that this loss never pushes a candidate organ toward absence and never favors one member of the set, which leaves the decision to labeled evidence. ExiST outperforms the current state-of-the-art methods and reaches 77.1 mean Dice on Synapse with 20% labeled scans and 75.9 on AMOS with 5% labeled scans.</summary>

    <title>EviSlide-MIL: Multi-Query Pooling and Shared Prediction for Class-Incremental Whole-Slide Image Classification</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T18:50:42Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23212v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.23212v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Histopathological analysis of whole-slide images (WSIs) plays a critical role in cancer diagnosis, and multiple instance learning (MIL) is widely adopted for WSI analysis under weak supervision. As new tumor subtypes are introduced, extending existing MIL models requires learning new classes while retaining knowledge of previously learned ones. This presents a class-incremental learning challenge, where models must acquire new classes with limited access to historical training data and recognize all learned classes without task identifiers at inference. A major obstacle is forgetting, as updates to feature aggregation and prediction modules can degrade performance on previously learned classes. To address this challenge, we propose \textbf{EviSlide-MIL}, a class-incremental WSI framework that integrates multiple learnable queries per class with a shared prediction module. The queries aggregate frozen patch features into class-specific representations, while the shared prediction module limits parameter growth across incremental stages. By freezing queries associated with previously learned classes, EviSlide-MIL preserves their attention patterns for identical inputs, while experience replay and knowledge distillation further mitigate forgetting as shared parameters are updated. Experiments on eight tumor subtypes from The Cancer Genome Atlas demonstrate that EviSlide-MIL achieves improved performance and reduced forgetting compared with competing methods across most learning settings, demonstrating its potential for scalable and knowledge-preserving WSI classification. Code and pretrained models will be released.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22773v1</id>
    <title>Guarded Swarms in the Loop: A ROS 2/PX4 Digital Twin for Hybrid Digital-Analog Coordination of UAV/UGV Swarms</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T13:40:51Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22773v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.22773v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Swarms of unmanned aerial and ground vehicles (UAV/UGV) operating in contested environments cannot rely on software alone for physical safety, since the software stack and its networks are part of the attack surface. The Guarded Swarms architecture addresses this by pairing a digital coordination layer, built on Topic-Based Communication Space Petri Nets (TB-CSPN), with an independent analog safety layer that can veto unsafe actuation commands. So far, the architecture has been specified and argued for, but not executed. We present the first executable instantiation of Guarded Swarms as a digital twin built on ROS 2, the PX4 autopilot in software-in-the-loop mode, and Gazebo, with two UAVs and one UGV in a coastal counter-UAS scenario. The TB-CSPN transition chain, from multi-modal sensing through human authorization to vehicle tasking, is mapped one-to-one onto ROS 2 nodes, and the analog layer is modeled as a per-vehicle Virtual Safety Board that gates every command. Eight groups of experiments show that the three negative guarantees of the architecture (no mission from conflicting, temporally incoherent, or unauthorized evidence) hold at three distinct stages of the chain in all 60 counterfactual runs; that threat confirmation is bounded by the narrowest sensing modality; that the safety layer exercises its full modeled envelope independently of the coordination layer; and, under fault injection, that it prevents every collision caused by a forged mission or a compromised worker once its veto is enforced by an independent gate, whereas a veto left to the compromised worker prevents none. The twin also exposes implementation-level hazards that the architectural specification does not address, and it draws an explicit line between the properties that simulation can validate and those that only hardware can.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20773v1</id>
    <title>When Does Interaction Help? Toward a Reynolds Number for Collective Intelligence</title>
    <updated>2026-11-16T09:22:24Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20773v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.20773v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Multi-agent systems combine distributed information through interaction, which can improve performance but also spread errors or suppress useful differences. Predicting when interaction helps is central to understanding and designing collective intelligence. We investigate whether a few dimensionless parameters can predict gains over explicitly defined non-communicating baselines across group sizes, network structures, and tasks, toward a Reynolds-number-like description of collective intelligence. Using distributed classification tasks, stochastic tracking networks, and neural cellular automata, we combine analytical and empirical evidence to examine information sufficiency, dynamical applicability, and finite-sample prediction. We construct inference systems with bounded random variables and matching specified joint moments up to total degree three, yet opposite interaction gains under a fixed readout. These moments alone cannot generally determine the gain sign. Tracking networks likewise exhibit gain reversals despite matched candidate parameters when task power occupies different spectral modes. Under concentrated task spectra and aligned observation noise, however, we derive a low-dimensional similarity relation with an explicit zero-delay error bound and test it across network sizes and topologies under frozen protocols. The relation does not directly apply to the neural cellular systems, where a separate moment-based predictor underperforms direct gain measurement at matched calibration sample budgets. These results establish conditions and limits for low-dimensional gain prediction, providing a restricted similarity law while leaving a general Reynolds-number-like description of collective intelligence open.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08971v1</id>
    <title>Phantom Consensus: Measuring Social Reasoning in Multi-Agent LLM Decision-Making</title>
    <updated>2026-11-06T04:33:59Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08971v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08971v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Multi-agent LLM systems increasingly aggregate judgments across model instances, but reasoning about other agents can itself introduce failure. We study a setting in which LLMs shift their public decisions after observing ambiguous social signals while reporting inaccurate estimates of what other agents privately judged, even when the group's recorded private judgments do not support the apparent consensus. We call this failure phantom consensus and study it as a pluralistic-ignorance-style pattern in controlled LLM collectives. To measure this phenomenon, we introduce PHANTOM-Bench, a benchmark that separates isolated private judgments, public decisions after ambiguous social signals, elicited estimates of the group's private judgment, transparency-based recovery, and controls for neutral public text and explicit vote-following. Across nine closed- and open-weight models, ambiguous public signals consistently degrade decision quality and can turn correct private group judgments into incorrect public collective outcomes. Public accuracy drops by as much as 47.8 percentage points, and collective rationality failures reach 47.3% in the most susceptible setting. We observe substantial errors in reported group-private beliefs alongside public-stage failures, while control conditions reveal model-dependent differences in susceptibility to ambiguous and explicit peer signals. Revealing the agents' recorded private decisions repairs many failures without revealing the gold label, although recovery varies across models. Our results show that evaluating multi-agent LLM systems requires measuring not only final agreement, but whether that agreement reflects independently measured private judgments or an apparent consensus.</summary>

    <title>s$^3$: Simple Scaling of Swarms via Cooperative Multi-agent RL</title>
    <updated>2026-11-05T19:07:15Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08615v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08615v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Groups can achieve more than individuals in the same amount of time, but only if their members coordinate: they must decide who works on what and what to share. However, this organization in multi-agent systems today usually comes from arbitrary, static harnesses designed a priori without adapting to agent behaviors or task specifications. We ask whether agents can instead learn to organize themselves. We introduce s$^3$, the first multi-agent reinforcement learning method in which agents decide for themselves how long to work alone and when to share findings or read teammates' messages, with no predefined organization or roles. Our s$^3$ agents learn to take different approaches, read each other's work, exhibit emergent roles that complement each other in the swarm, and generalize to bigger teams. We study both coordination, where agents must combine private information, and parallel exploration, where sharing discoveries can make search more efficient. With matched training and inference budgets, s$^3$, swarms evaluated with twice as many agents as in training solve over 25$\times$ more coordination problems than the strongest baseline, and in exploration, communicating agents reduce repeated work by nearly 50% and outperform best-of-N by up to 9.4 percentage points. Rather than being designed in advance, s$^3$ enables organization to emerge from a shared goal. This opens the door to capable systems built from many models that learn to work together.</summary>

    <title>SEER: A Scalable Event-Driven Runtime for Parallel Execution of Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Environments</title>
    <updated>2026-11-05T13:24:57Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07996v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.07996v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is increasingly used in systems where many entities interact in a shared environment. In these workloads, policy inference can be batched on GPUs, but the CPU-side environment path still updates entity states, resolves local interactions, and builds observations inside each $\mathrm{env.step}$. This path can dominate latency in interaction-intensive workloads after policy batching. Existing vectorized environment interfaces and general event-driven runtimes do not directly address the fine-grained cross-entity work inside one bounded MARL step while preserving the step-level semantics expected by learning systems. We present SEER (Scalable Event-Driven Environment Runtime), a runtime for MARL environment execution under an explicit event-locality contract. SEER models each environment step as a bounded stream of timestamped events. If direct state updates are entity-local and cross-entity effects are represented as ordered future events, SEER can run independent events in parallel while preserving serial-equivalent boundary outputs. To make this contract practical, SEER uses a CAS-based dual-layer event queue: local event queues preserve per-entity causal order, while a parallel executive list exposes ready work to global worker threads. SEER further uses STPA, a preflight-guided thread-pool selection mechanism that combines short runtime traces with static workload and hardware features. We evaluate SEER on two parameterized MARL workloads: compute-intensive UAV swarm control (Aircraft) and communication-intensive wireless management (PCS). On Aircraft, SEER reduces inference latency by 16.2\% over the baseline. On PCS, SEER reduces environment-execution latency by 46.9\%, 19.5\%, and 64.9\% over ROSS-T, NBSE, and ROOT-Sim, respectively.</summary>

    <summary>This paper proposes a bilevel particle swarm optimization (PSO)-neurodynamic method for solving the distributed sparse least-squares problem regularized by the smoothly clipped absolute deviation (SCAD) penalty to global optimality. The SCAD penalty is nonsmooth and nonconvex, so existing distributed neurodynamic methods have not been extended to it directly. Through two-time-scale singular perturbation analysis, a rigorous full-trajectory convergence theory with explicit convergence rates is established for the inner collaborative multi-agent neurodynamic system without requiring the second-order sufficient condition. A theory-guided inner-outer collaborative optimization framework is further developed, in which a red-light green-light sensitivity mechanism is embedded in the outer PSO search to enhance global search while concentrating computational effort on the SCAD shape parameters, thereby improving recovery accuracy and computational efficiency. Simulation results on four sparse-recovery scenarios demonstrate that the proposed method accurately recovers the true sparsity pattern and achieves faster convergence and lower relative error than competing neurodynamic methods.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18693v1</id>
    <title>Swarm Shepherd: Securing Multi-Agent Ecosystems Against Persistent Latent Compromise</title>
    <updated>2026-11-04T21:37:57Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18693v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.18693v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Agentic ecosystems are emerging as a new platform layer in which agents maintain persistent memory, retrieve from shared knowledge bases, execute through tool interfaces, and coordinate through shared states. These capabilities create a security problem that per-turn defenses miss: compromise can accumulate across sessions, agents, and system layers before visible failure. We define this threat as Agentic Sleeper, a system-level adversary that first behaves legitimately, gains routing trust, and later activates across memory, agent logic, and infrastructure. We formulate defense as inference under partial observability and propose Swarm Shepherd, a system-level defense framework centered on an inference filter for early warning, paired with a backward trace-back module for entry attribution. Our analysis yields a two-scale deployment rule that balances longer event histories against broader agent coverage. Across LangGraph, CrewAI, and AutoGen, Agentic Sleeper drift begins 2.7--8.9$\times$ faster than natural baselines, propagates across agents on most topologies, and evades per-turn and stateful defenses above 80\%. Swarm Shepherd warns at least three sessions before visible degradation (2.6 sessions when failure is scored by the benchmark's own task grader), while trace-back reaches 0.69 top-1 accuracy and 0.72 macro-F1 over 24 variants. The two-scale deployment rule is empirically confirmed, and in live end-to-end runs on LangGraph and AutoGen the posterior-guided defense stack drives cross-agent propagation below the self-sustaining regime, which removing only the visibly compromised agent does not achieve.</summary>

    <title>AttriSwarm: Orchestrating Agent Swarms for Cross-Page Visual Attribution</title>
    <updated>2026-11-03T08:31:44Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.04504v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.04504v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) increasingly address knowledge-intensive tasks by integrating evidence scattered across multiple document pages into a final answer. Because such answers are synthesized from many pages, the link between the answer and its supporting visual evidence can become obscured, hindering verification and trust. Cross-page visual attribution is therefore essential: it requires identifying the supporting pages and localizing fine-grained evidence regions within them, thereby making multi-page reasoning transparent and auditable. Existing approaches either process multiple pages jointly or iteratively refine evidence within a single trajectory, risking cross-page context pollution and, for interactive methods, substantial sequential overhead. We introduce \textbf{AttriSwarm}, an agent-swarm framework that assigns these concerns to separate roles: a leader handles global cross-page reasoning, while subagents perform page-wise attribution in isolation and in parallel. To support training and evaluation, we construct \textbf{AttriDoc}, a cross-page QA dataset linking supporting pages to their annotated evidence regions, and use it for role-specific training of AttriSwarm, improving answer accuracy, page-level $F_1$, and region-level IoU over its training-free counterpart by an average of 18.94, 29.34, and 23.04 percentage points, respectively, across three open-source backbones and three datasets.</summary>

    <title>Old Matches, New Frames: Schedule-Gated Stereo Memory from Human Vision to Machine Matching</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T18:09:03Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24848v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24848v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Human vision and video stereo networks both reuse disparity evidence across time, yet a refresh of the input can invalidate a match formed milliseconds earlier. What tells a system whether an old match still counts? We answer this from limited human data in three steps. First, nine temporal mechanisms share a frozen binocular-energy front end and an equal-capacity readout, so held-out behavior isolates the temporal selection rule: on 240 conditions from 10 observers, down-weighting aged evidence that has lost binocular support lowers subject RMSE from 12.6% to 10.3% and reproduces a period-dependent reversed-depth illusion, across all 59 readings of the unpublished protocol and 8 front-end perturbations. Second, four propositions establish what such data can identify: gating is identified at the level of the refresh schedule, and candidate binding is invisible to standard stimuli but exposed by a single-eye geometry flip that separates the readouts by up to 7.1%. Third, the identified rule becomes a two-field stereo memory that separates sample validity from hypothesis support. It removes a 50 ms recovery lag after geometry flips, and its regime analysis explains why plain integration stays preferable on MPI-Sintel, where 71.1% of pixels change appearance but not disparity.</summary>

    <title>Clover-35B-A3B-Preview Technical Report</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T15:46:14Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24636v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24636v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We introduce Clover-35B-A3B-Preview (Clover), a mixture-of-experts diffusion language model with 35 billion total parameters and 3 billion activated parameters, supporting thinking-mode generation. Clover adapts Gated Delta Networks to block diffusion by combining recurrent memory of previously generated context with bidirectional softmax attention inside the current block. Historical memory readout competes with current-block tokens in a shared softmax, with learnable block-size calibration and a separate, zero-initialized right-context convolution branch. Clover leads the seven evaluated agent metrics, including 73.6 on SWE-bench Verified and 51.7 on Terminal-Bench 2.1. On internal agent workloads, it reaches a reported generation speed of 680 tokens/s using one NVIDIA GB300 GPU at BF16 precision and batch size one. We organize the evaluation around model quality, drafting and verification costs, and deployment under constrained memory. We also describe a decision-model variant that generates answers to related questions in one denoising pass. On an internal set of 500 groups, joint prediction raises question accuracy from 90.37% to 93.88% and all-correct group accuracy from 65.4% to 77.0%.</summary>

    <title>Do Frontier Model Ingredients Add Up? A Replicated Factorial Study of Small Language Models</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T14:48:52Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24540v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24540v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Building a small language model requires choosing which published improvements to combine. We compare five changes in the same model, using the same data and training budget. We test selected combinations and repeat each one with a second random seed. Mixture-of-experts layers, Muon optimisation and a Gated DeltaNet hybrid give the largest gains. Extra normalisation also helps, while an attention gate with a matched parameter budget adds little on average. The gains mostly combine, but small interactions between changes appear again in the repeated runs. Repetition also reveals benefits that an initial statistical estimate treated as noise. These findings apply to our small-model training setting; the expert models also have greater total capacity. The practical lesson is to test promising components together and repeat the comparisons before deciding which ones to keep.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24496v1</id>
    <title>Harvesting Expert-Parallel Bubbles for Fine-Tuning</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T14:24:23Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24496v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24496v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>GPUs are expensive, yet latency-critical large language model (LLM) inference leaves part of them idle. Colocation reclaims this capacity by running best-effort work, such as fine-tuning, alongside serving. Many leading LLMs now use a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture, which adds a new source of idle time. Under expert parallelism, MoE experts are spread across GPUs, and because the router sends uneven numbers of tokens to each GPU, lightly loaded GPUs wait for the most loaded one. Even after applying load balancing solutions, such bubbles still take 8--13% of prefill time.
  We present BubbleTea, the first colocation system that leverages expert-parallel bubbles for fine-tuning. Unlike existing colocation systems, which make one scheduling decision for all GPUs per forward pass, BubbleTea predicts each GPU's bubble at every layer from the router's token assignment, and fills it with short chunks of fine-tuning work that reuse the weights already loaded for serving. We also introduce compiler passes that automatically derive these chunks from the served LLM as-is, without porting each model architecture to a separate training engine.
  Our evaluation on three MoE models, served on four A100 GPUs, shows that fine-tuning throughput with BubbleTea is 1.9--6.2$\times$ faster than with LLMStation, a state-of-the-art colocation system. BubbleTea keeps p90 inference latency within 10% of serving alone in 50 of 63 workloads, compared to 44 for LLMStation. On bursty production traces, BubbleTea trains 3.3$\times$ faster than LLMStation and 14$\times$ faster than a stock trainer colocated under CUDA MPS, with p90 inference latency staying within 7% of serving alone.</summary>

    <title>Neural-Network Identification of LIGO Noise Transients Using Binary Auxiliary-Channel Activity</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T14:20:03Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24485v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24485v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Transient noise artifacts ("glitches") in the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO), Virgo and KAGRA (LVK) detectors can mimic astrophysical signals and reduce confidence in gravitational-wave detections. The LVK's iDQ pipeline identifies these glitches by analyzing correlations between auxiliary sensors and the strain channel using the Ordered Veto List (OVL) algorithm. We revisit neural-network approaches to this problem using modern training infrastructure and introduce two architectures: GIANTS, a single network trained on all auxiliary-channel features, and TITAN, a mixture-of-experts model composed of subsystem-specific networks and a learned combiner. Evaluated on ten independent test periods spanning LIGO's third observing run, both models outperform OVL on most test sets, with TITAN providing the most consistent performance over time. We further show that nearly all predictive information contained in Omicron trigger features is captured by a simple binary indicator of auxiliary-channel activity. Networks trained on these binary inputs achieve essentially the same performance as models using the full 8,440-dimensional feature set while reducing the input dimensionality by an order of magnitude. These results demonstrate that modern neural networks provide a robust alternative to OVL and suggest that substantially simpler data representations are sufficient for accurate glitch identification in future iDQ deployments.</summary>

    <title>automodel: A Skill for Agentic Model Discovery</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T12:43:45Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24347v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>

    <summary>The search for better models, whether expressed as analytical equations or neural architectures, has increasingly shifted from manual design toward data-driven automation. While a multitude of algorithms exist, ranging from exhaustive search to AlphaEvolve, recent advances in general-purpose coding agents such as Claude Code and OpenAI Codex raise the question: could providing such systems with a "model discovery recipe" be enough to discover or improve models? We present automodel, an agent skill for general model discovery. With case studies in astrophysics, cardiovascular dynamics, precision agriculture, traffic flow, and vehicle tire dynamics, we show how commercial agents equipped with automodel can successfully identify novel and scientifically-relevant models. Our findings suggest that encoding model-discovery methodology as a portable agent skill can provide a simple, interactive, powerful and broadly applicable alternative to domain-specific automated discovery pipelines. The skill is available at: https://github.com/unlayer-ai/automodel.</summary>

    <title>Analysis of the (1+1)-EA-ES-Bilevel on Mixed Discrete-Continuous Optimization Problems with Interactions</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T11:28:23Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24251v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24251v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Mixed discrete-continuous optimization problems can pose challenges -- especially for previous integrated approaches -- when interactions cause beneficial discrete changes to be rejected before sufficient continuous adjustment. We introduce ProximityOneMax as a simple benchmark with pairwise discrete-continuous interactions. On this function, we prove an exponential lower bound on the expected time for the (1+1)-EA-ES-Integrated to reach the target accuracy when initialized near a continuous optimum for a suboptimal discrete configuration with a sufficiently small step size. Experiments show frequent entries into such states from random initialization. We introduce the (1+1)-EA-ES-Bilevel, which uses an upper-level (1+1)-EA to optimize discrete variables and a lower-level (1+1)-ES to optimize continuous variables for each fixed discrete offspring before selection. For several interaction benchmarks and sufficiently small target values $ε> 0$ that require an optimal discrete configuration, using fixed continuous initialization and a suitable fixed budget per lower-level call, we prove that the expected number of fitness evaluations to reach objective value at most $ε$ is $Θ(n_d \cdot \log n_d \cdot n_c \cdot \log(R/\sqrtε))$, where $n_d$ is the number of discrete variables, $n_c$ is the number of continuous variables, and $R$ bounds the distances from the fixed continuous starting point to all relevant continuous optima for fixed discrete configurations.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24718v1</id>
    <title>Meta-LSQ: A Closed-Form Sobolev Inner Solver for Few-Shot Meta-Learning</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T16:39:44Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24718v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24718v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Gradient-based meta-learners such as model-agnostic meta-learning (MAML) adapt to a new task with an inner loop of gradient descent that has to be differentiated through, and they meta-learn every network weight. Meta-LSQ instead fits each task with one regularised least-squares solve over a fixed random Fourier basis and meta-learns only three scalars, a bandwidth, a ridge and a derivative weight. Since the derivative of a sinusoid is again a sinusoid, the same solve can also take derivative observations, and the fitted model has exact closed-form derivatives of any order. On 10-shot sinusoid regression Meta-LSQ trains in 14 s and ends with a 5.5 times lower error than a first-order MAML baseline that trains 36 times longer, and a Gaussian-process control suggests that most of this gain comes from sharing one kernel across tasks. In simulated beam tuning at DESY's ARES facility with model derivatives it is slightly more accurate than an ALPaCA-style model and well ahead of gradient descent. Over DESY's full range of target beams, again in simulation and from measurements alone, its best setting has a median error of 7.3 $μ$m, against 14.4 for the published final beams of their reinforcement-learning agent, which has the lower median on their 300 trials of small targets. On real sensor-calibration data a learned prior mean puts it ahead of MAML on two of four targets, but an exact Gaussian process with the same change and an ALPaCA-style model stay more accurate on most targets, and it breaks down on non-smooth targets. On noiseless targets outside the span of the basis, in-sample criteria such as generalised cross-validation choose too small a ridge.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24093v1</id>
    <title>UCLIR: Unsupervised Continual Learning using Independent Representations</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T09:19:21Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24093v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24093v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>In continual learning, regularization-based methods aim to mimic neuroplasticity by updating network weights to learn new tasks while constraining changes to parameters that are important for previously learned tasks through penalty terms. However, as the number of tasks increases, preserving knowledge from earlier tasks becomes less effective. This is mainly because updates for new tasks are distributed across the entire network, where parameters are highly interdependent due to the dense connectivity between neurons. Inspired by the Exponential Distance Rule (EDR), which states that the number of neural connections decreases with increasing physical distance, learning is naturally locally correlated while inter-area updates remain less task-dependent. Motivated by this principle, in this paper we demonstrate that applying weight regularization to multiple small and independently learned complementary representations is more effective than regularizing a single large shared representation. By decomposing the input into independently learned components, learning new tasks induces only localized parameter updates within specific representation, which limit interference and improve knowledge retention across tasks. We employ independent autoencoders that learn different parts of the input independently through unsupervised regularization. At inference time, a linear classifier is used for evaluation. The experimental results on a sequence of tasks using 5-Splits MNIST, sequence of 5-datasets, 5-Splits CIFAR-10, 10-Splits Tiny ImageNet shows competitive results with supervised and replay-based methods. Code is available.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23525v1</id>
    <title>Reinforcement Learning Optimized Flight Control for Interception of High-Altitude Maneuvering Targets</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T21:26:26Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23525v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.23525v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We implement and compare two approaches to improving flight control system (FCS) performance using reinforcement meta-learning (meta-RL). Both approaches are evaluated in a terminal phase hypersonic intercept engagement requiring hit-to-kill accuracy against a highly agile maneuvering target. In the first approach (FCS-RL), meta-RL is used to optimize a full FCS that maps acceleration tracking error and other measurements directly to commanded channel deflection rates of change, combining pitch, yaw, and roll control into a single policy. In contrast, the second approach (FCS-3L-RL) starts with a standard FCS (FCS-3L) implementing a three-loop autopilot for pitch and yaw control, but adapts the scheduled autopilot gains in real time using a policy optimized with meta-RL. Both approaches are compared to the FCS-3L in a 6-DOF simulator that captures most factors relevant to guidance and flight control. Simulations show that under ideal conditions the three systems have comparable performance. However, under conditions of aerodynamic uncertainty, radome refraction, or target evasive maneuvers, the FCS-RL significantly outperforms the FCS-3L-RL with improved intercept probability and less control effort. In turn, the FCS-3L-RL outperforms the FCS-3L by a similar margin. Importantly, we demonstrate that both FCS-RL and FCS-3L-RL generalize well to novel engagement scenarios, flight conditions, and target maneuvers that are not experienced during the optimization process.</summary>

    <title>From Perception to Simulation: Unveiling and Empowering Mental Spatial Dynamics in MLLMs</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T10:31:56Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22541v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.22541v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Spatial reasoning is a fundamental component of world understanding for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). While existing research has advanced the perception of spatial relations in static scenes, the domain of dynamic spatial simulation remains relatively unexplored. To bridge this gap, we introduce MentalGrid, a benchmark focused on spatial reasoning tasks that require models to simulate evolving spatial states without intermediate visual feedback. Extensive evaluation on our benchmark reveals a significant deficiency in the spatial simulation capabilities of existing models. Specifically, we find that performance is constrained by perceptual limitations in simple simulation scenarios and hindered by inadequate multi-step reasoning as complexity increases. To address these challenges, we propose a three-stage curriculum learning framework utilizing 16k specialized spatial reasoning samples. This approach yields SpatialWalker, which achieves a 33.8% average improvement over its base model, surpassing proprietary models like Gemini-3-Flash in spatial simulation. Furthermore, SpatialWalker demonstrates robust generalization, maintaining a 4.9% average gain on out-of-domain benchmarks, demonstrating the pivotal role of spatial simulation as a fundamental building block for broader spatial intelligence.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22250v1</id>
    <title>PCGRL for Complex Platformers: Synthesizing Playable and Diverse Levels via Inflated Envelopes and Forward Curricula</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T05:55:23Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22250v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.22250v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Procedural Content Generation via Reinforcement Learning (PCGRL) has emerged as a promising paradigm for automated game development. However, existing PCGRL frameworks still suffer from severe exploration bottlenecks and scaling limitations when faced with long-sequence generation tasks governed by strict rigid-body rules and non-linear kinematic boundaries (e.g., platformer constraints). Consequently, traditional approaches frequently fail to maintain reliable level solvability on large-scale canvases. To address these challenges, we present a physics-aware, curriculum-guided PCGRL framework. First, we construct an "Inflated Volume Envelope" mechanism, which provides a physics-constrained representation that incorporates continuous kinematic feasibility into the discrete state space of the MDP. Second, to alleviate the sparse reward challenge induced by extremely long decision sequences, we introduce intermediate state-transition feedback and a multi-stage forward extension curriculum learning framework, enabling informative value estimation and stable credit assignment over long-horizon trajectories. Finally, to resolve the issue where deterministic policies after convergence generate highly monotonous map paths with a lack of diversity, we activate high-entropy stochastic inference during the synthesis phase, regularized by a post-hoc parallel rejection filtering mechanism. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework significantly enhances structural diversity while maintaining high physical playability across multi-scale environments. Comparative evaluations across multi-scale canvases demonstrate that our framework maintains superior convergence stability and dimensional scalability, reliably synthesizing solvable levels where traditional PCGRL baselines degrade.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20609v1</id>
    <title>Newton-PINet: A fast physics-informed neural network with Newton linearization for meta-learning nonlinear PDEs</title>
    <updated>2026-11-16T06:33:53Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20609v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.20609v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Scientific machine learning has opened new avenues for solving parameterized partial differential equations (PDEs), enabling models to learn a family of PDEs and generalize to unseen instances. In this context, data-driven operator learning methods typically require large training datasets, while physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) suffer from difficult optimization and limited generalization, especially for nonlinear PDEs. We propose Newton-PINet, a physics-informed network enhanced by Newton linearization, offering an effective meta-learning framework for nonlinear PDEs. Newton-PINet (i) employs a physics-informed multilayer network with skip connections, where the output-layer weights are solved by least squares; (ii) adopts a two-stage learning strategy that first leverages gradient-based training to learn robust representations from the available training tasks, and then performs gradient-free fine-tuning on the output layer for fast task-specific generalization; and (iii) incorporates a Newton linearization method to speed up the least-squares iteration for nonlinear PDE problems. On a challenging nonlinear reaction-diffusion benchmark, Newton-PINet achieves up to three orders of magnitude lower relative error than recent neural solvers, while using 16x fewer training tasks and over an order of magnitude less training time (about 5 minutes versus several hours). This work advances the meta-learning of PINNs toward data-efficient, fast, and generalizable physics solvers. The code and datasets are publicly available at: https://github.com/fycAIwj/Newton-PINet.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20019v1</id>
    <title>D'BEAST: Logged Bad Experiences as Explanation for Autonomous Driving Agents</title>
    <updated>2026-11-15T14:05:02Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20019v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.20019v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Reinforcement learning agents learn from mistakes, yet their decisions can be difficult to trace back to those experiences. We investigate whether a tabular agent's decisions can be explained by its bad experiences, defined as the training transitions associated with safety or task events. A fixed training log is replayed from the same initial Q-table under three conditions. FULL retains all updates, SKIP omits bad-experience updates, and NEUTRALIZE retains those updates without their event penalties. We illustrate the method on six classic Markov decision processes and evaluate it in closed-loop driving in CARLA. On the full driving task, FULL reached the goal from 33 of 40 test starts, whereas SKIP and NEUTRALIZE reached it from none, indicating that the bad experiences carry decision-relevant information. At the local level, for 47 decisions shortly before a failure of SKIP or NEUTRALIZE, removing or neutralizing a small group of bad experiences, with a median size of one, caused the trained agent to select the failing policy's action in 46 cases. For this agent, the results indicate that its decisions can be explained by its bad experiences.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23321v1</id>
    <title>Error Analysis of Deep Learning</title>
    <updated>2026-11-15T12:23:47Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23321v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.23321v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>This review examines deep learning theory through the lens of error decomposition, systematically addressing approximation, statistical, and optimization errors. We trace the development of error analyses from bounds on individual error components to frameworks that account for all three. Using nonparametric regression and the Deep Ritz Method as dual running examples, we demonstrate how these analyses apply across fundamentally different loss structures. We then review representative analyses in scientific machine learning, generative learning, reinforcement learning, representation learning, and large language models, showing how learning errors affect solutions, distributions, and predictions through problem-specific arguments. Throughout, we clarify which error components are controlled, how they are combined, and what assumptions are needed to obtain guarantees for trained networks.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23177v1</id>
    <title>Déjà View: A Shared Working-Memory Model for Visual Tasks</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T18:23:14Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23177v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.23177v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>A working-memory model must remember stimuli and use its memory flexibly to perform different tasks. Here we introduce a model of working memory for images that combines dynamic activity with temporary associations between image features. We train the model on five tasks, including remembering a sample while other images are presented, categorizing distractor images while remembering the sample, and determining whether an image is new or has been presented before. The same trained model performs all tasks, guided by explicit cues about which response is required. We use this flexible memory model to ask how delay, distraction, and image history affect performance. Delays have little effect on sample-memory performance for the delays we tested, while seeing more images leads to more false alarms even when the target image appeared equally recently in all cases. On the sample-memory-plus-categorization task, the probability of correct responses on all questions decreases as more questions are asked, despite robust sample-memory performance. Finally, the model maintains stable performance across 40 brief trials of each task under the tested conditions. Together, these results demonstrate how a single working-memory system can be flexibly used to perform different tasks, and how its errors depend on both previous images and task demands.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22054v1</id>
    <title>A single inference process underlies the behavior and neural circuits of working memory</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T01:29:43Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22054v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.22054v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Working memory holds past inputs online for future behavior. Despite decades of research, accounts of working memory remain divided across levels of analysis, with long-standing debates on whether its capacity reflects discrete slots or continuous resources, how attention improves recall, and whether its representations rely on persistent neural firing or activity-silent states. Here we show that MemGP, a theory that is specified at the computational, algorithmic, and circuit levels of analysis simultaneously, can explain diverse behavioral and neural phenomena in working memory. At the computational level, MemGP casts working memory as probabilistic inference over a continuous function on feature space, with a variational objective that balances memory strength against a Gaussian-process prior. At the algorithmic level, writing, storing, and reading of memories correspond to approximating this posterior with a finite set of inducing points, the resource that all items share. In simulations, MemGP reproduces load-dependent precision loss, attentional benefits during maintenance, and inter-item attraction and repulsion, in each case revealing multiple complex computational dependencies. At the circuit level, the algorithm analytically (without training) maps onto a recurrent circuit, including its architecture and dynamics. Beyond reproducing neural phenomena such as delay-dependent drift, this analytical map deduces center--surround connectivity, a property long assumed in attractor models, and a structured combination of persistent activity and synaptic weights to hold memories. Thus, a single inference objective not only jointly predicts the behavioral and neural signatures of working memory, but also addresses, across several instances and different levels of analysis, existing competing explanations.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16057v2</id>
    <title>Pyramidal Columns Acting as Attention Heads</title>
    <updated>2026-11-14T20:39:15Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16057v2" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.16057v2" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Can the functional architecture of a Transformer attention head be given a biological construction? More specifically, could a suitable group of pyramidal columns in posterior temporal language regions (PTLRs) constitute the biological construction of a neuromorphic mechanical realization of an attention head, under a mathematical instantiation that need not coincide with its standard Transformer instantiation? This paper investigates this hypothesis by examining possible correspondences between the functional organization of attention heads and neurophysiological mechanisms operating within and across pyramidal columns involved in human language processing. Our analysis builds on a mechanical-structural description of Transformer attention heads as systems of simple neural networks linked through output-input and output-weight interconnections. We examine the functional organization of an attention head and the input-dependent transformations it produces, and ask how the corresponding processing relations could be constructed in biological neural tissue. We then identify candidate neural mechanisms of signal transmission and modulation within and across pyramidal columns that may jointly support such a construction. On this basis, we propose that a suitably organized group of pyramidal columns in PTLRs could constitute a biological construction of a neuromorphic mechanical realization of an attention head. Whether the required functional organization actually exists in PTLRs remains an open empirical question. The hypothesis does not require the biological system to reproduce the standard mathematical instantiation of Transformer attention: the same functional architecture may be mechanically realized and mathematically instantiated in a different way, consistent with its biological construction.</summary>

    <title>ScaleBrain: A Scale-Consistent Framework for EEG Foundation Models</title>
    <updated>2026-11-10T13:03:41Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14035v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.14035v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Foundation models pre-trained on large unlabeled electroencephalography (EEG) corpora have emerged as a transformative paradigm for Brain-Computer Interface (BCI) applications. Recent EEG foundation models have shown that multi-scale representations derived from fixed-length patches can improve EEG representation learning. Existing frameworks commonly construct temporal scales through feature-level operations. However, these operations leave the correspondence between learned features and scale-specific characteristics of the original EEG signals implicit. Moreover, when the self-supervised objective is not aligned with the multi-scale input representations, information at some temporal scales may receive insufficient supervision during pre-training. In light of this, we propose ScaleBrain, a scale-consistent pre-training framework that explicitly coordinates multi-scale representations of EEG from both the model input and optimization objective sides. Specifically, ScaleBrain introduces multi-scale EEG tokenization to represent the same EEG segment through analysis windows with different temporal spans and shared temporal anchors, and pairs these representations with scale-specific reconstruction to align with the multi-scale input structure and provide supervision across temporal resolutions during self-supervised learning. We further develop an axial spatio-temporal attention mechanism to contextualize the fused multi-scale representation along spatial and temporal dimensions. Extensive evaluations on six public BCI benchmarks against 12 representative baselines show that ScaleBrain achieves the highest mean Balanced Accuracy on five datasets and ranks third on the remaining one, with only 5.0M parameters, demonstrating strong performance and favorable parameter efficiency.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13637v1</id>
    <title>Human and Machine Annotations Predict Brain Responses to Naturalistic Movies Across Development</title>
    <updated>2026-11-10T06:25:00Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.13637v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.13637v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Naturalistic movie watching provides a powerful framework for studying dynamic brain function, but linking movie content to neural responses typically relies on labor-intensive human annotation. We investigated whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can provide scalable socio-affective and semantic annotations for naturalistic fMRI. We compared MLLM-generated theory-of-mind (ToM) and valence ratings with human ratings and with regional BOLD responses across three animated movies. For two of these movies, we combined machine-derived visual features, natural-language scene descriptions, and socio-affective ratings in an ROI-wise encoding model of fMRI data from 66 participants aged 5--22 years. MLLM ratings partially tracked human judgments, but their neural correspondence differed by construct and model: ToM showed the most consistent human--machine overlap in visual cortex, whereas valence correspondence was largely movie dependent. In the encoding model, visual features yielded the strongest and most widespread prediction, whereas scene descriptions were more spatially selective, concentrated in dorsal-attention and visual regions and extending into right lateral temporal cortex. Age-group comparisons suggested feature-specific developmental differences: scene-description encoding in dorsal-attention cortex was higher in the oldest group, whereas visual-feature encoding in salience/ventral-attention, limbic, and control networks peaked in the middle group. Together, these findings indicate that MLLM-generated annotations capture meaningful aspects of human judgments and neural responses, supporting MLLMs as a scalable complement to, rather than a replacement for, human annotation in naturalistic neuroimaging.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11011v1</id>
    <title>Learning Actionable Information Landscapes for Multimodal Active Sensing in Hawkmoths</title>
    <updated>2026-11-07T23:16:56Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11011v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.11011v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Animals integrate information across sensory modalities to guide exploration, suggesting that they maintain internal estimates of where actions are expected to reduce uncertainty. However, how such action-conditioned information maps are learned from multimodal sensory experience remains unclear, as previous studies have been largely confined to unimodal sensing frameworks. We introduce a multimodal predictive-coding framework for learning uncertainty-reduction maps from visual and mechanosensory observations in hawkmoth flower interaction tasks. A variational generative model trained on simulated environments recovers modality-specific information landscapes over the action space, capturing how visual patterns, surface geometry, and mechanosensory cues shape the value of exploratory actions. These learned maps are consistent with several features of hawkmoth behavior, including nonzero tracking offsets, probing along visual patterns, and geometry-dependent exploration. Applying the model to behavioral data from flower tracking and nectary search, we find that natural trajectories tend to occupy regions of high uncertainty reduction in these learned maps. Building on these observations, we develop an uncertainty-gated lexicographic algorithm that switches between information gathering and reward exploitation based on perceptual uncertainty. In nectary search, uncertainty gating improves learning relative to exploit-only, $ε$-greedy, fixed-time, and uncertainty-calibrated non-lexicographic controls, with better generalization and robustness to sensory and curvature shifts. These results link information landscapes learned through generative modeling to biological sensing and embodied exploration.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.10565v1</id>
    <title>Pixels over Symbols: Sensory Realism Improves Behavioral Alignment in Models of Cognition</title>
    <updated>2026-11-07T08:13:37Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.10565v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.10565v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Computational models of cognition have traditionally relied on abstract symbolic inputs that approximate sensory experiences with simplified vector representations. This simplification reflects historical computational constraints and a long-held assumption that the details of sensory realism are incidental to the study of cognitive processes. Recent advances have enabled the development of sensory-realistic models capable of performing diverse cognitive tasks, yet whether sensory realism meaningfully shapes cognition has not been formally established. We address this gap through a large-scale empirical comparison of abstract and sensory-realistic neural network models trained on a battery of memory-dependent decision-making tasks. Our results show that sensory-realistic models mirror human behavioral response patterns significantly more than their abstract counterparts, though a substantial gap to human internal behavioral consistency remains even for the best tested models. By analyzing the internal dynamics of these systems, we find that the learned recurrent weights are not the main source of this divergence. In fact, frozen abstract-trained weights driven by sensory-realistic inputs recover the human consistency of sensory-realistic models. The resulting dynamics are also within the seed-to-seed variability of sensory-realistic models. Together, our findings argue that across a broad set of visual working-memory tasks, sensory realism accounts for a substantial portion of the model-human behavioral agreement, more than the choice of sequence architecture and comparable to the choice of vision encoder. These results suggest that findings obtained from abstract task models in neuroscience should be more carefully interpreted in light of their potential behavioral limitations.</summary>

    <title>Intrinsic network dynamics catalyze switching in functional connectivity states of the brain</title>
    <updated>2026-11-02T12:58:21Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.03071v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.03071v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Dynamic functional connectivity (dFC) reflects ongoing reconfiguration of large-scale brain networks, but the temporal organization and network processes underlying spontaneous state transitions remain poorly understood. We developed functional connectivity state switching (FCSS), a phase-coherence-based framework that tracks multiscale changes in dominant whole-brain connectivity configurations. In Human Connectome Project fMRI, FCSS was strongly evoked by cognitive state and condition switches, and distinct transition dynamics differentially predicted working-memory performance. During rest, spontaneous FCSS was characterized by progressive changes in network segregation, integration, and cross-network communication as connectivity approached a switching event. Critically, event-related analysis time-locked to spontaneous FCSS revealed opposing pre-switch dynamics: salience-network contribution increased while default-mode-network contribution decreased, suggesting coordinated engagement and disengagement of these networks before switching. This reciprocal reweighting may provide a network-level mechanism for spontaneous FC reconfiguration. Together, these findings identify both global reorganization and network-specific processes underlying spontaneous and task-evoked brain-state transitions in the human brain.</summary>
