    <title>Piccolo: Co-Evolving Decision Models and Data through Recursive Self-Improvement</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T15:53:39Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24651v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24651v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We present Piccolo, a family of multimodal decision models (0.8B to 27B) that coevolves model capabilities and training data via Agentic Data Engineering and recursive self-improvement (RSI). The models predict probabilities over candidate answers for general-purpose text and visual judgments, agent harnesses, data workflows, and interactive games. Piccolo-27B tops the Decision Index Vision Full leaderboard with a score of 75.59, while Piccolo-9B and Piccolo-4B achieve 68.35 and 67.46, respectively. All three rank first on the Private benchmark in their respective model-size categories. Research agents analyze model behavior, construct training data, conduct experiments, and use the results to refine subsequent proposals. Semantic slices and a shared research memory connect these actions across the model family's development. With training recipes comprising hundreds of thousands of examples, data selection and feedback-driven refinement are central to the self-improvement process. Our large-scale RSI exploration yields three counter-intuitive insights for decision-model development: (1) Backbone-recipe co-adaptation outweighs raw model recency: earlier backbones can surpass newer generations on visual tasks under identical recipes; (2) Targeted data curation enables 4B-9B models to rival 27B baselines on specialized workflows; and (3) Continuous loss reduction can decouple from and even degrade discrete decision accuracy. Together with the released weights and tools from the Data-Juicer and AgentScope ecosystems, Piccolo provides an actionable blueprint for building frontier decision models and scaling data-driven RSI.</summary>

    <title>Think Offline, Act in Real Time: Self-Improving Visual Game Agents through Code</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T15:18:22Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24590v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24590v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Pre-trained models can read screens and reason about games, yet on an unfamiliar game, an agent still has to learn to play. We ask how an agent can self-improve on such a game from a few of its own attempts, in real-time visual games where the agent sees only the screen and the game keeps running while the agent thinks. We study two kinds of policy that can carry this improvement. In model as policy, a model selects actions during play; we adapt real-time chunking so that committed actions keep executing while the model reasons, and train a 2B controller for this interface. In code as policy, a model writes, tests, and revises a program between attempts, and the program acts during play. Across 170 GameWorld tasks, with at most eight one-minute executions per run, code as policy reaches 47.80% mean progress, against 30.90% for our trained controller, and leads in all five game categories. Improving the controller's weights on a single game, by contrast, yields only modest gains. These results favor letting a model think offline and storing what it learns in a program that acts in real time. Project repository: https://github.com/TabibitoQZP/SIGame</summary>

    <title>BaseRSI: Recursive Self-Improvement of a Base Vision-Language Model via Training-Free Harness Internalization</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T15:10:11Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24578v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24578v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Recursive self-improvement (RSI) is moving from the harness of prompts and tools around a base model toward the model itself. However, existing RSI still faces key challenges, including harness-bound gains that stay outside the base model, black-box supervision that reads only the model's outputs, and imprecise edits whose site and strength are fixed in advance. To address these challenges, we propose BaseRSI, a new paradigm of Recursive Harness Internalization: the base model improves its harness, then writes what the harness adds into its own weights through training-free edits, round after round on its own responses. To support this paradigm, we introduce ReGap, a mechanism that supervises every transformer block with the high-dimensional activation difference that the harness makes at that block alone, and updates the block's weights along this signal in a low-dimensional subspace. Building on this mechanism, we further propose ReKey, an algorithm that writes this signal by regression into a few key-value neurons of every block, and measures the site and strength of each edit on the model's own responses. Moreover, the base model fills every role of this recursion with forward passes alone, and its edits, written at different sites, compose in one checkpoint without refitting. Experimental results on ten visual reasoning benchmarks show that BaseRSI consistently improves a base vision-language model both in distribution and on held-out benchmarks. Our code is available at https://github.com/beita6969/BaseRSI.</summary>

    <title>RSIBench-Infra: Can Agents Optimize Their Own Training and Inference Infrastructure at Production Scale?</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T13:29:44Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24395v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24395v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Improving the efficiency of training and inference infrastructure is a practical component of recursive self-improvement. Existing benchmarks for agent-driven optimization largely focus on individual software layers such as kernel, leaving unclear whether agents can deliver end-to-end performance gains under production workloads. We introduce RSIBench-Infra, a benchmark of 20 training and inference tasks spanning diverse model families and modalities, with deployments of up to 32 accelerators on NVIDIA GPUs and Ascend NPUs. Agents start from runnable baselines derived from official recipes and can modify the software stack across engine, kernel, and instruction levels. An OCI image-layer submission protocol captures these changes for reproducible deployment, while independent evaluation measures end-to-end performance under task-specific quality constraints. Across all task results, 66.2% exceed $1.10\times$ validated speedup. These results demonstrate that current agents can improve production-scale training and inference performance, but identifying effective optimization strategies and consistently translating local improvements into end-to-end gains remain challenging.</summary>

    <title>From Self-Play RL to Constrained Control: Distilling DiffMPC Students with DAgger</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T21:17:04Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.25197v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.25197v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Self-play reinforcement learning (RL) produces strong driving policies, but these policies are hard to verify or interpret. Differentiable model predictive control (DiffMPC) can enforce explicit constraints, but it is usually trained by imitating logged data or with costly RL. To add constraints to an already trained policy, we keep a PPO teacher's backbone and replace its action head with a DiffMPC that enforces road boundary half-planes and agent ellipses. We then distill the student with DAgger in the teacher's self-play simulator. Over 9 seeds, the constrained student of a smaller teacher matches its teacher on nuPlan and beats it on CARLA and on out-of-distribution Waymo scenes. For a stronger teacher, the student has fewer failures on nuPlan and Waymo, while staying level on CARLA. Its distillation takes no more than 30% of the teacher's training time.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24876v1</id>
    <title>Learning to Interact in Multi-Agent Self-Play for Controllable Autonomous Driving Scenario Generation</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T18:23:29Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24876v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24876v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Large-scale, multi-agent self-play trains robust driving policies effectively in simulation, but controlling these models to generate specific, safety-critical edge cases remains a key challenge. Existing goal-conditioned self-play frameworks rely primarily on static map-location goals and fail to reliably produce complex agent interactions such as aggressive tailgating or adversarial cut-offs. These agent interactions are necessary for rigorous autonomous vehicle (AV) testing. To address this, we present an extended multi-agent self-play framework that introduces agent-relative dynamic goals. By conditioning policies on this extended goal representation, our framework enables targeted, controllable scenario synthesis. We demonstrate that our approach successfully generates interactive driving behaviors that static-goal baselines cannot simulate, providing a flexible tool for long-tail scenario generation in AV testing.</summary>

    <title>Reliable Tree Recruitment from Scarce Annotations for Forest Inventory Expansion</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T13:31:37Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24401v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24401v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Species-level inventories of individual tree crowns (ITCs) from UAV imagery are limited by annotation cost: in tropical forests, many species are represented by only a handful of field-validated crowns. We propose a reliable tree recruitment framework that expands a small annotated inventory by iteratively self-training a multi-task DeepLabV3 network, combining semantic segmentation with a crown-distance regression head, on RGB UAV orthomosaics. At each iteration, candidate crowns enter the training inventory only if they pass a confidence filter on class probability and distance map and a morphology filter on crown area and solidity, with at most five new crowns per species, keeping recruited samples consistent with the reference inventory. We evaluate the framework at two Brazilian sites: an Amazonian rainforest in Acre (17 species, 355 annotated crowns, 4 cm GSD) and a forest site in the Cerrado of Maranhão (4 species, 51 annotated crowns, 1.8 cm GSD). Over 20 iterations, the number of retained crowns grew from about 500 to 960 in Acre and from about 700 to over 3100 in Maranhão, while crown-level F1 exceeded single- and multi-task DeepLabV3 baselines (53.5% vs. 50.0% and 45.2%; 92.2% vs. 79.7% and 83.6%). The framework offers a low-cost route to expanding species inventories with consumer-grade UAVs and limited fieldwork.</summary>

    <title>Semi-Supervised GAN-Based Segmentation of CTPA Scans for Pulmonary Emboli Boundary Extraction</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T08:09:43Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24018v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24018v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Pulmonary embolism (PE) is a pulmonary vascular disease associated with high morbidity and mortality, where delayed diagnosis can be fatal. While computed tomography pulmonary angiography (CTPA) is the clinical gold standard for PE detection, interpreting these scans manually is time-consuming and error-prone. In this work, we propose a semi-supervised segmentation method, employing generative adversarial networks (GANs) to leverage large pools of unlabeled CTPA scans. The proposed method addresses more effectively the challenges of CTPA image segmentation than previous methods by employing the dice loss and the cross-entropy loss to tackle the highly imbalanced nature of CTPA scans, the feature matching loss to encourage the generator to produce anatomically plausible segmentation maps that are indistinguishable from ground truth, as well as the self-training loss to reinforce learning from highly-confident pseudo-labeled samples. The experimental evaluation on a publicly available dataset shows that the proposed method maintains accurate segmentation, despite a limited number of labeled CTPA scans. with a Dice coefficient of 88.75% and a 95th percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95) of 1.74, outperforming fully supervised baselines.</summary>

    <title>SWE-growth: Teacher-Guided Adaptive Self-Play for Software Engineering Agents</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T05:29:18Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23876v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.23876v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Self-play offers a scalable way to train software engineering agents by generating repository-level repair tasks. However, with binary repair rewards and finite rollout budgets, all-fail groups provide no reward-based group-relative advantage. Such tasks may still offer learning opportunities when a Teacher can provide verified repairs absent from the Student's own attempts. We introduce SWE-Growth, a teacher-guided adaptive self-play framework that uses verified Teacher outcomes to identify learning opportunities for the current Student. Tasks with all students failure but reliable Teacher success provide demonstrations for supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and post-SFT Student rollouts identify mixed-outcome tasks with a positive Teacher--Student gap for reinforcement learning. Task eligibility also guides Injector updates, connecting Student training with subsequent task generation. Starting from 101 seed issues, \textsc{SWE-Growth} improves Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct from 27.7% to 31.7% on SWE-bench Pro and from 11.0% to 17.2% on held-out TerminalBench 2.1 by Round~2. It exceeds Student-only self-play by 2.6 and 4.1 percentage points, respectively, and Teacher-augmented self-play by 1.8 and 2.5 points under approximately matched budgets. These results support adapting both supervision and task selection to the Student's evolving repair capability.</summary>

    <title>A Comparison of Heuristic, Human-Sensitive, and Self-Play DRL Policies in Human-Agent Teaming</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T02:59:54Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23747v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.23747v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Dynamical Perceptual-Motor Primitives (DPMPs) offer a tractable framework for generating human-like movement dynamics in artificial agents (AAs) and have been used to support coordination in human-AI teaming tasks. Traditionally, DPMP controllers rely on heuristic (rule-based) decision policies derived from human behavior to guide goal selection and action sequencing. Although effective in structured tasks, such heuristics can be difficult to generalize to more complex settings, motivating interest in deep reinforcement learning (DRL) approaches for learning decision policies for human-AI interaction. A key challenge, however, is ensuring that DRL policies remain aligned with human strategies, particularly when agents are trained through self-play. To examine this issue, we compared three target-selection policies governing DPMP-based AAs in a first-person herding task: (1) a human-derived heuristic policy, (2) a self-play DRL policy (SP-DRL), and (3) a human-sensitive DRL policy (HS-DRL) trained alongside a heuristic agent. Results showed that heuristic agents most closely matched typical human-human coordination patterns, followed by HS-DRL agents, whereas SP-DRL agents deviated most. These findings highlight the importance of human-informed training when developing DRL-based teammates and suggest that simple heuristic policies may remain an effective approach for designing human-aligned AAs capable of human-AI collaboration.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23631v1</id>
    <title>FairPGT: Partitioned Graph Transformers for Dual-Level Fair Graph Clustering</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T23:41:54Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23631v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.23631v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Clustering on attributed graphs can produce demographically biased clusters, particularly when communities align with protected groups. Graph transformers can amplify this bias through same-group attention, while global attention limits scalability. We propose FairPGT, a partitioned graph transformer for fair graph clustering. FairPGT restricts attention to METIS partitions and connects them through routing tokens, which divides the quadratic cost of attention by the number of partitions. A graph-aware self-training target guides clustering, with a provably bounded deviation from the standard DEC target. Fairness is imposed at two levels: a mutual-information term promotes demographic parity in cluster assignments, while a normalized cross-group attention ratio (nCGAR) guides attention toward group neutrality through self-distillation. We prove that the nCGAR correction moves attention toward neutrality and establish a condition preventing overshooting. Across seven benchmarks, FairPGT achieves the best clustering performance and statistical parity on the three largest graphs (Credit, Pokec-n, Pokec-z), with a statistical-parity gap approximately ten times lower than DMoN, and is Pareto-dominated on only one dataset. On controlled stochastic block models, FairPGT attains 97% of the derived upper bound on NMI for exactly fair clustering when communities and protected groups coincide. These graphs further show that, under strong alignment, assignment-level fairness alone makes the attention group-heterophilous, whereas attention-level fairness alone improves neutrality without ensuring fair clusters. Code for reproducibility is available at https://github.com/SiamakGhodsi/FairPGT.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23581v1</id>
    <title>ExiST: Existence-Aware Self-Training for Semi-Supervised Multi-Organ Segmentation</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T22:27:46Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23581v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.23581v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Semi-supervised multi-organ segmentation should learn more than a dozen organs from a handful of labeled scans, and the smallest organs occupy less than one percent of the foreground. We identify a failure mode of self-training that is specific to this regime. When a teacher misses a small organ in a scan, every voxel of that organ receives the confident pseudo-label background, and the student is trained toward the organ absence. Repeated over many scans, this loop extinguishes tail organs. In a pilot study, removing the gallbladder from the pseudo-labels reduced its Dice on AMOS from 36.5 to 1.0. We argue that a missing organ should be treated as unresolved rather than absent and propose Existence-aware Self-Training (ExiST). It builds pseudo-labels by leave-one-out consensus of independently trained networks, screens them with a quality gate on validation scans, and infers, per scan and per organ, whether the organ was found. For every unresolved organ, the background voxels of that scan receive the set-valued target, trained with a marginal cross-entropy that accepts either answer and a Dice term that skips uncertain voxels. We show that this loss never pushes a candidate organ toward absence and never favors one member of the set, which leaves the decision to labeled evidence. ExiST outperforms the current state-of-the-art methods and reaches 77.1 mean Dice on Synapse with 20% labeled scans and 75.9 on AMOS with 5% labeled scans.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22773v1</id>
    <title>Guarded Swarms in the Loop: A ROS 2/PX4 Digital Twin for Hybrid Digital-Analog Coordination of UAV/UGV Swarms</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T13:40:51Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22773v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.22773v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Swarms of unmanned aerial and ground vehicles (UAV/UGV) operating in contested environments cannot rely on software alone for physical safety, since the software stack and its networks are part of the attack surface. The Guarded Swarms architecture addresses this by pairing a digital coordination layer, built on Topic-Based Communication Space Petri Nets (TB-CSPN), with an independent analog safety layer that can veto unsafe actuation commands. So far, the architecture has been specified and argued for, but not executed. We present the first executable instantiation of Guarded Swarms as a digital twin built on ROS 2, the PX4 autopilot in software-in-the-loop mode, and Gazebo, with two UAVs and one UGV in a coastal counter-UAS scenario. The TB-CSPN transition chain, from multi-modal sensing through human authorization to vehicle tasking, is mapped one-to-one onto ROS 2 nodes, and the analog layer is modeled as a per-vehicle Virtual Safety Board that gates every command. Eight groups of experiments show that the three negative guarantees of the architecture (no mission from conflicting, temporally incoherent, or unauthorized evidence) hold at three distinct stages of the chain in all 60 counterfactual runs; that threat confirmation is bounded by the narrowest sensing modality; that the safety layer exercises its full modeled envelope independently of the coordination layer; and, under fault injection, that it prevents every collision caused by a forged mission or a compromised worker once its veto is enforced by an independent gate, whereas a veto left to the compromised worker prevents none. The twin also exposes implementation-level hazards that the architectural specification does not address, and it draws an explicit line between the properties that simulation can validate and those that only hardware can.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20773v1</id>
    <title>When Does Interaction Help? Toward a Reynolds Number for Collective Intelligence</title>
    <updated>2026-11-16T09:22:24Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20773v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.20773v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Multi-agent systems combine distributed information through interaction, which can improve performance but also spread errors or suppress useful differences. Predicting when interaction helps is central to understanding and designing collective intelligence. We investigate whether a few dimensionless parameters can predict gains over explicitly defined non-communicating baselines across group sizes, network structures, and tasks, toward a Reynolds-number-like description of collective intelligence. Using distributed classification tasks, stochastic tracking networks, and neural cellular automata, we combine analytical and empirical evidence to examine information sufficiency, dynamical applicability, and finite-sample prediction. We construct inference systems with bounded random variables and matching specified joint moments up to total degree three, yet opposite interaction gains under a fixed readout. These moments alone cannot generally determine the gain sign. Tracking networks likewise exhibit gain reversals despite matched candidate parameters when task power occupies different spectral modes. Under concentrated task spectra and aligned observation noise, however, we derive a low-dimensional similarity relation with an explicit zero-delay error bound and test it across network sizes and topologies under frozen protocols. The relation does not directly apply to the neural cellular systems, where a separate moment-based predictor underperforms direct gain measurement at matched calibration sample budgets. These results establish conditions and limits for low-dimensional gain prediction, providing a restricted similarity law while leaving a general Reynolds-number-like description of collective intelligence open.</summary>

    <title>Phantom Consensus: Measuring Social Reasoning in Multi-Agent LLM Decision-Making</title>
    <updated>2026-11-06T04:33:59Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08971v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08971v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Multi-agent LLM systems increasingly aggregate judgments across model instances, but reasoning about other agents can itself introduce failure. We study a setting in which LLMs shift their public decisions after observing ambiguous social signals while reporting inaccurate estimates of what other agents privately judged, even when the group's recorded private judgments do not support the apparent consensus. We call this failure phantom consensus and study it as a pluralistic-ignorance-style pattern in controlled LLM collectives. To measure this phenomenon, we introduce PHANTOM-Bench, a benchmark that separates isolated private judgments, public decisions after ambiguous social signals, elicited estimates of the group's private judgment, transparency-based recovery, and controls for neutral public text and explicit vote-following. Across nine closed- and open-weight models, ambiguous public signals consistently degrade decision quality and can turn correct private group judgments into incorrect public collective outcomes. Public accuracy drops by as much as 47.8 percentage points, and collective rationality failures reach 47.3% in the most susceptible setting. We observe substantial errors in reported group-private beliefs alongside public-stage failures, while control conditions reveal model-dependent differences in susceptibility to ambiguous and explicit peer signals. Revealing the agents' recorded private decisions repairs many failures without revealing the gold label, although recovery varies across models. Our results show that evaluating multi-agent LLM systems requires measuring not only final agreement, but whether that agreement reflects independently measured private judgments or an apparent consensus.</summary>

    <title>s$^3$: Simple Scaling of Swarms via Cooperative Multi-agent RL</title>
    <updated>2026-11-05T19:07:15Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08615v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08615v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Groups can achieve more than individuals in the same amount of time, but only if their members coordinate: they must decide who works on what and what to share. However, this organization in multi-agent systems today usually comes from arbitrary, static harnesses designed a priori without adapting to agent behaviors or task specifications. We ask whether agents can instead learn to organize themselves. We introduce s$^3$, the first multi-agent reinforcement learning method in which agents decide for themselves how long to work alone and when to share findings or read teammates' messages, with no predefined organization or roles. Our s$^3$ agents learn to take different approaches, read each other's work, exhibit emergent roles that complement each other in the swarm, and generalize to bigger teams. We study both coordination, where agents must combine private information, and parallel exploration, where sharing discoveries can make search more efficient. With matched training and inference budgets, s$^3$, swarms evaluated with twice as many agents as in training solve over 25$\times$ more coordination problems than the strongest baseline, and in exploration, communicating agents reduce repeated work by nearly 50% and outperform best-of-N by up to 9.4 percentage points. Rather than being designed in advance, s$^3$ enables organization to emerge from a shared goal. This opens the door to capable systems built from many models that learn to work together.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07996v1</id>
    <title>SEER: A Scalable Event-Driven Runtime for Parallel Execution of Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Environments</title>
    <updated>2026-11-05T13:24:57Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07996v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.07996v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is increasingly used in systems where many entities interact in a shared environment. In these workloads, policy inference can be batched on GPUs, but the CPU-side environment path still updates entity states, resolves local interactions, and builds observations inside each $\mathrm{env.step}$. This path can dominate latency in interaction-intensive workloads after policy batching. Existing vectorized environment interfaces and general event-driven runtimes do not directly address the fine-grained cross-entity work inside one bounded MARL step while preserving the step-level semantics expected by learning systems. We present SEER (Scalable Event-Driven Environment Runtime), a runtime for MARL environment execution under an explicit event-locality contract. SEER models each environment step as a bounded stream of timestamped events. If direct state updates are entity-local and cross-entity effects are represented as ordered future events, SEER can run independent events in parallel while preserving serial-equivalent boundary outputs. To make this contract practical, SEER uses a CAS-based dual-layer event queue: local event queues preserve per-entity causal order, while a parallel executive list exposes ready work to global worker threads. SEER further uses STPA, a preflight-guided thread-pool selection mechanism that combines short runtime traces with static workload and hardware features. We evaluate SEER on two parameterized MARL workloads: compute-intensive UAV swarm control (Aircraft) and communication-intensive wireless management (PCS). On Aircraft, SEER reduces inference latency by 16.2\% over the baseline. On PCS, SEER reduces environment-execution latency by 46.9\%, 19.5\%, and 64.9\% over ROSS-T, NBSE, and ROOT-Sim, respectively.</summary>

    <title>A Bilevel Neurodynamic Approach for Distributed SCAD-Regularized Sparse Least Squares</title>
    <updated>2026-11-05T08:01:08Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07618v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.07618v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>This paper proposes a bilevel particle swarm optimization (PSO)-neurodynamic method for solving the distributed sparse least-squares problem regularized by the smoothly clipped absolute deviation (SCAD) penalty to global optimality. The SCAD penalty is nonsmooth and nonconvex, so existing distributed neurodynamic methods have not been extended to it directly. Through two-time-scale singular perturbation analysis, a rigorous full-trajectory convergence theory with explicit convergence rates is established for the inner collaborative multi-agent neurodynamic system without requiring the second-order sufficient condition. A theory-guided inner-outer collaborative optimization framework is further developed, in which a red-light green-light sensitivity mechanism is embedded in the outer PSO search to enhance global search while concentrating computational effort on the SCAD shape parameters, thereby improving recovery accuracy and computational efficiency. Simulation results on four sparse-recovery scenarios demonstrate that the proposed method accurately recovers the true sparsity pattern and achieves faster convergence and lower relative error than competing neurodynamic methods.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18693v1</id>
    <title>Swarm Shepherd: Securing Multi-Agent Ecosystems Against Persistent Latent Compromise</title>
    <updated>2026-11-04T21:37:57Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18693v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.18693v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Agentic ecosystems are emerging as a new platform layer in which agents maintain persistent memory, retrieve from shared knowledge bases, execute through tool interfaces, and coordinate through shared states. These capabilities create a security problem that per-turn defenses miss: compromise can accumulate across sessions, agents, and system layers before visible failure. We define this threat as Agentic Sleeper, a system-level adversary that first behaves legitimately, gains routing trust, and later activates across memory, agent logic, and infrastructure. We formulate defense as inference under partial observability and propose Swarm Shepherd, a system-level defense framework centered on an inference filter for early warning, paired with a backward trace-back module for entry attribution. Our analysis yields a two-scale deployment rule that balances longer event histories against broader agent coverage. Across LangGraph, CrewAI, and AutoGen, Agentic Sleeper drift begins 2.7--8.9$\times$ faster than natural baselines, propagates across agents on most topologies, and evades per-turn and stateful defenses above 80\%. Swarm Shepherd warns at least three sessions before visible degradation (2.6 sessions when failure is scored by the benchmark's own task grader), while trace-back reaches 0.69 top-1 accuracy and 0.72 macro-F1 over 24 variants. The two-scale deployment rule is empirically confirmed, and in live end-to-end runs on LangGraph and AutoGen the posterior-guided defense stack drives cross-agent propagation below the self-sustaining regime, which removing only the visibly compromised agent does not achieve.</summary>

    <title>AttriSwarm: Orchestrating Agent Swarms for Cross-Page Visual Attribution</title>
    <updated>2026-11-03T08:31:44Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.04504v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.04504v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) increasingly address knowledge-intensive tasks by integrating evidence scattered across multiple document pages into a final answer. Because such answers are synthesized from many pages, the link between the answer and its supporting visual evidence can become obscured, hindering verification and trust. Cross-page visual attribution is therefore essential: it requires identifying the supporting pages and localizing fine-grained evidence regions within them, thereby making multi-page reasoning transparent and auditable. Existing approaches either process multiple pages jointly or iteratively refine evidence within a single trajectory, risking cross-page context pollution and, for interactive methods, substantial sequential overhead. We introduce \textbf{AttriSwarm}, an agent-swarm framework that assigns these concerns to separate roles: a leader handles global cross-page reasoning, while subagents perform page-wise attribution in isolation and in parallel. To support training and evaluation, we construct \textbf{AttriDoc}, a cross-page QA dataset linking supporting pages to their annotated evidence regions, and use it for role-specific training of AttriSwarm, improving answer accuracy, page-level $F_1$, and region-level IoU over its training-free counterpart by an average of 18.94, 29.34, and 23.04 percentage points, respectively, across three open-source backbones and three datasets.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27751v1</id>
    <title>Budgeted Subset Selection with a Transferable Learned Value Model</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T15:42:07Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27751v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27751v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Subset selection is a fundamental task in machine learning, statistics and combinatorial optimisation, with applications in active learning, band selection, input selection and experimental design. The utility of a subset depends on information revealed only after the selection, such as labels or responses, and on interactions among selected candidates. Existing approaches combine value estimation and redundancy control in application-specific ways, which limits their use in other domains. This paper introduces Subset Acquisition with Learned Value Estimates and Search (SALVES), a framework that decomposes subset selection into two components. First, a value model is trained by supervised learning on tasks where the hidden information is known. On a new task, it predicts the utility each candidate would add to the current selection. Second, a selection step chooses the subset from these predictions, typically by simulated annealing with a diversity term penalising redundancy. The value model transfers to new classes, pretrained networks, datasets and sensors, and from synthetic to real data. On the four applications, SALVES matches or outperforms application-specific baselines on average. It requires substantially fewer bands for equal accuracy and remains reliable in input selection where individual baselines fail.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27656v1</id>
    <title>Beyond Sample Hardness: Adaptive Data Selection through Learning Dynamics</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T14:21:10Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27656v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27656v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Data selection has emerged as an effective approach to reducing the model training costs. However, most existing methods often rely heavily on sample hardness, which may overlook differences in sample learning dynamics and lead to suboptimal sample selection. In this paper, we propose LeDAS, an end-to-end Learning Dynamics-Aware Selection framework for dynamic data selection, which jointly characterizes sample importance through hardness, learning progress, and deterioration, enabling adaptive sample prioritization throughout training with marginal additional computational overhead. Specifically, we track per-sample loss dynamics using exponential moving averages (EMA) to obtain three complementary signals that capture current learning difficulty, ongoing learning improvements, and potential degradation. To accommodate evolving training dynamics, we introduce Adaptive Metric Fusion, a contextual bandit-based mechanism that dynamically adjusts the relative importance of these signals based on training feedback. Furthermore, a bounded staleness compensation mechanism accounts for historical selection patterns by increasing the selection priority of samples that have not been selected for extended periods. Extensive experiments across diverse vision and language tasks demonstrate the effectiveness and generality of LeDAS. Compared with state-of-the-art baselines, LeDAS consistently achieves superior performance, matching or surpassing full-dataset training at a 50\% selection ratio on ImageNet-1K and in LLM supervised fine-tuning. Moreover, its modular and task-agnostic design enables the integration of complementary selection signals, demonstrating strong robustness to noisy and corrupted datasets.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27492v1</id>
    <title>Learning Unknown Oscillators From Bandit Feedback</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T11:37:16Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27492v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27492v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We study semi-bandits driven by unknown oscillators. Each round, a learner selects two of four reward channels and observes their individual rewards. Frequency errors change future reward rankings and the resulting measurements. We show when committing to one fitted oscillator lets its greedy choices expose prediction errors. Our controller bounds reward loss (regret) over a continuous confidence set and holds the longest block within budget. An online regression policy gathers observations when the check fails. Regret grows at a square-root rate, up to logarithmic factors, across all frequencies and extends to two competing oscillators. On 96 fresh synthetic instances, checked commitment uses 49 fits instead of 1,023, with 1.5% higher mean regret than fitting every round. Matched isolated timings give a 4.69-fold speedup. The confidence sets also certify trajectory regret.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27436v1</id>
    <title>THRIFTY: Cost-Constrained Reasoning-Data Synthesis for Small Language Models</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T10:32:38Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27436v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27436v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Small language models (SLMs) are increasingly attractive for efficient, specialized deployment, and are typically trained on reasoning trajectories distilled from a larger teacher LLM. Generating this synthetic data is a major cost of the pipeline, especially when the teacher is a frontier model. Existing collection methods, however, are largely cost-unaware, or at best spread a fixed sampling budget uniformly across queries. Such allocation ignores the wide variation in problem difficulty and the strategic over- or under-sampling it invites. Thus, we propose THRIFTY, a Thompson-sampling bandit controller that spends a fixed generation-token budget to collect diverse correct reasoning trajectories, casting the task as a bandits-with-knapsacks problem with a novel diversity-aware objective. It tracks each problem's success probability with an online Beta posterior and spends each token where it expects the most new distinct correct solutions. Because repeated solutions add progressively less value, THRIFTY adaptively stops resampling saturated problems, concentrates budget on under-covered ones, and retires the unsolvable at the budget's opportunity cost. On math (AIME, MATH-500) and code (LiveCodeBench) benchmarks, THRIFTY gathers up to 22% more diverse correct trajectories per generation token than both the standard uniform-sampling recipe and the strongest adaptive baseline, with the largest gains in the scarce-budget and hard-problem regimes.</summary>

    <title>Quantum computing for gearing down complex many-fermion problems</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T10:10:07Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27402v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27402v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Quantum computing unlocks exciting opportunities to extend first-principles calculations of quantum many-body systems beyond classical computing limits. Despite advances in algorithms and proof-of-principle experiments, large-scale {\it ab initio} calculations on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices remain challenging. We introduce a quantum-classical framework that identifies compact single-particle bases to bring otherwise intractable many-fermion problems within classical reach while preserving an accurate ground-state description. We develop an efficient adaptive search scheme driven by simulated annealing that jointly optimizes natural-orbital-guided transformations and active-space selections. A quantum-assisted ground-state estimator provides search guidance using low-depth circuits and relaxed accuracy requirements, making the framework promising for NISQ devices. We demonstrate the framework's applicability for the nuclear structure of the oxygen isotopes. Our framework opens a new route to tackling complex {\it ab initio} many-fermion problems across disciplines through quantum-assisted basis reduction.</summary>

    <title>A Matter of Representation: Evolving Partial Spreads for Bent Functions</title>
    <updated>2026-11-19T12:29:34Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26011v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>

    <summary>Partial spread ($\mathcal{PS}$) bent functions are Boolean functions of maximum nonlinearity built from families of subspaces that pairwise intersect only in the null vector. We design an Evolution Strategy (ES) to construct such partial spread families, comparing two encodings: one based on generator matrices of the subspaces, and one based on spread sets. With the latter, combined with a ruin-and-rebuild operator, the ES finds $\mathcal{PS}$ functions up to $n=10$ variables. An ablation study shows that mutation is necessary, while the population size is not, and that a restarted look-ahead greedy heuristic outperforms the ES on the hardest instance. We investigate this finding with a landscape analysis of the stagnation points, and we also introduce a quality-diversity variant of the ES which finds $\mathcal{PS}$ functions of low algebraic degree for 8 variables. Interestingly, the bent functions evolved by the ES have higher 2-ranks and mostly higher degrees than those obtained by a baseline Genetic Programming optimizer.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.25625v1</id>
    <title>QUBO-based feature selection for MRI undersampling pattern design</title>
    <updated>2026-11-19T07:10:59Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.25625v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.25625v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We formulate undersampling mask design for Cartesian magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) as a feature subset selection problem. Each sampling line is represented by a binary feature indicating whether it is included in each candidate mask. Using candidate masks and their training-set evaluations, we estimate mutual information (MI) and conditional mutual information (CMI). These estimates and a sampling-count penalty define a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) model. The model is solved using simulated annealing and quantum annealing to determine a feature subset and its corresponding sampling mask. We assess the selected subsets on the test set through zero-filled reconstruction in Fourier undersampling simulations using fastMRI knee magnitude reference images, with patient-disjoint training and test sets. At all six tested target sampling rates from 15% to 40%, the resulting reconstructions have lower mean root mean square error than those obtained with four conventional sampling methods. They also have higher mean structural similarity than those obtained using univariate mutual-information ranking at all tested rates. These results support information-theoretic feature selection as an approach to MRI undersampling mask design under the tested zero-filled simulation settings.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.25424v1</id>
    <title>Coordinate Basis Linear Bandits with Sublinear Regret over Low-Rank Clusters</title>
    <updated>2026-11-19T03:03:52Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.25424v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.25424v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We study the problem of computational efficiency for linear bandits in high-dimensional settings with a finite arm set. In linear bandits, the increase in the dimension $d$ of the feature vectors leads to growing computational costs of $O(d^2)$ at each round of update. Traditional low-rank approximation methods such as SOFUL reduce computation via fixed-size matrix sketching, yet run the risk of incurring vacuous linear regret when the spectral tail of the data is heavy and the approximation rank is inadequately selected. To guarantee regret convergence and effectively reduce computational costs, we introduce a clustering mechanism and propose the Coordinate Basis Linear Bandit (CBL) algorithm. Our method preserves the full covariance information in each cluster by maintaining an exact orthonormal basis of the cluster's column space together with a low-dimensional coordinate representation, which guarantees robust sublinear regret without spectral-tail vulnerabilities. It performs cluster switching by assigning a sentinel for each cluster, and reduces per-round update computation to $O(\bar r^2)$ in the cluster's effective dimension $\bar r=\min(r,l)$, where $r$ is the intrinsic rank of the data and $l<d$ is a tunable rank bound.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27601v1</id>
    <title>PromptTTSD: Controllable Text to Spoken Dialogue Synthesis with Open-Ended Text Descriptions</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T13:29:30Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27601v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27601v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Spoken dialogue synthesis aims to generate multi-turn conversational speech from dialogue scripts while maintaining speaker consistency and contextual appropriateness. However, existing models largely lack fine-grained controllability, which is critical for capturing the dynamic, context-dependent style shifts in natural conversations. While prompt-based TTS has enabled such control for single-speaker speech, existing datasets heavily rely on predefined tags, which fundamentally limits their capacity to capture open-ended styles. To address this gap, we propose a scalable pipeline for extracting conversational speech from multi-narrator audiobooks, featuring an improved two-stage alignment algorithm to preserve dialogue continuity, paired with LLM-based extraction of style descriptions directly from narrative text. We release PromptDialog, a large-scale multi-speaker conversational speech dataset comprising 8,383 hours of Chinese speech and 120 hours of English speech, with open-ended style descriptions for 79% of utterances. We further introduce PromptTTSD, a spoken dialogue synthesis model built via a prompt-aware fine-tuning strategy that integrates style prompts into text-speech interleaved sequences. PromptTTSD is an open-source spoken dialogue synthesis model that supports both zero-shot voice cloning and natural language style control. Experiments demonstrate that PromptTTSD not only maintains strong fundamental synthesis capabilities but also achieves competitive open-ended style control compared with proprietary models, and substantially improves contextual appropriateness in multi-turn dialogues.</summary>

    <title>PathOPEN: A pathologist-curated histopathology dataset for visual question answering</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T11:19:44Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27469v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27469v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>PathOPEN is a histopathology dataset for visual question answering. Two clinical pathologists selected 157 cases with 229 available original images and wrote open-ended, five-option multiple-choice and close-ended (yes/no) questions. They supplied both a correct and a wrong answer for 201 of the 309 open-ended questions. Each case records the organ, pathology category and regional anatomy, and each image records its magnification. The dataset includes 6,870 augmented images and four manifests that select subsets to improve balance by individual metadata field. Five additional pathologists and two vision-language model judges rated items with scoring rubrics, and six models answered questions zero-shot across the three formats. The metadata support subgroup evaluation, and the paired answers can be used to construct preference examples.</summary>

    <title>WePM: Hierarchical Conflict Reconciliation for Unified MLLMs</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T09:34:56Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27365v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27365v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Bringing multimodal intelligence from the cloud to users' devices keeps sensitive data local and reduces inference cost, but deploying a specialized model per capability duplicates vision-language capacity under tight memory and compute budgets. We formalize heterogeneous capability density (HCD), measuring how broadly and effectively a model serves heterogeneous task families per unit of resident inference memory. High HCD across representation, generation, and decision raises two challenges: these capabilities need visual evidence at different spatial granularities under a fixed token budget, and separately collected task corpora yield conflicting updates to shared parameters, while cross-task paired supervision is costly and ambiguous for open-ended inputs. We present WePM, a family of pocket models unifying representation, generation, and decision within one vision-language backbone. Multi-Granularity Visual Budgeting (MGVB) allocates a fixed visual-token budget across global, regional, and fine-grained banks; Unified Listwise Knowledge Distillation (ULKD) enriches separately collected data with soft teacher guidance, avoiding cross-task paired annotation; Stable and Efficient Multitask Optimization (SEMO) regulates each task's contribution through explicit loss weights and exposure schedules, with sequential gradient accumulation under memory constraints. In the joint representation-generation setting, WePM outperforms all baselines across five evaluation groups, raising the Joint score from 38.15 to 52.74. In single-task evaluation, WePM-4B attains the best average score over 30 embedding, 39 generation, and seven typed-decision benchmarks (72.86, 62.41, 61.11). Against the separate-model stack with the highest HCD, WePM achieves slightly higher balanced performance with 61.9% less resident weight memory, a 2.64-fold higher HCD.</summary>

    <title>H-MSAE: Hierarchical Sparse Concept Coverage for Efficient and Diverse Instruction Data Selection</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T09:08:19Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27329v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27329v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Large instruction-tuning corpora contain substantial semantic redundancy, motivating the selection of compact subsets that preserve useful supervision while reducing training cost. Existing diversity-aware selectors often rely on generated semantic tags and explicit graph structures, introducing considerable annotation and preprocessing overhead. We introduce H-MSAE, a hierarchical sparse instruction selection framework that organizes multi-resolution concepts learned by a Matryoshka sparse autoencoder into a coarse-to-fine hierarchy. Quality-weighted, diminishing-return coverage with ancestor propagation promotes high-quality and non-redundant semantic coverage, while pool-relative length constraints regulate subset composition. We motivate this design through a local quality-diversity analysis of subset SFT utility and examine it using example-quality and representation-space diversity diagnostics. On Tulu 3 data pool, H-MSAE achieves the highest Final Avg among the evaluated 50K selectors across scales and initialization. The selected subset also exhibits the highest mean quality and effective rank among the evaluated methods. By avoiding full-pool generative tagging and supporting efficient sparse selection, H-MSAE reduces measured end-to-end runtime by approximately $5\times$ relative to MIG.</summary>

    <title>Scalable Evaluation of Medical AI using Evidence-based Practice Recommendations</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T02:36:36Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27007v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27007v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Rigorously evaluating medical artificial intelligence (AI) requires testing open-ended clinical management across diverse presentations and stages of care. However, existing benchmarks rely on manual expert authoring, limiting coverage across conditions, conditional care pathways, and evolving guidelines. We develop an automated pipeline that extracts and verifies structured clinical criteria and branching decision trees from practice recommendations to generate scenarios spanning the care continuum, including nuanced presentations and practice variations across regions and guideline editions. Applied to 436 BMJ Best Practice clinical monographs (354 US, 82 International), this yields 3,200 scenarios spanning differential diagnosis, investigations, treatment, and complications, plus targeted suites for regional specificity (731 US/International pairs) and temporal freshness (630 scenarios). To grade responses, we develop a clinician-calibrated autorater that scores management plans on a 4-point rubric stratifying deviations by clinical severity. Across Gemini models, scaling improves adherence, while web search (+0.8 percentage points [pp] on average) and multi-sample synthesis (+2.2 pp) combine additively (+2.8 pp). In context, full monographs consistently trail condensed excerpts. On targeted suites, web search narrows international performance gaps (+4.2 pp) and improves adherence to newly updated guidance (+4.6 pp). In a study with Primary Care Physicians (n = 9) across 200 scenarios, AI assistance raises adherence from 50.5% to 70.0%, driven largely by fewer clinical omissions. Overall, our results demonstrate a scalable evaluation setup using an evidence-based corpus originally written to guide human clinical decision-making, and demonstrate its viability to assess medical AI and its assistance on clinician decision-making.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26954v1</id>
    <title>Learning Video Foresight Reasoning from Unlabeled Videos via On-Policy Self-Distillation</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T01:08:12Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26954v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.26954v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Video foresight reasoning requires vision-language models to anticipate future events or next actions from currently observed videos. Existing methods fit future captions, rationales, or full visual states, but face two limitations. First, they rely on annotations or external large models for supervision, limiting scalability. We address this with an on-policy self-distillation framework that turns past-future video pairs into a natural self-supervised signal without extra annotations or LLM supervision. Second, they treat the whole future clip as equally valuable, although most of it is irrelevant context information. We address this by defining a foresight score, from which we obtain a contrastive privilege advantage that drives the model to learn the most valuable future information. Since the score is intractable, we optimize a tractable lower-bound surrogate that interpolates this advantage, computed between the true and a random reference future, with a teacher-student distillation advantage; together, they amplify decision-relevant content information and suppress irrelevant context information. We call the resulting framework Future-OPSD. On open-ended prediction and closed-ended planning, Future-OPSD improves base models by up to 14.2 and 15.9 points without compromising general video understanding. Code will be available at https://jingchensun.github.io/future-opsd/</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26881v1</id>
    <title>Your Judge Inherits Your Prompt: In-Context Label Bias in an LLM-as-Judge Is Directional, Not Symmetric</title>
    <updated>2026-11-19T22:48:23Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26881v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.26881v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>LLM-as-judge has become a standard way to score open-ended model outputs, yet the judge is itself a frozen language model steered by a few in-context examples, and such models are known to absorb the label balance of their demonstrations rather than treat them as neutral illustrations. We ask whether this label bias reaches an LLM judge used inside a multimodal (video question answering) evaluation pipeline, and what form it takes. Using a fully frozen generator-judge pipeline, we hold the generated answers fixed and vary only the Yes/No balance of the judge's few-shot examples across four demonstration sets. Each verdict is validated against a two-annotator human consensus on 200 examples per dataset. The judge's acceptance rate stays close to human consensus when its examples are balanced or skewed toward rejection, but jumps sharply (by about 30 points on NExT-QA and 20 on MSVD-QA, with a strongly one-sided error profile) when the examples are skewed toward acceptance; the opposite skew produces no matching drop. The bias is therefore one-directional within the tested range of label ratios. A separate five-draw analysis shows that results from a single example draw are unreliable, varying by up to 18 points, more than any difference between prompting conditions. We conclude that demonstration label bias in an LLM judge is a directional, inflation-only failure mode that can fabricate apparent benchmark gains but not losses, and that it is cheaply avoided by balancing the judge's examples and reporting results averaged over several draws.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26874v1</id>
    <title>How Language Models Compress and Compare: Understanding Selection with Token Covariance Maps</title>
    <updated>2026-11-19T22:39:02Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26874v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.26874v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Many language-model tasks reduce to selecting among structured alternatives, yet we still lack a simple picture of how a decoder-only transformer organizes an entire selection prompt across depth. We introduce token covariance maps, a prompt-level geometric view that tracks how token positions co-vary in hidden-state space at each layer. This turns a structured prompt into a depth-indexed sequence of maps whose spectral and block structure can be aligned with instructions, context, and candidate answers. Across 14 decoder-only models from 4 families and 12 structured-selection benchmarks, token covariance maps reveal a robust compress-then-compare organization. Early layers represent prompts diffusely, middle layers compress them into a shared low-rank bottleneck, and late layers re-expand into context-option and option-option geometry. This organization recurs across larger fixed-template samples, deterministic prompt rewrites, pairwise reranking reformulations, and controlled answer-set manipulations, while also emerging during training from an initially flat depth profile. Its timing aligns with behavior: useful answer discrimination appears well after the bottleneck, and low-rank intervention around the bottleneck preferentially disrupts late comparison geometry. We additionally show that the same geometric profile appears in instruction-tuned models, across several languages, and during open-ended generation. We further show that changing the internal representation of one candidate around the compressed region can shift which candidate the model later prefers. These results show that token covariance maps are a diagnostic tool for comparing how models organize information across prompts, model families, and stages of training.</summary>

    <title>SLICR: Strategy Logic-Guided Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T17:13:50Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27865v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27865v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Specification-guided reinforcement learning (RL) translates formal specifications of desired behavior of agents into shaped rewards. This paper introduces SLICR, a significant paradigm shift that advances the state of the art to specification-guided RL in adversarial settings under partial observability. We employ Strategy Logic (SL), which allows explicit quantification over agents' strategies and uses the linear temporal logic (LTL) to specify the agents' objectives and constraints. This enables reasoning not only about how agents should act to satisfy a specification, but also about how they should respond to the strategies and behaviors of other agents. We evaluate SLICR on three popular benchmarks: Predator-Prey, Google Research Football, and our home-grown extension of SMAC-HARD, demonstrating its effectiveness, scalability, and ability to adapt to diverse adversarial strategies.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27814v1</id>
    <title>Pushdown Reachability Requires $N^{3/2}$ Time on Multitape Turing Machines</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T16:41:49Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27814v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27814v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Pushdown reachability, or equivalently, language non-emptiness of pushdown automata (PDA), is a fundamental problem in automata theory and program analysis. We show that, for every $ε>0$, no deterministic multitape Turing machine can decide pushdown reachability in $O(N^{\frac{3}{2}-ε})$ time, where $N$ is the input size. The lower bound already holds for \emph{sparse instances}, i.e., instances in which the number of transitions is linear in the number of states. This gives the first unconditional super-linear lower bound for pushdown reachability. Furthermore, we also extend this result and show that for any $ε> 0$ and $k \ge 1$, no deterministic multitape Turing machine can decide the intersection non-emptiness problem of one PDA and $k-1$ NFAs in time $O(N^{\frac{3k}{2}-ε})$, where $N$ is the input size.
  Finally, pushdown reachability is well-known to be quasi-linear time equivalent to many different problems in program analysis. Our result translates to all of those problems as well and provides the first unconditional super-linear lower bounds for those problems on multitape Turing machines.</summary>

    <title>Can Vision-Language Models Synthesize Executable Game-Playing Programs?</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T15:36:12Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27741v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27741v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Recent advances in vision-language models (VLMs) have endowed multimodal agents with increasingly strong visual perception and long-horizon reasoning capabilities, making VLM-based autonomous game playing feasible. Existing game benchmarks primarily evaluate whether an agent can select appropriate actions from the current visual state across different scenarios and games. However, most of them adopt a step-by-step interaction paradigm where the current visual observation is sent to the agent before each action. In practical deployment, this paradigm introduces two fundamental limitations: the game loop must wait for model inference, making real-time interaction impractical, and repeated VLM calls incur substantial cost. Therefore, we propose PlayScriptBench, a script-based game benchmark that evaluates whether VLMs can synthesize an executable game-playing program from game states. This setting jointly evaluates visual grounding, understanding of game dynamics, long-horizon strategic reasoning, and executable program synthesis, providing a more comprehensive assessment of game-playing agents. To support more tractable evaluation for current general-purpose VLMs, we further introduce a four-stage pipeline --- Explore, Perception, API Construction, and Strategy Composition --- that decomposes controller synthesis into game exploration, state perception, interface construction, and strategic control, enabling agents to progressively construct an executable program. Experiments on 16 games spanning 4 genres show that even strong VLMs struggle on our benchmark, revealing a substantial gap between passive visual game understanding and executable closed-loop game control. These results establish script-based controller synthesis as a complementary direction for benchmarking VLM-based game-playing agents.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27489v1</id>
    <title>Efficient Natural Language to Temporal Logic Translation for Real-Time Physical AI</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T11:35:56Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27489v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27489v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Robots can be controlled to perform tasks with guaranteed correctness when the task instructions are stated in a formal language. Large language models (LLMs) have been widely used to allow users to provide such instructions in natural language (NL), by translating NL into formal language. When deploying such translators on a robot, however, we face limited computing and energy resources, while offloading computation or data to the cloud may be infeasible or undesirable. Yet an LLM is a general-purpose text generator, whereas a formula in a fixed formal language fragment follows a well-defined syntax. We therefore ask whether text generation is needed at all. For the formal language of linear temporal logic (LTL), we show that this translation can instead be broken down into answering a set of questions with pre-defined answers. We then construct a System-One model, a recent class of NL-based classifier, to provide such answers and enable us to translate a natural language instruction into an LTL instruction. On three benchmarks, our translator matches or exceeds the accuracy of the best local LLMs available, at up to one order of magnitude lower runtime and energy consumption. We show that it generalizes to unseen atomic propositions and temporal patterns.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27461v1</id>
    <title>Bounded Treewidth Rulesets Are Not Finitely Controllable</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T11:10:28Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27461v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27461v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>An ontology language $O$ is finitely controllable with respect to a query language $Q$ if the finite and unrestricted variants of the query entailment problem for $\langle O, Q\rangle$ coincide. In this paper, we study finite controllability (FC) in its classical sense for existential rules, where $O$ is a class of existential rules and $Q$ is the class of all Boolean conjunctive queries (BCQs).
  A natural question in this line of work is whether the class of bounded treewidth sets (BTS) is finitely controllable with respect to BCQs. We answer this question negatively: we exhibit a simple set of rules over a binary signature and prove that it is BTS but not FC. Moreover, using the same set of rules, we show that two subclasses of BTS, namely GBTS and pieceful, are not FC either.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27260v1</id>
    <title>No Perfect Guardrail & No Perfect Guard: On the Decidability of Output Policies for Large Language Models</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T08:01:29Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27260v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27260v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Expecting guardrails to provide a general guarantee of safety fails to recognize the limits of computational enforcement and policy specification. We argue that promising such perfection is an ethical failure of precision, and that invoking it to abdicate responsibility is a moral failure. Guardrails can support responsible action, but cannot relieve researchers, developers, policymakers, or users of their obligations to examine what they claim, permit, and prevent.
  We establish a precise computational boundary. If every finite string is a possible output of a language model, a computable guard that blocks every forbidden output and passes every permitted one exists if and only if the policy is decidable. For an undecidable policy, every guard misclassifies infinitely many strings, and every guard that blocks all forbidden outputs excludes infinitely many permitted ones. We apply this characterization to arithmetic truth, program behavior, and harmful instructions to an idealized recipient. We distinguish guards from execution monitors, identify bounded and interceptable cases admitting exact enforcement, and explain why the results establish no positive lower bound on average error.
  Exact enforcement does not establish that a policy adequately captures safety. Conservative exclusion may withhold warnings, remedies, or challenges needed to recognize the policy's own defects. Human oversight cannot substitute for judgment: an apparent controller can become an instrument of purposes they have ceased to examine. Responsible governance requires continued critical challenge and the intellectual and moral humility to recognize possible flaws in our machines, rules, policies, and ourselves. The impossibility of a general assurance of perfection is a condition responsible practice must confront, not a responsibility that another guardrail - or another guard - can remove.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27001v1</id>
    <title>Moonshine Conjecture Formalized</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T02:31:15Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27001v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27001v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>The celebrated and intimidating Moonshine Conjecture has now been formalized in Lean. This achievement might suggest that, once a sufficiently large library compiles, the principal mathematical work is complete. This paper tells a less optimistic story.
  During our formalization project, we repeatedly encountered two problems that a formally checked proof alone does not settle: (1) whether the formal statements actually express the mathematics we humans expect, and (2) how that meaning survives as the repositories and their dependencies evolve.
  We argue that there is no magic pill that turns a large agent-produced library into mathematics a community can trust. Even after the proofs are checked by the Lean kernel, someone must judge whether the definitions and statements express the intended mathematics and whether future updates preserve that meaning. This work, even when done, can only be trusted. We must therefore return to the usual trust model: relying on the mathematical judgment of maintainers and expert communities.
  But semantic review is expensive, making it tempting to keep producing code and take successful kernel checks as sufficient grounds for trust. This shortcut accumulates semantic debt: definitions and results with unchecked mathematical interpretations are reused as foundations for further work. A library may keep compiling and produce the desired formal theorem while users lose track of which mathematical claims they can responsibly rely on.
  Reliable reuse is also a prerequisite for Terence Tao's vision of formal mathematics as something people can navigate, explain, learn from, and build with. This paper takes our work connecting the VOA and CFSG repositories for the Moonshine Conjecture as a case study of the challenges of reliable reuse as formal developments scale.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26906v1</id>
    <title>Budget-Aware Predict-and-Verify Theorem Proving with Heterogeneous LLM Solvers</title>
    <updated>2026-11-19T23:43:38Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26906v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.26906v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Large language model (LLM) theorem solvers differ in both proving capability and inference cost. Applying an expensive solver to every subgoal wastes computation when cheaper models are sufficient, while always starting from the cheapest solver wastes attempts on subgoals that require stronger models. We present BudgetPV, an agentic budget-aware predict-and-verify system that allocates computation across unresolved subgoals and heterogeneous LLM solvers. BudgetPV uses a cross-solver predictor to guide solver selection for each subgoal and revises the allocation as verification feedback becomes available.
  The allocation problem changes as proving progresses. Early decisions mainly determine which solver should handle an untried subgoal, while later decisions determine which previously attempted subgoals should receive additional computation. We train the predictor with two objectives for these two stages. Class-weighted cross-entropy improves assignment to less frequent stronger solvers during the initial stage, while plain cross-entropy provides better calibrated probabilities for later allocation among previously attempted subgoals.
  We evaluate BudgetPV on Lean Workbook, miniF2F, ProofNet, and PutnamBench using three progressively expanded solver settings: a strong but expensive solver alone, adding a medium-cost solver with intermediate solving capability, and further adding a cheap solver with lower solving capability. BudgetPV requires less LLM generation computation than uniform allocation to solve the same number of subgoals across the evaluated settings. The experiments further show the computation savings obtained as medium- and lower-cost solvers are added.</summary>
