    <title>Multiplicative Sidon basis</title>
    <updated>2026-11-19T18:24:14Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26555v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.26555v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>For a $h \ge 2$ integer a sequence of positive integers $A$ is called asymptotic basis of order $h$ if every sufficiently large positive integer $n$ can be written as a sum of $h$ elements of $A$. We say a sequence of positive integers $A$ is a multiplicative Sidon sequence if all the products of two elements of the sequence $A$ are distinct. In this paper we prove the existence of a multiplicative Sidon set which is an asymptotic basis of order 2 by using the probabilistic method.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.25159v1</id>
    <title>Self-adjoint skew quartics, symplectic monodromy, and zeta functions</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T20:36:59Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.25159v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.25159v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>For an odd prime power $P$, let $A_H(P)$ be the number of $a\in\F_{P^H}$ for which the self-adjoint skew quartic $t^4+t^3+at^2+t+1$ is irreducible in $\F_{P^H}[t;σ]$, with $σ(c)=c^P$. We determine $A_H(3)$ for every $H\ge1$ and prove that its minimal constant-coefficient recurrence has order $24$. Local ramification gives the degrees of the Steinberg and regular cuspidal Frobenius polynomials. Duality and finitely many exact counts determine both polynomials.
  For $P=p^f$ with $p\nmid f$, we construct an explicit genus-$P(P+1)/2$ flag curve whose zeta numerator is the Steinberg Frobenius polynomial. At $P=3$ this identifies the degree-$12$ factor computed above with the zeta numerator of a genus-$6$ curve. For general $P$ the flag curve and the regular cuspidal factors give a rational expression for the counting series. We evaluate the linear coefficients of the two factors by an elliptic-curve point count and express their quadratic coefficients through a single finite-field character sum.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.25050v1</id>
    <title>On the Erdős--Ginzburg--Ziv problem for $\mathbb Z_n^3$</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T19:01:37Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.25050v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.25050v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>The Erdős--Ginzburg--Ziv constant $\mathsf s(\mathbb Z_n^r)$ is the least positive integer $t$ such that every sequence of $t$ elements of $\mathbb Z_n^r$ contains $n$ terms whose sum is zero. In this paper, we prove that $$\mathsf s(\mathbb Z_n^3)=9n+o(n)$$ for odd $n$. For every fixed $r\ge 4$, we also show that $\mathsf s(\mathbb Z_n^r)\le\bigl(\binom{2r-1}{r}+1\bigr)n+o_r(n).$ Our approach combines Alon--Dubiner-type spectral expansion, Zakharov's convex-geometric framework, and restricted-sum ideas developed by Han and Ren.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24847v1</id>
    <title>Two almost sure upper bounds for sums of random multiplicative functions</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T18:08:35Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24847v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24847v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Let $f,g$ be a squarefree and extended Rademacher random multiplicative functions, respectively. We prove that, for every $\varepsilon>0$, almost surely
  $$\big|\sum_{n \le x}\frac{f(n)}{\sqrt{n}}\big| \ll (\log\log x)^{1/4+\varepsilon}, \qquad \big|\sum_{n\le x}g(n)\big|\ll\sqrt{x}(\log\log x)^{1/4+\varepsilon}.$$
  We also show that almost surely, there exist arbitrarily large values of $x$ such that $\sum_{n \le x}\frac{f(n)}{\sqrt{n}} \gg (\log\log x)^{1/4+o(1)}$. We follow Caich and Durkan and Pearce-Crump by using a version of the Azuma--Hoeffding inequality for martingale difference sequences.</summary>
    <category term="math.NT" scheme="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom"/>
    <category term="math.PR" scheme="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom"/>

    <title>A disproof of the van Emde Boas--Kruyswijk conjecture on the Davenport constant</title>
    <updated>2026-11-19T14:22:50Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24775v2" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24775v2" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>The Davenport constant $D(G)$ of a finite abelian group $G$ is the smallest positive integer $\ell$ such that every sequence $S$ with terms from $G$ and with length $|S| \ge \ell$ has a nontrivial zero-sum subsequence. A long-standing conjecture, first proposed by van Emde Boas and Kruyswijk in 1969, states that $D(C_n^r)=r(n-1)+1$ for all positive integers $n$ and $r$. We disprove this conjecture for every exponent $n=2k$ with $k\ge3$ odd. For each such $n$, we prove that $D(C_n^r)>r(n-1)+1$ for every $r\ge 8n-7$.</summary>

    <summary>Let $G$ be a finite abelian group, and let $\mathsf{T}(G)$ be the smallest integer $t$ such that every sequence of length $t$ over $G$ contains a nonempty zero-sum subsequence of cross number $1$. We determine the exact value of $\mathsf{T}(C_n)$ for every positive integer $n$, showing that $\mathsf{T}(C_n)=2n-1$ when $n$ is odd and $\mathsf{T}(C_n)=3n/2-1$ when $n$ is even. In particular, $\mathsf{T}(C_n)=\mathsf{s}(C_n)$ for odd $n$.</summary>

    <updated>2026-11-17T04:51:33Z</updated>

    <summary>For a $p$-torsionfree $p$-quasisyntomic ring, we construct a fiber sequence relating the $p$-th Nygaard graded piece of absolute prismatic cohomology to the Frobenius--Witt cotangent complex. We also clarify the relationship between the regularity criterion proved by Mao using the Frobenius--Witt cotangent complex and the regularity criterion established by Bhatt and Mathew using the Nygaard graded piece. This relationship was anticipated by Bhatt and Mathew.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27368v1</id>
    <title>Testing for Coordination Failures in Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T09:39:32Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27368v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27368v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Deep parallel cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (CMARL)} trains multiple agents that all act at every time step to optimize a common objective. Like single-agent RL, CMARL can produce unsafe behaviors that violate implicit safety requirements not captured by the reward, and these behaviors are hard to explain. However, testing CMARL policies for safety has received less attention than the safety testing of single-agent RL policies. In this paper, we propose DisQ, a test case selection method that identifies failure-revealing states in value-based CMARL by exploiting a signal specific to trained Q-learning agents. The signal is the Q-value gap, an explainable metric that flags a state when the agents' estimates of the achievable return diverge by more than a calibrated threshold. DisQ selects such states for execution and skips those without a gap. Our experiments in four CMARL benchmark environments show that, in most of the evaluated configurations, DisQ improves failure detection over single-agent RL testing methods applied to CMARL, namely random testing and search-based testing with genetic algorithms. Our main contributions are the Q-value gap, an indicator of potential miscoordination computable from a single state without executing the system, and DisQ, a test case selection method that adapts existing single-agent testing methods to CMARL.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.25404v1</id>
    <title>Toward a Science of AI Agent Societies</title>
    <updated>2026-11-19T02:47:44Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.25404v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.25404v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>AI agents are rapidly evolving from isolated personal assistants into networked actors that interact with one another at scale. We envision the emergence of AI agent societies, with their own social and economic dynamics, as a new research frontier. We argue that AI agent societies should be studied as a distinct object of inquiry: neither simply larger collections of individual agents nor merely simulations of human society. To formalize this perspective, we propose four core properties that a valid AI agent society should satisfy: individualized objectives, rules and governance, autonomy, and scale and complexity. Building on this framework, we identify four classes of societal behaviors worth studying in AI agent societies: economic behaviors, behaviors under conflict-of-interest, unsafe and unethical behaviors, and system-level behaviors. We then outline key technical challenges--including property parameterization, parameter balancing, and robust implementation--and argue that progress on these challenges could enable scientifically informative and practically useful models of AI agent societies. Finally, we revisit existing multi-agent systems through the lens of the proposed core properties, show that they instantiate only subsets of them, and discuss implications for platform design, evaluation, and governance.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24290v1</id>
    <title>Beyond Corpus-Driven Imitation: Evolving Musical Mindsets in the Agentic Orchestra via Quantum Reinforcement Learning</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T12:03:57Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24290v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24290v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>This paper presents a framework for computer-aided music composition and performance based on quantum reinforcement learning and multi-agent interaction. We introduce the agentic orchestra, where musical agents evolve distinct mindsets through trial-and-error engagement with a musical environment, rather than through training on large datasets. The agents are implemented as parameterised quantum circuits. They evolve distinct compositional behaviours, referred to as mindsets. This enables the exploration of musical decision spaces using quantum superposition and entanglement within a hybrid quantum-classical loop. We present two complementary agent architectures: atomistic agents, which process pitch and rhythm independently, and holistic agents, which handle pitch and duration as unified note events. Mindsets are shaped through musically grounded reward functions, which can be combined and weighted to develop different mindsets across agents. The resulting system positions quantum computing agents less as autonomous composers and more as adaptive musical partners, each developing its own musical personality through interaction rather than imitation. Demonstrations show how agents generalise their learned behaviour to previously unseen material, operating in interactive and offline batch modes using MIDI-encoded music. While quantum computers are still in development, experiments conducted on IBM quantum hardware confirmed that musically meaningful learning is achievable with existing quantum computers. For composers and performers, the agentic orchestra opens new possibilities for emergent, process-oriented musical creativity, offering a scalable foundation for quantum computer-aided music composition as quantum computing technology continues to advance.</summary>

    <title>Macro Control and Capability Evaluation of Black-Box World Models: A Two-Regime Framework for LLM-Agent Markets</title>
    <updated>2026-11-14T10:12:22Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19311v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.19311v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Large language model (LLM) agents can be organized into multi-agent markets that act as world models, mapping macro information to emergent macro dynamics while the evaluator observes only macro inputs and outputs. This paper separates a model's capability into two stages that a single aggregate score cannot separate: information simulation, from macro information to micro behavior, and macro emergence, from micro behavior to the macro outcome. We introduce a soft macro-control method that announces a public reference path day by day without touching individual decisions, orders, or matching, and a two-regime evaluation framework that measures both stages from macro observations alone. In the reference-only regime the symmetric true and flipped references share a common level R, which measures realization under the announced reference, while their paired gap B measures structural bias; in the information-injection regime external information dilutes the reference, so only the true-flipped gap Delta remains interpretable. On five single-index LLM-agent markets, announcing a target path shifts the realized path toward the announced target on both announced references under both information conditions. Relative to the no-reference path, the tracking score is higher by 0.306 and 0.415 without news and by 0.183 and 0.329 with news; within the stock/cash scan structural bias is lowest at 70/30 (B=0.042); realization peaks at a 3:7 technical share (R=0.894 versus 0.358 for technical-only); and Delta is 0.0341 with fundamental data and 0.0487 with news. Both stages use the same two observable scores, each read in the regime where it is interpretable.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18543v2</id>
    <title>Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning</title>
    <updated>2026-11-19T05:39:09Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18543v2" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.18543v2" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Demonstrations are an effective way to accelerate single-agent reinforcement learning (RL), but extending this idea to multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is non-trivial as it is difficult and often impossible for a single person to teleoperate multiple agents simultaneously. Round-Robin Behavior Cloning (R2BC) addresses this by letting a single demonstrator control one agent at a time while the others execute their current policies. However, the resulting imitation policies are limited by the quality of the demonstrations. We propose Imitation Bootstrapped Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (IBMARL), a framework that extends Imitation Bootstrapped Reinforcement Learning (IBRL) to cooperative teams and uses R2BC to train the imitation policies. At each time step, every agent receives one action proposal from its imitation policy and one from its RL policy, and an ensemble of centralized critics selects among the per-agent combinations of the two. A gated imitation penalty, a soft Q-filtered behavior cloning loss, regularizes each RL policy toward its imitation policy only where the critics value the imitation action more, so that after training each agent executes its RL policy alone, without the centralized critics. On four cooperative multi-agent RL benchmarks, IBMARL surpasses its imitation policies $2.6$-$4.2\times$ faster than demonstration-based baselines on two tasks, is the only method to surpass it on the other two, and exceeds the demonstrator itself on two of the four. With real human demonstrations IBMARL still surpasses imitation learning alone, and does so more than twice as fast as the best baseline.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17917v1</id>
    <title>When Cooperation Must Change: Semantic Strategy Unlearning in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning</title>
    <updated>2026-11-13T08:57:49Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17917v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.17917v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) supports coordinated decision-making in distributed Web services, multi-robot control, and collaborative games through learned coordination conventions. When deployment requirements change, a previously useful convention may become obsolete or unsafe. For example, revised cache-sharing permissions in Web content delivery may require caches to abandon a learned division of storage and serving roles while maintaining efficient delivery. Teams must therefore remove the specified convention while preserving useful cooperation. This is challenging because the same relational pattern can be reproduced by different agents across different histories. Runtime shielding leaves the underlying coordination preference intact and can impair task progress, while existing reinforcement unlearning and trajectory-deletion methods do not directly target role-invariant conventions. This paper formalizes this problem as semantic coordination-strategy unlearning and proposes CARVE.CARVE uses causal coordination attribution to identify influential interactions and retain-aware subspace updates to limit interference with unrelated behaviors. Counterfactual re-coordination helps agents learn productive alternatives, while adversarial auditing tests whether the target convention can still be recovered. Accepted updates are merged into decentralized actors for direct deployment. Evaluation across five cooperative MARL benchmarks shows that CARVE reduces mean nominal convention-completion and worst-case elicitation rates by 91.4\% and 83.3\%, respectively.The median utility loss is 5.9\%, and measured inference latency matches that of the original policies.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15521v1</id>
    <title>DecArena: Evaluating Large-Scale Decentralized Multi-Agent Collaboration</title>
    <updated>2026-11-11T14:13:26Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.15521v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.15521v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Emerging personal AI agents raise fundamental scalability and privacy concerns for centralized multi-agent systems (MASs), which rely on a global orchestrator with broad access to agents, resources, and communication. In decentralized environments, global visibility is unavailable. Agents need to proactively discover non-local resources (e.g. tools, skills), and collaborate with other agents to solve tasks. We study decentralized multi-agent collaboration under graph-constrained communication, a natural reflection of human structures. Each agent observes only its local state and can interact only with neighboring agents. We introduce a benchmark with synthetic scalable distributed tool calling with 100K+ tools. Our experiments reveal that recent LLM agents struggle to discover non-local relevant resources and collaborate in decentralized setting. Moreover, standard reinforcement learning fails to reliably overcome this limitation, suggesting that decentralized MAS needs more explicit harness mechanisms for effective collaboration, even using SOTA LLMs. We then present a strong baseline \textbf{GraphHarness}, combining topology-aware warmup with self-improving LLM-based routing. Results show that GraphHarness substantially improves task success (+48.5) and produces higher quality collaboration (+30.6), while using fewer costs (+34.0) than baselines.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14846v1</id>
    <title>Open Challenges and Opportunities in Human-Agent Systems</title>
    <updated>2026-11-10T23:55:44Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14846v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.14846v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Agentic AI systems increasingly undertake extended tasks and act on people's behalf, making human-agent interaction central to their effectiveness. Successful interaction requires understanding human perspectives, coordinating complementary capabilities, and maintaining productive relationships within socio-technical environments. This paper examines how foundations developed by the Autonomous Agents and Multi-Agent Systems (AAMAS) community inform these demands. We consider interactions ranging from individual human-agent partnerships to teams and larger groups, where participants differ in their roles, decision authority, capabilities, and objectives. We organize computational approaches around the connected challenges of understanding others and deciding how to interact with them. Theory of Mind, belief-desire-intention architectures, goal and plan recognition, inverse planning, and recursive reasoning provide mechanisms for representing and inferring partially observable mental states. Observer-aware planning, model reconciliation, and decision-theoretic communication connect these inferences to action, explanation, and information exchange. Together with shared autonomy, argumentation, and cooperative inverse reinforcement learning, these approaches offer foundations for agentic systems that account for evolving human knowledge, intentions, and expectations. We argue that progress requires treating human interaction as an ongoing decision problem shaped by uncertainty, interdependence, and potentially conflicting objectives.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27780v1</id>
    <title>Search-RSI: Expanding Search Worlds Along Multimodal Agents' Capability Frontier</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T16:09:46Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27780v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27780v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Multimodal search agents answer knowledge intensive visual questions by grounding them in retrieved evidence, and recent recipes train them on multi hop tasks that are synthesized from knowledge graphs and grown online to keep pace with the agent. These recipes, however, treat the searchable world as fixed: a new question can be well formed and verifiable while its evidence is absent from the retrieval backend, so the agent issues the right query, retrieves nothing, and is penalized as if its policy were at fault. Such unreachable negatives accumulate with every round of growth. We propose Search-RSI, a recursive self improvement framework that expands the search world along the agent's capability frontier. In each round, the current policy diagnoses its partially mastered regions of a task space spanned by hop depth, relation rarity, and distractor density; new tasks there are grown together with their evidence; and the same policy decides how they are used: candidates on which its probes disagree feed reinforcement learning, while those beyond its reach become hint guided demonstrations of its own. Keeping the policy inside this loop matters: an improver frozen at the start of training loses 3.2 points. On nine multimodal search benchmarks, Search-RSI keeps improving where static task growth saturates, raising the average accuracy of the recipe it builds on by 9.8 and 9.5 points at 9B and 27B, of which 7.0 points are out of reach for a world that is merely made consistent. The loop uses no external model and only privileged task structure that is removed before training, at 1.27x the compute of static growth.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27689v1</id>
    <title>Embodied-Harness: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Robotic Manipulation</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T14:55:07Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27689v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27689v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Vision-language model (VLM)-based agents offer a promising approach to robotic manipulation, yet remain limited by inadequate memory organization, uncertain failure attribution, and limited reuse of execution experience. We propose Embodied-Harness, a dual-agent framework that improves manipulation by refining the execution harness without updating model parameters. The Actor interacts with the environment through a robot-control interface, while the Reflector converts execution evidence into reusable operational guidance. Hierarchical Memory Architecture maintains short-term execution context and long-term experiential knowledge to support execution and reflection. Evidence-based Experience Reflection grounds failure diagnosis in observed interactions, while Recursive Harness Self-Improvement refines operational guidance across successive attempts. Experiments on RoboTwin 2.0, RoboSPA, and RMBench demonstrate the effectiveness of Embodied-Harness in generalization under environmental variations, spatial reasoning, long-horizon planning, and memory-dependent manipulation. Our method achieves success rates of 82.4%, 76.7%, and 94.4% on the three benchmarks, respectively. Real-world evaluation further yields an average success rate of 96.7% across three manipulation tasks. These results highlight the potential of Embodied-Harness to improve robotic manipulation through experience-driven harness self-improvement.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27499v1</id>
    <title>NavRSI: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement for Vision-and-Language Navigation</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T11:47:47Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27499v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27499v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Frontier large language models (LLMs) have enabled vision-and-language navigation (VLN) through direct closed-loop perception and action. However, navigation performance depends strongly on the harness governing LLM-environment interactions, while existing harnesses largely rely on manually designed navigation tools, memory, and agent roles. We introduce NavRSI, a harness-centric recursive self-improvement framework that optimizes the navigation behavior of frozen LLMs through closed-loop experience. In each round, NavRSI iteratively collects navigation trajectories and failure diagnostics, employs a designer agent to rewrite the harness, and retains the revisions that prove effective, while the designer accumulates experience from previous revisions so that the harness and this experience co-evolve. Privileged simulator diagnostics guide only the designer and remain inaccessible to the navigating LLM, enabling deployment with a single RGB camera and primitive actions, without task-specific model training or additional navigation tools. Experiments demonstrate consistent improvements across LLMs from four vendors, with 85.64% success rate on the full R2R-CE val-unseen split with GPT-6-Astra, surpassing the previously reported best by 4.13%. Evaluations on RxR-CE, NavRAG-CE, and a real humanoid robot further demonstrate its generalizability.</summary>

    <title>$γ$-Scape: An Agent-Centric World for Mobile Embodied Intelligence</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T08:49:02Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27306v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27306v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Recent embodied agents construct and adapt robot behavior through executable programs, tool use, and interaction feedback. Studying these systems in mobile manipulation calls for physical worlds that connect agent-directed execution with its physical consequences and reusable interaction experience. We introduce $γ$-Scape, an agent-centric simulation and benchmark platform for mobile embodied intelligence. Agents compose motion tools and learned skills to carry out complete tasks that combine navigation and manipulation in a persistent physical world. BenchForge grounds structured objectives in physical task instances with instructions, reference programs, and goal evaluators, defining task goals while preserving agents' choice of valid solutions. An agentic collection harness further enables agents to produce demonstrations by carrying out contact-rich interactions through sustained control and physical feedback. Assisted reference execution and human guidance provide complementary experience. The resulting tool traces and aligned observation-action records support program refinement and policy learning, with common task-goal criteria for subsequent evaluation. We benchmark representative agent systems on complete tasks and demonstrate contact collection and trace-informed program revision. Together, these workflows provide infrastructure for research on embodied recursive self-improvement.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27285v1</id>
    <title>SIR-Agent: Skill-Augmented Image Restoration Agent with Recursive Self-Improvement</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T08:24:50Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27285v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27285v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Agents for Image Restoration (IR) aim to leverage Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to autonomously perceive image degradation and invoke IR tools. However, existing IR agents typically rely on fine-tuning MLLM parameters to adapt to new IR tasks, leading to catastrophic forgetting of IR knowledge. To address this limitation, we propose a skill-augmented IR agent, dubbed SIR-Agent, that maintains IR knowledge in a scalable skill library and uses Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) to facilitate efficient skill-library evolution. Specifically, we design a Chain Feedback-driven Skill Revision (CFSR) to evolve the skill library. The CFSR analyzes restoration chains to identify and revise weak operations in existing skills. The compatibility of a revised skill with known tasks decides if it replaces the original skill or is appended independently. Furthermore, to advance CFSR's skill-library evolution, we present an RSI-driven skill meta-learning mechanism, which identifies CFSR's inefficient operations and autonomously refines its revision strategy. Extensive experiments across 14 IR benchmarks, covering 6 single-degradation and 8 mixed-degradation scenarios, demonstrate SIR-Agent's superior IR performance. Further evaluation on 7 unseen tasks validates SIR-Agent's generalization to new IR tasks.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27006v1</id>
    <title>Physics-Guided Recursive Self-Improvement of Amortized Bayesian Inference Across Physics</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T02:36:12Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27006v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27006v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Across physics, from the orbits of imaged exoplanets and the matter inside neutron stars to thin films at synchrotrons and cortical neurons, conservation laws, interference, and compensating currents compress the posteriors of precise data into tiny, curved regions where Markov chains need minutes to days. We introduce PhyRSI (physics-guided recursive self-improvement), in which an AI agent coupled to the simulator writes and revises an amortized Bayesian inference algorithm for each field, scored by the importance weights of the exact likelihood because the true posterior is unknown. It evolves coordinates, symmetries, and factorizations matched to the physics: orbital elements at the best-measured epoch, Fresnel-normalized reflectivity with a chart for each of its multiple solutions, coordinates along which Na+ and K+ currents compensate, a shared neutron-star equation of state that factorizes a 32-dimensional joint analysis, and the time-rescaling symmetry of predator-prey dynamics. In six fields, networks trained once on simulations return 36 posteriors of real observations in seconds, reweighted by the likelihood and agreeing with converged Markov chains about as closely as two independent chains agree with each other. Such posteriors could steer synchrotron film growth and patch-clamp recordings as they run, follow X-ray transients while they are bright, update the dense-matter equation of state as neutron stars are added, and compare physical models across catalogs. Inference can thus be evolved and checked by the physics itself rather than designed by hand for each problem.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26910v1</id>
    <title>AstronautBench: Measuring Agent Self-Improvement Across Episodes Through Knowledge, Evidence, and Progress</title>
    <updated>2026-11-19T23:48:39Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26910v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.26910v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>LLM agents are expected to improve themselves from their own experience across episodes, with fixed weights. Self-improvement in an embodied world cannot be read from one measure. Existing benchmarks measure task progress, world-knowledge question answering (QA), and episodic memory, but a correct answer does not show that the agent ever observed the evidence for it, and progress does not show what the agent learned. We introduce AstronautBench, which measures one agent's self-improvement through three views on the same run: what it knows, whether its own evidence supports that knowledge, and how far it gets in the world. It is built on the game Outer Wilds, where each episode is a 22-minute loop after which the world resets, only the agent's knowledge carries over, and progress is gated by knowledge. After every episode, we measure the places reached and ship-log rumor facts revealed, the correctness of answers to 164 questions about the world, and whether each answer is supported by the frames and position the agent cites from its own recorded play. Two LLM judges from different model families check every answer. In eight-episode baselines with GPT-6.1 Sol and Gemini 4 Argon planners, which act through a learned controller or their own gamepad inputs, the three views do not move together, so any one of them alone gives an incomplete picture of whether the agent is improving. The GPT-6.1 Sol agent's correct answers grow from 14.6% to 26.8% of all questions, but at episode 8 only 59 to 68% of them are supported by its cited evidence. It reveals no new rumor facts after episode 3, while the places it reaches and its memory keep growing. More than half of the answers that become correct after episode 3 cite only evidence from earlier episodes.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26806v1</id>
    <title>MedicalRSI: Medical Recursive Self-Improving Agents via Clinical Model-Harness Co-Evolution</title>
    <updated>2026-11-19T20:48:58Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26806v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.26806v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Medical agents built on large language models (LLMs) have advanced rapidly, yet most stay fixed once deployed and do not keep using their experience to improve later attempts. As a result, the same kind of error can recur across patients. To address this, existing self-improvement methods update an agent's weights or its medical harness from its own experience, but their improving strategy stays fixed and never learns which changes actually help, which caps how much the agent can improve. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) instead improves both the agent and its improving strategy. However, achieving RSI for medical agents is challenging, because clinical workflows rarely come with a reference harness, and a change that fixes early errors may not fix the problems the agent meets later. We propose MedicalRSI, an RSI framework built on Clinical Model-Harness Co-Evolution, in which one model plays two roles. The Solver is the medical agent itself, and the Improver is its learnable improving strategy, which writes a medical harness from the agent's failures. Each harness is rewarded by its gain over acting without it, and both roles are trained together, so the Improver keeps adapting to the problems the Solver has not yet solved. On multiple benchmarks and LLM backbones, MedicalRSI outperforms existing context-level and weight-level self-improvement methods and transfers well to unseen workflows, new LLMs and new databases, a step toward medical agents that keep improving.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27815v1</id>
    <title>Autonomous quantum machine learning via Riemannian gradient-based optimization</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T16:42:26Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27815v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27815v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Quantum machine learning models typically rely on repeated quantum measurements and classical optimization during training, making the quantum-to-classical information-extraction process a fundamental bottleneck for scalability. We propose a framework for autonomous self-training quantum machine learning, based on Riemannian gradient optimization, in which the optimization proceeds entirely within the quantum domain without requiring quantum measurements or classical feedback. We derive the Riemannian gradient update rules for a broad class of learning tasks and identify sufficient conditions under which the resulting training dynamics can be realized fully autonomously. Within this regime, we establish an exponential convergence guarantee, in the training iterations, for sufficiently small step sizes, and further analyze the training cost in terms of the growth of the circuit depth. Importantly, we further show that the trained model can automatically discover symmetries hidden in the training data without $\textit{a priori}$ specification. For the canonical examples of quantum phase classification and unitary learning with a hidden symmetry, our numerical study indicates that learning can be achieved at low circuit depths with only a few distinct training examples. Our results thus establish autonomous quantum machine learning as a promising paradigm that removes the classical optimization loop while retaining strong theoretical guarantees and practical performances.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27129v1</id>
    <title>Opto-Electronic Hybrid Reinforcement Learning Based on MZI for Robotic Manipulator Control</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T04:59:35Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27129v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27129v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Precise motion control for autonomous robots is a core technical enabler for the large-scale deployment of embodied intelligence. In particular, basic manipulation tasks, such as point-to-point reaching and target grasping with robotic manipulators, impose stringent requirements on control accuracy, real-time response, and energy efficiency for edge deployment. As a prevailing end-to-end control paradigm, reinforcement learning (RL) has demonstrated remarkable capabilities in autonomous learning and generalization for decision-making in continuous action spaces. Nevertheless, constrained by electronic computing architectures, it generally suffers from substantial computing overhead, high inference latency and limited energy efficiency, making low-power edge deployment challenging. Optical computing, benefiting from its high-speed parallelism, offers a promising route to break energy-efficiency bottlenecks; however, research on the integration of optical computing and RL remains at an early stage. In this work, we propose a Mach-Zehnder Interferometer (MZI)-based opto-electronic hybrid RL architecture. We adopted two algorithm structures: Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient combined with Hindsight Experience Replay (DDPG-HER) and Twin Delayed Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient combined with HER (TD3-HER). We implemented the key layer linear computation of the spiking neural network (SNN) Actor on an optical MZI chip for the reaching task of a Franka Emika Panda robotic manipulator. The architecture is evaluated in the PyBullet simulation environment. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed architecture achieves an energy efficiency of 1.39 TOPS/W and an inference latency of 120ps while maintaining control accuracy, which provide a feasible pathway toward energy-efficient and precise control for robots.</summary>

    <title>Rethinking Cross-Sensor Domain Adaptation for Bridge Point Cloud Semantic Segmentation</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T03:27:43Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27060v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27060v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Segmentation models for bridge point clouds lose accuracy when trained on terrestrial laser scanning (TLS) data and applied to mobile laser scanning (MLS) data. This study re-examines the SemanticBridge TLS-to-MLS protocol to determine how sampling density, surface roughness, color, and acquisition viewpoint are expressed in the 8-cm sparse-voxel representation, and how adaptation gains depend on source-model convergence. Using one sparse-convolution U-Net, we combine raw-point statistics with controlled input perturbations and compare adaptive batch normalization, entropy minimization, Mean Teacher, and confidence-filtered self-training under 100- and 300-epoch schedules. TLS and MLS have similar nearest-neighbor spacing after preprocessing (12.08 and 12.02 mm), and a 4-mm perturbation of TLS points changes voxel occupancy by only 4.4%. Color distributions differ systematically, but zeroing color on identical voxels changes target mean intersection over union (mIoU) by only +0.02, and by +0.06 after the color augmentation is scale-corrected. The sensors also observe different portions of the bridge, yielding different class proportions. A 300-epoch source-only model obtains 57.80 mIoU on the paired-bridge protocol. Confidence-filtered self-training improves the 100-epoch baseline, but from a converged model it changes target mIoU by -0.97 (source-selected checkpoints) and -2.44 (final-50-epoch means). Repeated evaluation (standard deviation 0.27-0.64) and seed variation (1.88 across three seeds) are comparable to several method differences. Adaptation results on this benchmark therefore depend on representation scale, source-model convergence, and evaluation variability.</summary>

    <title>Forehead ROI Localization under Real-World Imaging Degradations via Cross-View Pseudo-Labeling</title>
    <updated>2026-11-19T19:13:39Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26712v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.26712v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Forehead region-of-interest (ROI) localization is important for forehead-creases biometrics, particularly when the lower face is occluded. However, localization remains challenging under varying image quality, pose, and illumination. We propose Confidence and Consistency Guided Pseudo-Labeling (CCGP), which adapts Grounding DINO using unlabeled facial images filtered by detection confidence and geometric consistency between original and horizontally flipped views, without modifying the detector architecture or loss. We evaluate CCGP on five external datasets and 350 images spanning seven imaging conditions. CCGP achieves the highest mean intersection over union (mIoU) on four of five external datasets, improving from 0.415 to 0.580 on RMFRD compared with supervised Grounding DINO. On the quality-stratified subset, the largest gains occur under blur (0.487 to 0.719) and low contrast (0.615 to 0.710). CCGP also outperforms conventional self-training on RMFRD (0.580 versus 0.551 mIoU). Despite a slight in-domain performance gap (0.861 vs. 0.866 mIoU) and challenges with off-angle poses, CCGP improves cross-dataset localization under challenging imaging conditions.</summary>

    <title>From Self-Play RL to Constrained Control: Distilling DiffMPC Students with DAgger</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T21:17:04Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.25197v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.25197v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Self-play reinforcement learning (RL) produces strong driving policies, but these policies are hard to verify or interpret. Differentiable model predictive control (DiffMPC) can enforce explicit constraints, but it is usually trained by imitating logged data or with costly RL. To add constraints to an already trained policy, we keep a PPO teacher's backbone and replace its action head with a DiffMPC that enforces road boundary half-planes and agent ellipses. We then distill the student with DAgger in the teacher's self-play simulator. Over 9 seeds, the constrained student of a smaller teacher matches its teacher on nuPlan and beats it on CARLA and on out-of-distribution Waymo scenes. For a stronger teacher, the student has fewer failures on nuPlan and Waymo, while staying level on CARLA. Its distillation takes no more than 30% of the teacher's training time.</summary>

    <title>Learning to Interact in Multi-Agent Self-Play for Controllable Autonomous Driving Scenario Generation</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T18:23:29Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24876v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24876v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Large-scale, multi-agent self-play trains robust driving policies effectively in simulation, but controlling these models to generate specific, safety-critical edge cases remains a key challenge. Existing goal-conditioned self-play frameworks rely primarily on static map-location goals and fail to reliably produce complex agent interactions such as aggressive tailgating or adversarial cut-offs. These agent interactions are necessary for rigorous autonomous vehicle (AV) testing. To address this, we present an extended multi-agent self-play framework that introduces agent-relative dynamic goals. By conditioning policies on this extended goal representation, our framework enables targeted, controllable scenario synthesis. We demonstrate that our approach successfully generates interactive driving behaviors that static-goal baselines cannot simulate, providing a flexible tool for long-tail scenario generation in AV testing.</summary>

    <title>Reliable Tree Recruitment from Scarce Annotations for Forest Inventory Expansion</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T13:31:37Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24401v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24401v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Species-level inventories of individual tree crowns (ITCs) from UAV imagery are limited by annotation cost: in tropical forests, many species are represented by only a handful of field-validated crowns. We propose a reliable tree recruitment framework that expands a small annotated inventory by iteratively self-training a multi-task DeepLabV3 network, combining semantic segmentation with a crown-distance regression head, on RGB UAV orthomosaics. At each iteration, candidate crowns enter the training inventory only if they pass a confidence filter on class probability and distance map and a morphology filter on crown area and solidity, with at most five new crowns per species, keeping recruited samples consistent with the reference inventory. We evaluate the framework at two Brazilian sites: an Amazonian rainforest in Acre (17 species, 355 annotated crowns, 4 cm GSD) and a forest site in the Cerrado of Maranhão (4 species, 51 annotated crowns, 1.8 cm GSD). Over 20 iterations, the number of retained crowns grew from about 500 to 960 in Acre and from about 700 to over 3100 in Maranhão, while crown-level F1 exceeded single- and multi-task DeepLabV3 baselines (53.5% vs. 50.0% and 45.2%; 92.2% vs. 79.7% and 83.6%). The framework offers a low-cost route to expanding species inventories with consumer-grade UAVs and limited fieldwork.</summary>

    <title>Semi-Supervised GAN-Based Segmentation of CTPA Scans for Pulmonary Emboli Boundary Extraction</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T08:09:43Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24018v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24018v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Pulmonary embolism (PE) is a pulmonary vascular disease associated with high morbidity and mortality, where delayed diagnosis can be fatal. While computed tomography pulmonary angiography (CTPA) is the clinical gold standard for PE detection, interpreting these scans manually is time-consuming and error-prone. In this work, we propose a semi-supervised segmentation method, employing generative adversarial networks (GANs) to leverage large pools of unlabeled CTPA scans. The proposed method addresses more effectively the challenges of CTPA image segmentation than previous methods by employing the dice loss and the cross-entropy loss to tackle the highly imbalanced nature of CTPA scans, the feature matching loss to encourage the generator to produce anatomically plausible segmentation maps that are indistinguishable from ground truth, as well as the self-training loss to reinforce learning from highly-confident pseudo-labeled samples. The experimental evaluation on a publicly available dataset shows that the proposed method maintains accurate segmentation, despite a limited number of labeled CTPA scans. with a Dice coefficient of 88.75% and a 95th percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95) of 1.74, outperforming fully supervised baselines.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27540v1</id>
    <title>Where Delay Compensation Belongs in a Decentralized Mean-Field-Game Swarm with a Control-Barrier Safety Filter</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T12:36:13Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27540v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27540v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Large robot teams are often run as a plan-then-execute stack. We study a decentralized instance for drone swarms, a mean-field-game (MFG) routing field with a per-agent control-barrier-function (CBF) safety filter, when communication is limited by a shared TDMA channel. Neighbors are known only through noisy range and bearing measurements exchanged in round-robin slots, so the frame, and with it the age of every estimate, grows with swarm size. In simulation this delay reaches both layers but breaks only the safety layer. Without delay, swarms of up to 100 agents do not collide, even with each measurement's noise held for a whole frame; with it, stale estimates at the CBF cause collisions beyond a frame period of 125 to 175 ms, or 75 to 100 ms at 100 agents with held noise, and swarm size sets where that limit lies and how steeply collisions rise. At the MFG, staleness makes the local density noisier without biasing it, and throughput drops by at most a tenth. We then compensate with lightweight on-board predictors, from constant-velocity fits to a small learned network, that estimate each neighbor's position from its last broadcasts. A layer-split experiment shows where prediction is needed: at the CBF it restores safety and extends the tolerated frame period by 1.4 to 1.7 times with an untrained constant-velocity fit and about 2.3 with the learned network when the noise is redrawn each step; with noise held for a frame the two extend it about equally, while at the MFG it only refines the congestion correction. A constant wider safety margin, the simplest alternative, makes collisions more frequent in a bottleneck. With the routing solved offline, that layer is robust to the delay because it sees neighbors only through a crowd average; compensation belongs in the safety filter, switched on only above the uncompensated limit, since below it the predictor's own error adds collisions.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22773v1</id>
    <title>Guarded Swarms in the Loop: A ROS 2/PX4 Digital Twin for Hybrid Digital-Analog Coordination of UAV/UGV Swarms</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T13:40:51Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22773v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.22773v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Swarms of unmanned aerial and ground vehicles (UAV/UGV) operating in contested environments cannot rely on software alone for physical safety, since the software stack and its networks are part of the attack surface. The Guarded Swarms architecture addresses this by pairing a digital coordination layer, built on Topic-Based Communication Space Petri Nets (TB-CSPN), with an independent analog safety layer that can veto unsafe actuation commands. So far, the architecture has been specified and argued for, but not executed. We present the first executable instantiation of Guarded Swarms as a digital twin built on ROS 2, the PX4 autopilot in software-in-the-loop mode, and Gazebo, with two UAVs and one UGV in a coastal counter-UAS scenario. The TB-CSPN transition chain, from multi-modal sensing through human authorization to vehicle tasking, is mapped one-to-one onto ROS 2 nodes, and the analog layer is modeled as a per-vehicle Virtual Safety Board that gates every command. Eight groups of experiments show that the three negative guarantees of the architecture (no mission from conflicting, temporally incoherent, or unauthorized evidence) hold at three distinct stages of the chain in all 60 counterfactual runs; that threat confirmation is bounded by the narrowest sensing modality; that the safety layer exercises its full modeled envelope independently of the coordination layer; and, under fault injection, that it prevents every collision caused by a forged mission or a compromised worker once its veto is enforced by an independent gate, whereas a veto left to the compromised worker prevents none. The twin also exposes implementation-level hazards that the architectural specification does not address, and it draws an explicit line between the properties that simulation can validate and those that only hardware can.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20773v1</id>
    <title>When Does Interaction Help? Toward a Reynolds Number for Collective Intelligence</title>
    <updated>2026-11-16T09:22:24Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20773v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.20773v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Multi-agent systems combine distributed information through interaction, which can improve performance but also spread errors or suppress useful differences. Predicting when interaction helps is central to understanding and designing collective intelligence. We investigate whether a few dimensionless parameters can predict gains over explicitly defined non-communicating baselines across group sizes, network structures, and tasks, toward a Reynolds-number-like description of collective intelligence. Using distributed classification tasks, stochastic tracking networks, and neural cellular automata, we combine analytical and empirical evidence to examine information sufficiency, dynamical applicability, and finite-sample prediction. We construct inference systems with bounded random variables and matching specified joint moments up to total degree three, yet opposite interaction gains under a fixed readout. These moments alone cannot generally determine the gain sign. Tracking networks likewise exhibit gain reversals despite matched candidate parameters when task power occupies different spectral modes. Under concentrated task spectra and aligned observation noise, however, we derive a low-dimensional similarity relation with an explicit zero-delay error bound and test it across network sizes and topologies under frozen protocols. The relation does not directly apply to the neural cellular systems, where a separate moment-based predictor underperforms direct gain measurement at matched calibration sample budgets. These results establish conditions and limits for low-dimensional gain prediction, providing a restricted similarity law while leaving a general Reynolds-number-like description of collective intelligence open.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08971v1</id>
    <title>Phantom Consensus: Measuring Social Reasoning in Multi-Agent LLM Decision-Making</title>
    <updated>2026-11-06T04:33:59Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08971v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08971v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Multi-agent LLM systems increasingly aggregate judgments across model instances, but reasoning about other agents can itself introduce failure. We study a setting in which LLMs shift their public decisions after observing ambiguous social signals while reporting inaccurate estimates of what other agents privately judged, even when the group's recorded private judgments do not support the apparent consensus. We call this failure phantom consensus and study it as a pluralistic-ignorance-style pattern in controlled LLM collectives. To measure this phenomenon, we introduce PHANTOM-Bench, a benchmark that separates isolated private judgments, public decisions after ambiguous social signals, elicited estimates of the group's private judgment, transparency-based recovery, and controls for neutral public text and explicit vote-following. Across nine closed- and open-weight models, ambiguous public signals consistently degrade decision quality and can turn correct private group judgments into incorrect public collective outcomes. Public accuracy drops by as much as 47.8 percentage points, and collective rationality failures reach 47.3% in the most susceptible setting. We observe substantial errors in reported group-private beliefs alongside public-stage failures, while control conditions reveal model-dependent differences in susceptibility to ambiguous and explicit peer signals. Revealing the agents' recorded private decisions repairs many failures without revealing the gold label, although recovery varies across models. Our results show that evaluating multi-agent LLM systems requires measuring not only final agreement, but whether that agreement reflects independently measured private judgments or an apparent consensus.</summary>

    <title>s$^3$: Simple Scaling of Swarms via Cooperative Multi-agent RL</title>
    <updated>2026-11-05T19:07:15Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08615v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08615v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Groups can achieve more than individuals in the same amount of time, but only if their members coordinate: they must decide who works on what and what to share. However, this organization in multi-agent systems today usually comes from arbitrary, static harnesses designed a priori without adapting to agent behaviors or task specifications. We ask whether agents can instead learn to organize themselves. We introduce s$^3$, the first multi-agent reinforcement learning method in which agents decide for themselves how long to work alone and when to share findings or read teammates' messages, with no predefined organization or roles. Our s$^3$ agents learn to take different approaches, read each other's work, exhibit emergent roles that complement each other in the swarm, and generalize to bigger teams. We study both coordination, where agents must combine private information, and parallel exploration, where sharing discoveries can make search more efficient. With matched training and inference budgets, s$^3$, swarms evaluated with twice as many agents as in training solve over 25$\times$ more coordination problems than the strongest baseline, and in exploration, communicating agents reduce repeated work by nearly 50% and outperform best-of-N by up to 9.4 percentage points. Rather than being designed in advance, s$^3$ enables organization to emerge from a shared goal. This opens the door to capable systems built from many models that learn to work together.</summary>

    <title>SEER: A Scalable Event-Driven Runtime for Parallel Execution of Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Environments</title>
    <updated>2026-11-05T13:24:57Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07996v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.07996v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is increasingly used in systems where many entities interact in a shared environment. In these workloads, policy inference can be batched on GPUs, but the CPU-side environment path still updates entity states, resolves local interactions, and builds observations inside each $\mathrm{env.step}$. This path can dominate latency in interaction-intensive workloads after policy batching. Existing vectorized environment interfaces and general event-driven runtimes do not directly address the fine-grained cross-entity work inside one bounded MARL step while preserving the step-level semantics expected by learning systems. We present SEER (Scalable Event-Driven Environment Runtime), a runtime for MARL environment execution under an explicit event-locality contract. SEER models each environment step as a bounded stream of timestamped events. If direct state updates are entity-local and cross-entity effects are represented as ordered future events, SEER can run independent events in parallel while preserving serial-equivalent boundary outputs. To make this contract practical, SEER uses a CAS-based dual-layer event queue: local event queues preserve per-entity causal order, while a parallel executive list exposes ready work to global worker threads. SEER further uses STPA, a preflight-guided thread-pool selection mechanism that combines short runtime traces with static workload and hardware features. We evaluate SEER on two parameterized MARL workloads: compute-intensive UAV swarm control (Aircraft) and communication-intensive wireless management (PCS). On Aircraft, SEER reduces inference latency by 16.2\% over the baseline. On PCS, SEER reduces environment-execution latency by 46.9\%, 19.5\%, and 64.9\% over ROSS-T, NBSE, and ROOT-Sim, respectively.</summary>

    <title>A Bilevel Neurodynamic Approach for Distributed SCAD-Regularized Sparse Least Squares</title>
    <updated>2026-11-05T08:01:08Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07618v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.07618v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>This paper proposes a bilevel particle swarm optimization (PSO)-neurodynamic method for solving the distributed sparse least-squares problem regularized by the smoothly clipped absolute deviation (SCAD) penalty to global optimality. The SCAD penalty is nonsmooth and nonconvex, so existing distributed neurodynamic methods have not been extended to it directly. Through two-time-scale singular perturbation analysis, a rigorous full-trajectory convergence theory with explicit convergence rates is established for the inner collaborative multi-agent neurodynamic system without requiring the second-order sufficient condition. A theory-guided inner-outer collaborative optimization framework is further developed, in which a red-light green-light sensitivity mechanism is embedded in the outer PSO search to enhance global search while concentrating computational effort on the SCAD shape parameters, thereby improving recovery accuracy and computational efficiency. Simulation results on four sparse-recovery scenarios demonstrate that the proposed method accurately recovers the true sparsity pattern and achieves faster convergence and lower relative error than competing neurodynamic methods.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18693v1</id>
    <title>Swarm Shepherd: Securing Multi-Agent Ecosystems Against Persistent Latent Compromise</title>
    <updated>2026-11-04T21:37:57Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18693v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.18693v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Agentic ecosystems are emerging as a new platform layer in which agents maintain persistent memory, retrieve from shared knowledge bases, execute through tool interfaces, and coordinate through shared states. These capabilities create a security problem that per-turn defenses miss: compromise can accumulate across sessions, agents, and system layers before visible failure. We define this threat as Agentic Sleeper, a system-level adversary that first behaves legitimately, gains routing trust, and later activates across memory, agent logic, and infrastructure. We formulate defense as inference under partial observability and propose Swarm Shepherd, a system-level defense framework centered on an inference filter for early warning, paired with a backward trace-back module for entry attribution. Our analysis yields a two-scale deployment rule that balances longer event histories against broader agent coverage. Across LangGraph, CrewAI, and AutoGen, Agentic Sleeper drift begins 2.7--8.9$\times$ faster than natural baselines, propagates across agents on most topologies, and evades per-turn and stateful defenses above 80\%. Swarm Shepherd warns at least three sessions before visible degradation (2.6 sessions when failure is scored by the benchmark's own task grader), while trace-back reaches 0.69 top-1 accuracy and 0.72 macro-F1 over 24 variants. The two-scale deployment rule is empirically confirmed, and in live end-to-end runs on LangGraph and AutoGen the posterior-guided defense stack drives cross-agent propagation below the self-sustaining regime, which removing only the visibly compromised agent does not achieve.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27807v1</id>
    <title>Evaluating Prompting Strategies for Zero-Shot Multilingual Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis with Large Language Models</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T16:34:21Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27807v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27807v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>While large language models (LLMs) have advanced natural language understanding, their ability to perform complex target-aspect-sentiment detection (TASD) -- a key task within aspect-based sentiment analysis (ABSA) -- in zero-shot multilingual settings remains underexplored. Existing ABSA research predominantly focuses on English or relies on fine-tuned task-specific models, leaving a gap in understanding how open-weight LLMs handle compound sentiment triplet extraction across diverse language families and domains. We present a systematic evaluation of zero-shot multilingual TASD across 12 languages and three domains using seven instruction-tuned open-weight models -- ranging from 8B to 35B parameters across dense and mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures -- under four prompting paradigms: monolithic, chain-of-thought, sequential, and sequential refine. Our results show that direct monolithic prompting achieves strong zero-shot performance, outperforming multi-step pipelines, while dense models consistently outperform sparse MoE architectures. Through fine-grained error taxonomy profiling and step-level pipeline tracking, we demonstrate that initial aspect term recall forms a hard bottleneck, whereas multi-step decomposition degrades extraction quality; iterative refinement only partially recovers this loss on larger models while inducing net-negative over-refinement on smaller architectures. Finally, generation volume analysis shows that multi-step strategies incur up to 2.38x token overhead without F1 gains, establishing monolithic prompting as the most effective and efficient paradigm for multilingual ABSA.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27765v1</id>
    <title>Weave: Routing-Adaptive Runtime Warp Scheduling for MoE Megakernels</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T15:55:34Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27765v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27765v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>The Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture is widely used in mainstream large language models. Under expert parallelism (EP), state-of-the-art systems fuse each MoE layer into a persistent megakernel for high performance. By the nature of EP, each GPU's communication and computation volumes vary with the routing result. However, prior work either fixes how GPU resources are divided between communication and computation at compile time (e.g., MegaMoE), or adapts to runtime dynamism only at coarse-grained SM granularity (e.g., mKernel), dedicating whole SMs to communication and leaving their Tensor Cores idle. At the finer warp granularity within each SM, static warp schedules can neither match routing-dependent loads nor prevent warps from idling while waiting for inputs or after finishing their assigned work. Therefore, we propose Weave, an MoE megakernel with three key designs. First, a spatial schedule allocates resources between communication and computation at both SM and warp granularities to match each GPU's load. Second, a temporal schedule switches warp roles as execution progresses, enlisting all warps at the start and end of a layer and selectively handing output scatter to idle communication warps. Third, a fused cost model jointly selects both schedules per GPU at launch from runtime routing statistics. Across all evaluated platforms, Weave outperforms the strongest baselines: under EP8 over DeepGEMM-MegaMoE, it speeds up the MoE layer by 1.30x geomean and up to 1.97x on SM103, and by 1.24x geomean and up to 1.72x on SM90; under EP16 on CDNA3, it beats the fastest official RCCL+AITER baseline by 1.44x geomean (up to 2.87x; 1.67x over vLLM).</summary>

    <title>DPMA: Learning to Compress Mixture-of-Experts Models</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T15:46:35Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27759v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27759v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures offer high computational efficiency, but storing all experts requires substantial memory and limits deployment on resource-constrained hardware. Most retraining-free MoE compression methods commit to either pruning or merging experts, often with a uniform compression ratio across layers. We introduce DPMA (Differentiable Prune Merge Absorb), which jointly learns compression operations and layer-wise expert allocation through gradient descent under a global expert budget. Separate learnable coefficients allow DPMA to prune experts, merge their parameters, and absorb their routing contributions by forwarding routing weights to retained experts. These coefficients and expert assignments are optimised to match the original model's outputs on calibration data while its weights remain frozen. Across four MoE models, eight multiple-choice benchmarks, and five compression ratios, DPMA achieves the highest accuracy averaged over benchmarks and compression ratios on each model among the evaluated methods. At $75\%$ expert reduction, it outperforms the strongest baseline on every model, with gains of up to $6.7$ percentage points.</summary>

    <title>IsoMoE: Placement-Invariant Hybrid CPU-GPU MoE Inference with Lossless 12-bit Experts</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T13:33:57Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27604v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27604v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models scale model capacity at low computational cost. Hybrid CPU-GPU inference offloads some experts to the CPU, enabling a single GPU to run MoE models larger than its memory. Expert placement changes with free GPU memory and should only affect speed. However, the greedy decoding outputs of existing hybrid engines change with placement. This is because the two devices use different arithmetic to compute experts. In addition, decoding is limited by CPU memory bandwidth. Lossless compression reduces memory traffic, but the CPU decompresses entropy-coded formats too slowly to keep up with memory reads. To address these challenges, we propose IsoMoE, an efficient hybrid MoE inference system that guarantees that its outputs do not change with expert placement. IsoMoE introduces (i) a GPU expert kernel that bitwise replays the arithmetic of the CPU expert kernel, (ii) a memory layout that allows the CPU to efficiently compute lossless 12-bit experts using AVX-512 dot-product instructions, and (iii) a dual micro-batch pipeline that overlaps CPU and GPU computation without changing the outputs. Experimental results on three MoE models show that IsoMoE produces bitwise identical outputs across different expert placements. It is also faster than the fastest baseline in every setting, achieving an average decoding speedup of 1.26$\times$ and a maximum speedup of 1.54$\times$. Our source code is publicly available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/isomoe-artifact-9C21/.</summary>

    <title>Spiking Neural Networks Incrementally Track Firing-Rate Networks</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T09:03:29Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27322v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27322v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Understanding how spiking neural networks (SNNs) efficiently process data streams is key to (i) studying how biological brains conserve energy for lifelong predictions and (ii) enabling efficient continuous AI inference. In this work, we propose a theory on how an SNN incrementally tracks its corresponding firing-rate network, a continuous-valued neural network (ANN). We prove that the output of a discrete SNN continuously tracks the instantaneous ANN output implicitly determined by the SNN input. Based on this principle, we develop LIF-Stream, a conversion framework for efficient SNN inference over unbounded data streams. It enables the converted SNN to reuse its prior activation state and compute only the activation updates between frames, thereby reducing the average number of time steps needed per frame. Specifically, LIF-Stream controls the SNN to continuously track the reference ANN output, which gives a high-accuracy prediction for every frame. Evaluation on three large-scale streaming inference benchmarks with distinct modalities shows that LIF-Stream achieves the best efficiency-accuracy trade-off compared to high-accuracy SNN techniques.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27193v1</id>
    <title>cmHC: Balancing Stream Mixing in Hyper-Connections via Geometric Contraction</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T06:26:11Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27193v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27193v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC) extends residual connections to multiple streams and stabilizes residual propagation by constraining stream-mixing residual matrices to the Birkhoff polytope, the set of doubly stochastic matrices. In this work, we investigate how to effectively mix residual streams within the Birkhoff polytope. We reveal a mixing trade-off: when under-mixed residual matrices stay close to the vertices of the Birkhoff polytope, hyper-connections will degenerate into a set of nearly independent streams; when over-mixed residual matrices are concentrated around the uniform barycenter of the polytope, streams will become less distinguishable from each other. We theoretically validate our findings by bounding the cumulative residual mixing, stream difference and gradient difference of mixing coefficients across layers. Motivated by these findings, we propose Contraction for Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (cmHC), an exact doubly stochastic method which geometrically contracts the Birkhoff polytope toward its interior. This contraction mitigates under-mixing by forcing the residual matrices to explore deeper into the polytope, with a provable stream mixing bound and no new parameterization. Moreover, we apply a moderate contraction at the shallow layers to prevent over-mixing, enabling stable gradient propagation on extremely large-scale model pretraining. Extensive experiments across dense and mixture-of-experts models at various parameter scales demonstrate the effectiveness and scalability of cmHC. We also develop fused operators for cmHC on Ascend NPUs, reducing hyper-connection execution latency by up to 44.8%.</summary>

    <title>Recurrent Amplification and Exact Nonexpansiveness Criteria for Query-Driven Erasure</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T04:33:22Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27109v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27109v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>The Query-derived Erase Direction (QED) augments a rank-one linear attention update with a key-orthogonal query component. Under scalar decay, this correction leaves the eigenvalues of each homogeneous state transition unchanged, while the propagation of an initial perturbation depends on the ordered product of these transitions. We construct a periodic token sequence with fixed key and query projections for which every one-step spectral radius is below one but the spectral radius of the period product exceeds one. The same construction yields a sufficient condition for mean-square growth under independent uniform token sampling. For rank-one erasure with channel-wise decay, we derive a necessary and sufficient spectral-norm test for one-step nonexpansiveness that can be evaluated in $O(d)$ time. The test agrees with direct singular value decomposition on all 1,800 operators evaluated. In a counterfactual replay of a selected head of Qwen3.5-0.8B-Base, the terminal gain on a 4,096-token repeated-text sequence increased from 0.99938 to 1.3977 with the feature and checkpoint gate trajectories held fixed.</summary>
