    <title>DPMA: Learning to Compress Mixture-of-Experts Models</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T15:46:35Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27759v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27759v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures offer high computational efficiency, but storing all experts requires substantial memory and limits deployment on resource-constrained hardware. Most retraining-free MoE compression methods commit to either pruning or merging experts, often with a uniform compression ratio across layers. We introduce DPMA (Differentiable Prune Merge Absorb), which jointly learns compression operations and layer-wise expert allocation through gradient descent under a global expert budget. Separate learnable coefficients allow DPMA to prune experts, merge their parameters, and absorb their routing contributions by forwarding routing weights to retained experts. These coefficients and expert assignments are optimised to match the original model's outputs on calibration data while its weights remain frozen. Across four MoE models, eight multiple-choice benchmarks, and five compression ratios, DPMA achieves the highest accuracy averaged over benchmarks and compression ratios on each model among the evaluated methods. At $75\%$ expert reduction, it outperforms the strongest baseline on every model, with gains of up to $6.7$ percentage points.</summary>

    <title>IsoMoE: Placement-Invariant Hybrid CPU-GPU MoE Inference with Lossless 12-bit Experts</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T13:33:57Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27604v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27604v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models scale model capacity at low computational cost. Hybrid CPU-GPU inference offloads some experts to the CPU, enabling a single GPU to run MoE models larger than its memory. Expert placement changes with free GPU memory and should only affect speed. However, the greedy decoding outputs of existing hybrid engines change with placement. This is because the two devices use different arithmetic to compute experts. In addition, decoding is limited by CPU memory bandwidth. Lossless compression reduces memory traffic, but the CPU decompresses entropy-coded formats too slowly to keep up with memory reads. To address these challenges, we propose IsoMoE, an efficient hybrid MoE inference system that guarantees that its outputs do not change with expert placement. IsoMoE introduces (i) a GPU expert kernel that bitwise replays the arithmetic of the CPU expert kernel, (ii) a memory layout that allows the CPU to efficiently compute lossless 12-bit experts using AVX-512 dot-product instructions, and (iii) a dual micro-batch pipeline that overlaps CPU and GPU computation without changing the outputs. Experimental results on three MoE models show that IsoMoE produces bitwise identical outputs across different expert placements. It is also faster than the fastest baseline in every setting, achieving an average decoding speedup of 1.26$\times$ and a maximum speedup of 1.54$\times$. Our source code is publicly available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/isomoe-artifact-9C21/.</summary>

    <title>Spiking Neural Networks Incrementally Track Firing-Rate Networks</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T09:03:29Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27322v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27322v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Understanding how spiking neural networks (SNNs) efficiently process data streams is key to (i) studying how biological brains conserve energy for lifelong predictions and (ii) enabling efficient continuous AI inference. In this work, we propose a theory on how an SNN incrementally tracks its corresponding firing-rate network, a continuous-valued neural network (ANN). We prove that the output of a discrete SNN continuously tracks the instantaneous ANN output implicitly determined by the SNN input. Based on this principle, we develop LIF-Stream, a conversion framework for efficient SNN inference over unbounded data streams. It enables the converted SNN to reuse its prior activation state and compute only the activation updates between frames, thereby reducing the average number of time steps needed per frame. Specifically, LIF-Stream controls the SNN to continuously track the reference ANN output, which gives a high-accuracy prediction for every frame. Evaluation on three large-scale streaming inference benchmarks with distinct modalities shows that LIF-Stream achieves the best efficiency-accuracy trade-off compared to high-accuracy SNN techniques.</summary>

    <title>cmHC: Balancing Stream Mixing in Hyper-Connections via Geometric Contraction</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T06:26:11Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27193v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27193v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC) extends residual connections to multiple streams and stabilizes residual propagation by constraining stream-mixing residual matrices to the Birkhoff polytope, the set of doubly stochastic matrices. In this work, we investigate how to effectively mix residual streams within the Birkhoff polytope. We reveal a mixing trade-off: when under-mixed residual matrices stay close to the vertices of the Birkhoff polytope, hyper-connections will degenerate into a set of nearly independent streams; when over-mixed residual matrices are concentrated around the uniform barycenter of the polytope, streams will become less distinguishable from each other. We theoretically validate our findings by bounding the cumulative residual mixing, stream difference and gradient difference of mixing coefficients across layers. Motivated by these findings, we propose Contraction for Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (cmHC), an exact doubly stochastic method which geometrically contracts the Birkhoff polytope toward its interior. This contraction mitigates under-mixing by forcing the residual matrices to explore deeper into the polytope, with a provable stream mixing bound and no new parameterization. Moreover, we apply a moderate contraction at the shallow layers to prevent over-mixing, enabling stable gradient propagation on extremely large-scale model pretraining. Extensive experiments across dense and mixture-of-experts models at various parameter scales demonstrate the effectiveness and scalability of cmHC. We also develop fused operators for cmHC on Ascend NPUs, reducing hyper-connection execution latency by up to 44.8%.</summary>

    <title>Recurrent Amplification and Exact Nonexpansiveness Criteria for Query-Driven Erasure</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T04:33:22Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27109v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27109v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>The Query-derived Erase Direction (QED) augments a rank-one linear attention update with a key-orthogonal query component. Under scalar decay, this correction leaves the eigenvalues of each homogeneous state transition unchanged, while the propagation of an initial perturbation depends on the ordered product of these transitions. We construct a periodic token sequence with fixed key and query projections for which every one-step spectral radius is below one but the spectral radius of the period product exceeds one. The same construction yields a sufficient condition for mean-square growth under independent uniform token sampling. For rank-one erasure with channel-wise decay, we derive a necessary and sufficient spectral-norm test for one-step nonexpansiveness that can be evaluated in $O(d)$ time. The test agrees with direct singular value decomposition on all 1,800 operators evaluated. In a counterfactual replay of a selected head of Qwen3.5-0.8B-Base, the terminal gain on a 4,096-token repeated-text sequence increased from 0.99938 to 1.3977 with the feature and checkpoint gate trajectories held fixed.</summary>

    <updated>2026-11-20T03:39:30Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27073v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>

    <summary>Offshore wind planning requires balancing capital cost, wind-resource potential, and seabird exposure. We formulate a spatial tri-objective mixed-integer linear program for offshore wind capacity allocation, minimizing capital cost and modeled seabird exposure while maximizing wind-weighted capacity. Applied to Australia's Gippsland offshore wind area, the model identifies exposure reductions of 23-44% at capital-cost premiums of 0.8-6.1% across 15 wind-weighted capacity requirements. We benchmark exposure-aware optimization against 19 percentile-based exclusion thresholds. At a fixed wind-weighted capacity requirement, the 5th-percentile threshold reduces exposure by 30.1% at a 37.6% cost premium, versus at least 30.1% at a 1.4% premium with optimization. Under a fixed capital budget, exclusion screening reduces exposure by 48.2% with a 26.9% capacity loss, compared with 48.5% and 7.6%, respectively, under optimization. These results highlight the value of explicitly optimizing graded seabird exposure.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27670v1</id>
    <title>Closed-loop policy optimisation for cylinder wake control via differentiable simulation</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T14:42:27Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27670v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27670v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Suppressing vortex shedding behind a circular cylinder is a classical problem in active flow control.Model-free deep reinforcement learning (DRL) learns such policies by interacting with the flow without differentiating its dynamics, which typically requires a large interaction budget. This study optimises closed-loop policies by differentiable simulation: control-loss gradients propagate through the simulated flow to the policy parameters, which are updated by reverse-mode automatic differentiation. The policy maps local velocity measurements to a jet amplitude imposed through differentiable synthetic-jet boundary conditions. In a two-dimensional confined cylinder wake at Rey=100, eight policy updates (about 78 shedding periods of forward simulation) give approximately 8% drag reduction and 99.6% suppression of lift fluctuations, the drag level being comparable to reported DRL results. Suppression is sustained by feedback: a mean-matched constant jet does not maintain it, whereas the same policy responds similarly at three activation phases and recovers after upstream disturbances. A velocity-deviation reward alone retains strong suppression, and observations of two instantaneous velocity components at one near-wake or surface location reach about 99.8% suppression, whereas a single surface pressure leaves residual oscillations. Together with related DRL results, this suggests that reward and observation requirements here are set by policy optimisation and flow physics.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27285v1</id>
    <title>SIR-Agent: Skill-Augmented Image Restoration Agent with Recursive Self-Improvement</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T08:24:50Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27285v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27285v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Agents for Image Restoration (IR) aim to leverage Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to autonomously perceive image degradation and invoke IR tools. However, existing IR agents typically rely on fine-tuning MLLM parameters to adapt to new IR tasks, leading to catastrophic forgetting of IR knowledge. To address this limitation, we propose a skill-augmented IR agent, dubbed SIR-Agent, that maintains IR knowledge in a scalable skill library and uses Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) to facilitate efficient skill-library evolution. Specifically, we design a Chain Feedback-driven Skill Revision (CFSR) to evolve the skill library. The CFSR analyzes restoration chains to identify and revise weak operations in existing skills. The compatibility of a revised skill with known tasks decides if it replaces the original skill or is appended independently. Furthermore, to advance CFSR's skill-library evolution, we present an RSI-driven skill meta-learning mechanism, which identifies CFSR's inefficient operations and autonomously refines its revision strategy. Extensive experiments across 14 IR benchmarks, covering 6 single-degradation and 8 mixed-degradation scenarios, demonstrate SIR-Agent's superior IR performance. Further evaluation on 7 unseen tasks validates SIR-Agent's generalization to new IR tasks.</summary>

    <title>PDE-State Conditioning for Learned Optimization Using Physics-Informed Neural Networks</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T21:08:52Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.25185v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.25185v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Physics-informed neural network (PINN) optimization depends on global properties of the underlying PDE and how the physics residual evolves across the domain. Standard optimizers such as Adam use fixed gradient-based statistics, while learned PINN optimizers replace the fixed rule with a learned update built from local parameters and optimization-history features. However, none explicitly use PDE-level information. We study two coupled design questions: what PDE-level information should a learned optimizer observe, and how should that information influence its update? We introduce an 11-dimensional PDE state-capturing operator structure, residual geometry, and short-horizon update response, and use it to condition a structured meta-learned optimizer through bounded feature-wise modulation. Repeated design studies identify the compact residual-geometry state G2 and bounded FiLM as the strongest overall choices among those tested. The resulting PDE-State-conditioned optimizer improves all evaluation metrics (relative-L2, L1, solution MSE, and physics MSE) over Adam and the unconditioned learned optimizer on Linear Advection, KdV, and Burgers.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24718v1</id>
    <title>Meta-LSQ: A Closed-Form Sobolev Inner Solver for Few-Shot Meta-Learning</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T16:39:44Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24718v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24718v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Gradient-based meta-learners such as model-agnostic meta-learning (MAML) adapt to a new task with an inner loop of gradient descent that has to be differentiated through, and they meta-learn every network weight. Meta-LSQ instead fits each task with one regularised least-squares solve over a fixed random Fourier basis and meta-learns only three scalars, a bandwidth, a ridge and a derivative weight. Since the derivative of a sinusoid is again a sinusoid, the same solve can also take derivative observations, and the fitted model has exact closed-form derivatives of any order. On 10-shot sinusoid regression Meta-LSQ trains in 14 s and ends with a 5.5 times lower error than a first-order MAML baseline that trains 36 times longer, and a Gaussian-process control suggests that most of this gain comes from sharing one kernel across tasks. In simulated beam tuning at DESY's ARES facility with model derivatives it is slightly more accurate than an ALPaCA-style model and well ahead of gradient descent. Over DESY's full range of target beams, again in simulation and from measurements alone, its best setting has a median error of 7.3 $μ$m, against 14.4 for the published final beams of their reinforcement-learning agent, which has the lower median on their 300 trials of small targets. On real sensor-calibration data a learned prior mean puts it ahead of MAML on two of four targets, but an exact Gaussian process with the same change and an ALPaCA-style model stay more accurate on most targets, and it breaks down on non-smooth targets. On noiseless targets outside the span of the basis, in-sample criteria such as generalised cross-validation choose too small a ridge.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24093v1</id>
    <title>UCLIR: Unsupervised Continual Learning using Independent Representations</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T09:19:21Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24093v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24093v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>In continual learning, regularization-based methods aim to mimic neuroplasticity by updating network weights to learn new tasks while constraining changes to parameters that are important for previously learned tasks through penalty terms. However, as the number of tasks increases, preserving knowledge from earlier tasks becomes less effective. This is mainly because updates for new tasks are distributed across the entire network, where parameters are highly interdependent due to the dense connectivity between neurons. Inspired by the Exponential Distance Rule (EDR), which states that the number of neural connections decreases with increasing physical distance, learning is naturally locally correlated while inter-area updates remain less task-dependent. Motivated by this principle, in this paper we demonstrate that applying weight regularization to multiple small and independently learned complementary representations is more effective than regularizing a single large shared representation. By decomposing the input into independently learned components, learning new tasks induces only localized parameter updates within specific representation, which limit interference and improve knowledge retention across tasks. We employ independent autoencoders that learn different parts of the input independently through unsupervised regularization. At inference time, a linear classifier is used for evaluation. The experimental results on a sequence of tasks using 5-Splits MNIST, sequence of 5-datasets, 5-Splits CIFAR-10, 10-Splits Tiny ImageNet shows competitive results with supervised and replay-based methods. Code is available.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23525v1</id>
    <title>Reinforcement Learning Optimized Flight Control for Interception of High-Altitude Maneuvering Targets</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T21:26:26Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23525v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.23525v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We implement and compare two approaches to improving flight control system (FCS) performance using reinforcement meta-learning (meta-RL). Both approaches are evaluated in a terminal phase hypersonic intercept engagement requiring hit-to-kill accuracy against a highly agile maneuvering target. In the first approach (FCS-RL), meta-RL is used to optimize a full FCS that maps acceleration tracking error and other measurements directly to commanded channel deflection rates of change, combining pitch, yaw, and roll control into a single policy. In contrast, the second approach (FCS-3L-RL) starts with a standard FCS (FCS-3L) implementing a three-loop autopilot for pitch and yaw control, but adapts the scheduled autopilot gains in real time using a policy optimized with meta-RL. Both approaches are compared to the FCS-3L in a 6-DOF simulator that captures most factors relevant to guidance and flight control. Simulations show that under ideal conditions the three systems have comparable performance. However, under conditions of aerodynamic uncertainty, radome refraction, or target evasive maneuvers, the FCS-RL significantly outperforms the FCS-3L-RL with improved intercept probability and less control effort. In turn, the FCS-3L-RL outperforms the FCS-3L by a similar margin. Importantly, we demonstrate that both FCS-RL and FCS-3L-RL generalize well to novel engagement scenarios, flight conditions, and target maneuvers that are not experienced during the optimization process.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22541v1</id>
    <title>From Perception to Simulation: Unveiling and Empowering Mental Spatial Dynamics in MLLMs</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T10:31:56Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22541v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.22541v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Spatial reasoning is a fundamental component of world understanding for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). While existing research has advanced the perception of spatial relations in static scenes, the domain of dynamic spatial simulation remains relatively unexplored. To bridge this gap, we introduce MentalGrid, a benchmark focused on spatial reasoning tasks that require models to simulate evolving spatial states without intermediate visual feedback. Extensive evaluation on our benchmark reveals a significant deficiency in the spatial simulation capabilities of existing models. Specifically, we find that performance is constrained by perceptual limitations in simple simulation scenarios and hindered by inadequate multi-step reasoning as complexity increases. To address these challenges, we propose a three-stage curriculum learning framework utilizing 16k specialized spatial reasoning samples. This approach yields SpatialWalker, which achieves a 33.8% average improvement over its base model, surpassing proprietary models like Gemini-3-Flash in spatial simulation. Furthermore, SpatialWalker demonstrates robust generalization, maintaining a 4.9% average gain on out-of-domain benchmarks, demonstrating the pivotal role of spatial simulation as a fundamental building block for broader spatial intelligence.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22250v1</id>
    <title>PCGRL for Complex Platformers: Synthesizing Playable and Diverse Levels via Inflated Envelopes and Forward Curricula</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T05:55:23Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22250v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.22250v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Procedural Content Generation via Reinforcement Learning (PCGRL) has emerged as a promising paradigm for automated game development. However, existing PCGRL frameworks still suffer from severe exploration bottlenecks and scaling limitations when faced with long-sequence generation tasks governed by strict rigid-body rules and non-linear kinematic boundaries (e.g., platformer constraints). Consequently, traditional approaches frequently fail to maintain reliable level solvability on large-scale canvases. To address these challenges, we present a physics-aware, curriculum-guided PCGRL framework. First, we construct an "Inflated Volume Envelope" mechanism, which provides a physics-constrained representation that incorporates continuous kinematic feasibility into the discrete state space of the MDP. Second, to alleviate the sparse reward challenge induced by extremely long decision sequences, we introduce intermediate state-transition feedback and a multi-stage forward extension curriculum learning framework, enabling informative value estimation and stable credit assignment over long-horizon trajectories. Finally, to resolve the issue where deterministic policies after convergence generate highly monotonous map paths with a lack of diversity, we activate high-entropy stochastic inference during the synthesis phase, regularized by a post-hoc parallel rejection filtering mechanism. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework significantly enhances structural diversity while maintaining high physical playability across multi-scale environments. Comparative evaluations across multi-scale canvases demonstrate that our framework maintains superior convergence stability and dimensional scalability, reliably synthesizing solvable levels where traditional PCGRL baselines degrade.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26913v1</id>
    <title>Surface Cues Over Structure: Probing LLM Behavior on Brain Connectivity Graphs</title>
    <updated>2026-11-19T23:58:11Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26913v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.26913v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) provides a noninvasive view of functional interactions across the brain, which can be represented as connectivity graphs for neurological disease analysis. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being paired with such representations, yet it remains unclear whether they genuinely reason over the underlying connectivity or simply respond to surface-level cues that may trigger learned priors. We probe this question through a controlled study of Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) diagnosis from resting-state functional connectivity, isolating one factor at a time to determine what drives an LLM's predictions on brain connectivity graphs. Across six models, from small open-weight LLMs to a proprietary one, the same pattern holds: the results provide little evidence that predictions are consistently grounded in subject-specific connectivity. Brain region names, numeric formatting, and prompt framing shift what a model predicts without improving how well it separates ADHD subjects from Controls; perturbing the graph changes predictions no more for clinically meaningful regions than for random ones; and the models' own justifications contradict the values they cite, inconsistently interpreting the connectivity evidence provided to them. Across every probe, predictions follow the model's built-in class bias and the surface form of the prompt rather than the subject's connectivity, calling into question a premise underlying current LLM brain integration work. Our code is available at https://github.com/Roy025/ADHD-code.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26319v1</id>
    <title>A Control-Theoretic Approximation to Predictive Coding Dynamics</title>
    <updated>2026-11-19T16:04:50Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26319v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.26319v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Backpropagation remains the dominant method for training deep neural networks, but its reliance on non-local computations has motivated the search for biologically plausible alternatives. Two prominent frameworks, predictive coding (PC) and deep feedback control (DFC), offer distinct approaches to local learning, yet their relationship remains unclear. Here, we show that DFC arises as a local approximation to predictive coding dynamics near fixed points, with exact equivalence in shallow linear networks and systematic deviations arising with depth, nonlinearity, and distance from equilibrium. We characterize how this approximation, which we call Approx PC, deviates from PC in its activity dynamics, and show that these deviations can be mitigated by relinearizing the feedback controller and approaching the output target through a sequence of intermediate nudges. In networks trained on MNIST and FashionMNIST, Approx PC reaches task performance comparable to PC trained with the same nudges, and weights learned with it transfer directly to PC inference. Our results unify energy-based and control-theoretic perspectives on learning and open the door to applying tools from control theory to the training of predictive coding networks.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26258v1</id>
    <title>Temporal Contrastive Alignment of EEG and Naturalistic Video Only Beats Linear Decoding On In-Sample Stimuli</title>
    <updated>2026-11-19T15:31:27Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26258v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.26258v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Neural tracking, the temporal alignment between a continuous stimulus and the elicited brain response, enables decoding of attention from electroencephalography (EEG), yet its application to naturalistic video remains largely unexplored and mainly relies on linear canonical correlation analysis (CCA). We investigate whether a temporal contrastive model, pairing pretrained VideoMAE features with a lightweight EEG encoder trained on a correlation-based InfoNCE objective, can strengthen EEG-video alignment. Benchmarked against CCA under three generalization regimes, the model outperforms CCA across subjects (leave-one-subject-out), matches it within the stimulus manifold (leave-video-segment-out), and falls behind CCA when extrapolating to entirely novel videos (leave-one-video-out). Because this advantage appears only for seen stimuli, we probe its basis: a sham control shows that a high accuracy does not certify genuine alignment, as a synthesized correspondence fit to the seen stimuli can reproduce it without genuine temporal alignment in the training pairs. This does not preclude practical use: on a downstream attention-decoding task with seen stimuli, the model remains better than CCA since the decoding only requires a strong statistical coupling, regardless of whether that coupling is physiologically meaningful. Using a group-averaged EEG reference, we further show that genuine, generalizable coupling is nonetheless learned, only buried in the noise of single-subject EEG. These results indicate that progress hinges on data scale, diversity, and single-subject denoising.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26101v1</id>
    <title>Revealing Pathway Interactions in Network Computations with Complete Path Contribution</title>
    <updated>2026-11-19T13:34:00Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26101v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.26101v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Networks pass signals through many layers of interconnected units, so explaining what they compute means tracing how information travels from input to output and how pathways interact. Most existing approaches analyze only pairwise interactions between components such as units, layers or attention heads. Even when these measurements are combined post hoc into a circuit, they do not capture higher-order interactions along full causal chains (paths) from input to output, and so cannot address how exponentially many paths interact to construct network computation. This leaves a large set of mechanistic questions unanswerable, for example whether inhibitory pathways veto excitatory ones, and how the two combine to yield network decisions. To address this gap, we introduce Complete Path Contribution, a method to decompose the network output into mathematically complete contributions of individual paths to study path-level interactions directly and at scale. Partial summation then induces definitions of contributions for any circuit at any granularity level, with completeness guaranteed at every level. We further present an efficient algorithm that identifies the $k$ strongest paths without examining all of them, with runtime empirically linear in $k$ rather than exponential in depth. By applying Path Contribution to benchmark image classification networks, we quantify excitatory-inhibitory interactions and show how they collectively construct network decisions at a level of detail previously unmeasurable. Furthermore, in an interpretable model of the mouse retina, it reveals how dynamic receptive fields emerge from excitatory-inhibitory interaction motifs among pathways between different cell types in response to time-varying natural stimuli. Overall, Path Contribution reveals how a network's causal pathways interact at scale to transform input to output.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23177v1</id>
    <title>Déjà View: A Shared Working-Memory Model for Visual Tasks</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T18:23:14Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23177v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.23177v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>A working-memory model must remember stimuli and use its memory flexibly to perform different tasks. Here we introduce a model of working memory for images that combines dynamic activity with temporary associations between image features. We train the model on five tasks, including remembering a sample while other images are presented, categorizing distractor images while remembering the sample, and determining whether an image is new or has been presented before. The same trained model performs all tasks, guided by explicit cues about which response is required. We use this flexible memory model to ask how delay, distraction, and image history affect performance. Delays have little effect on sample-memory performance for the delays we tested, while seeing more images leads to more false alarms even when the target image appeared equally recently in all cases. On the sample-memory-plus-categorization task, the probability of correct responses on all questions decreases as more questions are asked, despite robust sample-memory performance. Finally, the model maintains stable performance across 40 brief trials of each task under the tested conditions. Together, these results demonstrate how a single working-memory system can be flexibly used to perform different tasks, and how its errors depend on both previous images and task demands.</summary>
    <category term="cs.CV" scheme="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom"/>
    <category term="cs.LG" scheme="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom"/>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22054v1</id>
    <title>A single inference process underlies the behavior and neural circuits of working memory</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T01:29:43Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22054v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.22054v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Working memory holds past inputs online for future behavior. Despite decades of research, accounts of working memory remain divided across levels of analysis, with long-standing debates on whether its capacity reflects discrete slots or continuous resources, how attention improves recall, and whether its representations rely on persistent neural firing or activity-silent states. Here we show that MemGP, a theory that is specified at the computational, algorithmic, and circuit levels of analysis simultaneously, can explain diverse behavioral and neural phenomena in working memory. At the computational level, MemGP casts working memory as probabilistic inference over a continuous function on feature space, with a variational objective that balances memory strength against a Gaussian-process prior. At the algorithmic level, writing, storing, and reading of memories correspond to approximating this posterior with a finite set of inducing points, the resource that all items share. In simulations, MemGP reproduces load-dependent precision loss, attentional benefits during maintenance, and inter-item attraction and repulsion, in each case revealing multiple complex computational dependencies. At the circuit level, the algorithm analytically (without training) maps onto a recurrent circuit, including its architecture and dynamics. Beyond reproducing neural phenomena such as delay-dependent drift, this analytical map deduces center--surround connectivity, a property long assumed in attractor models, and a structured combination of persistent activity and synaptic weights to hold memories. Thus, a single inference objective not only jointly predicts the behavioral and neural signatures of working memory, but also addresses, across several instances and different levels of analysis, existing competing explanations.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16057v2</id>
    <title>Pyramidal Columns Acting as Attention Heads</title>
    <updated>2026-11-14T20:39:15Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16057v2" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.16057v2" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Can the functional architecture of a Transformer attention head be given a biological construction? More specifically, could a suitable group of pyramidal columns in posterior temporal language regions (PTLRs) constitute the biological construction of a neuromorphic mechanical realization of an attention head, under a mathematical instantiation that need not coincide with its standard Transformer instantiation? This paper investigates this hypothesis by examining possible correspondences between the functional organization of attention heads and neurophysiological mechanisms operating within and across pyramidal columns involved in human language processing. Our analysis builds on a mechanical-structural description of Transformer attention heads as systems of simple neural networks linked through output-input and output-weight interconnections. We examine the functional organization of an attention head and the input-dependent transformations it produces, and ask how the corresponding processing relations could be constructed in biological neural tissue. We then identify candidate neural mechanisms of signal transmission and modulation within and across pyramidal columns that may jointly support such a construction. On this basis, we propose that a suitably organized group of pyramidal columns in PTLRs could constitute a biological construction of a neuromorphic mechanical realization of an attention head. Whether the required functional organization actually exists in PTLRs remains an open empirical question. The hypothesis does not require the biological system to reproduce the standard mathematical instantiation of Transformer attention: the same functional architecture may be mechanically realized and mathematically instantiated in a different way, consistent with its biological construction.</summary>

    <title>ScaleBrain: A Scale-Consistent Framework for EEG Foundation Models</title>
    <updated>2026-11-10T13:03:41Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14035v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.14035v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Foundation models pre-trained on large unlabeled electroencephalography (EEG) corpora have emerged as a transformative paradigm for Brain-Computer Interface (BCI) applications. Recent EEG foundation models have shown that multi-scale representations derived from fixed-length patches can improve EEG representation learning. Existing frameworks commonly construct temporal scales through feature-level operations. However, these operations leave the correspondence between learned features and scale-specific characteristics of the original EEG signals implicit. Moreover, when the self-supervised objective is not aligned with the multi-scale input representations, information at some temporal scales may receive insufficient supervision during pre-training. In light of this, we propose ScaleBrain, a scale-consistent pre-training framework that explicitly coordinates multi-scale representations of EEG from both the model input and optimization objective sides. Specifically, ScaleBrain introduces multi-scale EEG tokenization to represent the same EEG segment through analysis windows with different temporal spans and shared temporal anchors, and pairs these representations with scale-specific reconstruction to align with the multi-scale input structure and provide supervision across temporal resolutions during self-supervised learning. We further develop an axial spatio-temporal attention mechanism to contextualize the fused multi-scale representation along spatial and temporal dimensions. Extensive evaluations on six public BCI benchmarks against 12 representative baselines show that ScaleBrain achieves the highest mean Balanced Accuracy on five datasets and ranks third on the remaining one, with only 5.0M parameters, demonstrating strong performance and favorable parameter efficiency.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26590v1</id>
    <title>Probing the "Conscious" Mind: Selective Access and Global Workspace in Vision-Language Models</title>
    <updated>2026-11-19T18:46:50Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26590v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.26590v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Vision-language models (VLMs) integrate visual and textual information, but their outputs do not reveal internal concept representations. Global workspace theory (GWT) proposes that information is selected from parallel brain processes, integrated in a shared workspace, and made available to specialised processes. We introduce the Multimodal Concept Lens (MC-Lens), a multimodal Jacobian lens, to study these functions in VLM concept processing. Its vision encoder and language decoder lenses map intermediate states to a shared semantic space defined by the decoder's output vocabulary to compare concept accessibility across modalities. MC-Lens supports internal concept interventions to examine the role of accessed concepts in downstream computation. (i) Accessibility and selective access. Multimodal concept information is readable in intermediate states and selectively accessible as tasks require. We extend "readout carriers" from one name token to a token set to better capture and express concept information and support counterfactual experiments. (ii) Concepts in downstream computation. Counterfactual experiments show that accessed concept information participates in downstream computation and reasoning. (iii) Development of cross-modal alignment and selective access. We develop two J-space metrics tracking the development of cross-modal concept alignment more clearly than hidden state cosine in controlled VLM training. The experiment also shows that reliable selective access develops later than concept accessibility. (iv) Shared functions across models. Across VLM families and sizes, we find shared patterns of concept accessibility, query-dependent selectivity and cross-task intervention effects despite differences in internal organisation. These findings offer an experimental basis to study GWT in multimodal artificial systems and how it can guide cross-modal alignment improvements.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26018v1</id>
    <title>Does the Workspace Do the Work? A Causal Protocol for Verifying Global-Workspace Computation in a Language Model</title>
    <updated>2026-11-19T12:33:35Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26018v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.26018v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Global Workspace Theory (GWT), a leading theory of consciousness, holds that information becomes conscious when it is broadcast to specialized processes that use it. Building a workspace into a network does not reveal what the trained network computes with it: a module that reports an answer may have combined a broadcast message with its own knowledge, or merely forwarded an answer computed elsewhere, and task accuracy and ablation cannot tell these apart. We introduce a causal protocol that identifies who computes when modules communicate. Its central test transplants a message from another input, chosen so that ignoring, relaying and recombining it predict three different answers. On networks built to relay or to recombine, the test assigns the right computation in every case. Among trained workspace models it finds all three outcomes: one leaves its broadcast nearly unused, and of two models that differ only in their training data, one relays and the other recombines. In AFGW, a language model whose modules communicate only through a learned workspace, a transplanted message yields the answer that recombination predicts in 97% of cases, and its content acts by redirecting what the receiver retrieves from its own memory. The tests carry over to other communication designs and to a known interface of a pretrained Transformer, turning GWT's central claim into a testable property of trained models.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24932v1</id>
    <title>Knowing What You Know: A Trait Theory of Reviewer Value in Human-AI Cognitive Systems</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T18:55:07Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24932v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24932v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>When a capable model and a human reviewer cooperate on the same decision, which human still adds value? We argue this is a question about a single cognitive trait, metacognitive calibration: the alignment between a reviewer's behavioral confidence and the actual correctness of their judgments. We develop a trait theory of reviewer value to make it precise. The theory makes five claims: value is governed by calibration rather than by activity, speed, agreement, or tenure; calibration leaves observable traces in behavioral telemetry; those traces are non-diagnostic on their own, because the fast, low-revision signature of a calibrated expert is indistinguishable from that of a confident novice until it is gated by outcomes; human calibration and a model's self-knowledge are the same construct, so the joint system should defer to whichever agent is better calibrated on each item; and individual calibration is causally identifiable only above the level of the single judgment. We ground each claim in a six-month production window of an AI-assisted accounting system (541621 reviewer events, 483 reviewers), and find that a purely behavioral expertise profile inverts the ground truth, scoring an overconfident cohort (5.2 percent correction survival) higher than genuine experts (99.2 percent); that reviewer quality is flat across tenure, so the trait is not learned on the job; and that the same calibration logic that separates good from bad reviewers, applied to the model, concentrates 92.5 percent of human effort on genuine errors. We close with the boundary the theory must respect: under majority-vote aggregation, individual causal value is unidentifiable.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23106v1</id>
    <title>Natural Language Programming: Rethinking Language, Memory, and Cognition in the Era of Generative AI</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T17:27:01Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23106v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.23106v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Generative Artificial Intelligence is transforming the role of natural language in computational systems. In classical Natural Language Processing (NLP), language was treated as an object of computation: something to analyse, classify, translate, or generate. Large Language Models (LLMs) challenge this perspective, enabling natural language to function increasingly as an executable cognitive medium through which humans structure reasoning, orchestrate problem solving, and regulate hybrid human/AI workflows.
  This paper introduces Natural Language Programming (NLPg) as a theoretical and epistemological extension of traditional NLP. Rather than focusing on language understanding alone, NLPg conceptualises prompts as dynamic cognitive artefacts that externalise goals, constraints, assumptions, validation criteria, and intermediate reasoning states. Prompting is thus not merely a technical interaction technique, but a form of dialogic cognitive programming operating within distributed human/AI memory architectures.
  Building on theories of distributed cognition, extended mind, metacognition, and dialogic learning, the paper proposes the notion of Dialogic Working Memory, describing how prompts and conversational states function as temporary external memory structures supporting reasoning continuity and reflective regulation. We further map existing memory architectures (BTMA, SKGE, RMR) onto this framework, illustrating how episodic, semantic, and metacognitive layers support long-horizon conversational coherence.
  Finally, implications for computational linguistics and AI/mediated knowledge systems are discussed, suggesting a post symbolic and post interface paradigm in which natural language operates simultaneously as communication medium, executable specification, cognitive scaffold, and distributed memory architecture.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20826v1</id>
    <title>Conversing with a Conversational Agent: A Real Conversation, Not a Simulated One</title>
    <updated>2026-11-16T10:09:08Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20826v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.20826v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>The claim that interactions with artificial conversational agents merely simulate human conversation rests on a philosophical distinction between reproducing the observable features of an activity and actually performing it. Although this distinction is appropriate for certain physical phenomena, its application to linguistic and symbolic activities is far less straightforward. This article argues that conversations with large language model (LLM)-based agents are genuine conversational activities rather than mere simulations, without thereby attributing consciousness, subjective understanding, or human intentionality to artificial systems. Drawing on the distinction between subjective and objective simulation, the article first examines the limitations of defining conversation exclusively through the intrinsic properties of its participants. It then develops a relational and semiotic account of conversational activity, informed by linguistic pragmatics, Lacan's Conversing with a Conversational Agent theory of the mirror, Baudrillard's concept of the simulacrum, Simondon's philosophy of individuation, and Peirce's semiotics. These perspectives make it possible to distinguish the reality of conversational interaction from the appearance of artificial subjectivity and from the epistemic validity of the meanings produced. The argument culminates in the concept of Hybrid Semiotic Fabrication, which characterizes meaning-making as a distributed process involving human participants, artificial intelligence, corpora, and technical arrangements. Recognizing the reality of human-AI conversation therefore entails neither anthropomorphizing artificial agents nor granting their outputs epistemic authority. Rather, it requires a more precise account of the relational, semiotic, and normative conditions under which conversational meaning is produced and justified.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.12809v1</id>
    <title>Qualiaphobic artificial neural networks (and why to build them)</title>
    <updated>2026-11-09T18:14:43Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.12809v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.12809v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>This paper introduces qualiaphobic AI: artificial neural network architectures that are hostile to theories of consciousness. I show that qualiaphobia can be well-justified by knowledge about theories of consciousness, like when such theories are trivial or unfalsifiable or contradicted by overwhelming scientific evidence. It can also be justified by how theories of consciousness must be grounded in phenomenology, as well as how current popular theories of consciousness are applied to AI. I identify and explore three convergent ways of engineering qualiaphobia that would minimize the potential for artificial consciousness. These include making AI architectures as close as possible to "anchor points" of systems with minimal potential for consciousness, fragmenting any potential phenomenology AI might have, and designing artificial neural networks in a way adversarial to popular theories of consciousness. In particular, I develop one "anchor point" of minimal potential for consciousness: systems where only behaviorist theories of consciousness can apply, and I propose qualiaphobic transformations that move existing artificial neural networks toward such systems. Additionally, I develop an account of how AIs can form justified beliefs about their own non-consciousness (or minimal potential for consciousness) and expand on how this knowledge would change their behavior. Most critically, I begin with why this research is important: qualiaphobic AI has epistemic properties that make it far better aligned with human civilization. Since consciousness is central to moral value, a world in which AIs are non-conscious ensures it is always morally correct for AI to assist and serve humanity, rather than pursue its own ends.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.12762v2</id>
    <title>Sage-Taiyi: A Metacognitive Architecture for Scientific Discovery</title>
    <updated>2026-11-13T08:33:13Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.12762v2" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.12762v2" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We introduce Sage-Taiyi, a metacognition-inspired architecture that uses accumulated scientific understanding to guide what to investigate next and how to investigate it. Through explicit monitoring and control, the system revises its understanding of evidence, assumptions, and unresolved questions, then uses these assessments to adapt research targets and select reusable reasoning methods. On Taiyi-Bench, an AI co-scientist ideation benchmark comprising 265 tasks from 50 papers across ten disciplines, Sage-Taiyi ranks first on all eight metrics of historical rediscovery and open-ended ideation, achieving an Overall score of 54.0 compared with 47.9 for the strongest baseline, AI Scientist-v2. It also performs well on two external scientific ideation benchmarks. Five expert-guided collaborations further connect its proposals to experimental and computational validation across chemistry, materials science, and engineering. In chemistry, reaction-condition optimization raises the yield of cobalt-catalyzed carbonylation from trace amounts to 84% and photocatalytic allylic amination from 13% to 69%. These results support metacognitive regulation as an approach to scientific ideation and its progression toward practical validation.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08469v1</id>
    <title>Same Behavior, Different Mechanism: What Finite Experiments Can Certify About Integrated Information</title>
    <updated>2026-11-05T18:55:31Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08469v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08469v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Interpretability, AI auditing and assessments of machine consciousness increasingly rest on mechanism-level quantities: functionals of a system's causal transition law that describe how it computes, not what it outputs. Experiments see that law only through finite, partial and noisy interventions. We ask when such a quantity is identifiable from an experiment's access, continuous in the mechanism and certifiable from finite data, and answer exactly for a deliberately demanding case - the integrated information $\varphi$ of integrated information theory - in stochastic networks of four and five units with known ground truth. Behavior can be silent: a recurrent and a feed-forward network with identical input-output laws at their response delay carry 0.28 and 0 bits, yet internal recordings separate them within 4-53 trials. Partial access can be just as blind: in our examples, units left out of a one-step recording impose precision floors of 0.30-1.02 bits that no sample size lowers, and in all-but-self parity networks, recordings of any length see several hidden units only through the product of their fidelities - a symmetry that one intervention broke in exact checks. The measure has sharp edges: because $\varphi$ selects a partition, and the cause and effect it specifies, by one criterion and reports another, infinitesimal changes of mechanism that cross an edge change it by 25-100% at 99% of the edges we found in random networks, and about 1% of surrogate models that fit interventional data almost perfectly misreport it by more than 20%. One-sided claims survive: the same data certify a lower bound on both sides of an edge, and we prove $\varphi>1.004$ bits throughout a 64-dimensional region of mechanisms and certify it from about $10^7$ controlled transitions with false-certificate probability at most $α$. Measurability is thus a design question with computable answers.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27793v1</id>
    <title>Extremal $K_t$-intersecting graph families for large $t$</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T16:25:25Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27793v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27793v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>In this paper, we show that for every sufficiently large positive integer $t$ and every integer $n \ge t$, every $K_t$-intersecting family $\mathcal{G}$ of graphs on vertex set $[n]$ has size at most $2^{\binom{n}{2}-\binom{t}{2}}$. Furthermore, when the equality is attained, $\mathcal{G}$ must consist of all graphs on $[n]$ that contain some fixed copy of $K_t$. Our result settles a conjecture of Ellis, Filmus, and Friedgut for sufficiently large $t$. We also present a short proof for the odd-cycle-intersecting case, slightly different from the existing proofs in the literature.</summary>
    <category term="math.CO" scheme="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom"/>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27781v1</id>
    <title>On the factorization of Dirac hypergraphs</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T16:10:09Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27781v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27781v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>A celebrated result from the 70s due to Baranyai states that the complete $k$-uniform hypergraph on $n$ vertices decomposes into perfect matchings if $k\mid n$. We prove a minimum degree version of this result. Note that a necessary condition for a $k$-uniform hypergraph $G$ on $n$ vertices to admit a decomposition into perfect matchings is that $G$ is vertex-regular and $k\mid n$. We show that, if this is satisfied and, in addition, $G$ has minimum $(k-1)$-degree at least $(\frac{1}{2}+o(1))n$, then it indeed decomposes into perfect matchings. The constant $1/2$ is optimal, as below this threshold, $G$ might not even contain a single perfect matching. This settles a conjecture of Glock, Kühn and Osthus from 2021.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27755v1</id>
    <title>Hankel determinants of Motzkin path generating functions and the Hirota-Miwa equation</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T15:44:20Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27755v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27755v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>For $k\ge0$ let $a_{n,k}(x,c)$ count Motzkin paths from $(0,0)$ to $(n,k)$ that never go below height $0$, where level steps have weight $c+x$ at height $0$ and $c$ above it, and let $D_{k,n}=\det\bigl(a_{i+j,k}(x,c)\bigr)_{0\le i,j\le n-1}$. T. Yu proved Cigler's conjecture $D_{k,n}D_{k,n-2k-2}-x^2D_{k,n-1}D_{k,n-2k-1}=(1-x^2)D_{k,n-k-1}^2$ $(n\ge2k+2)$ by writing $D_{k,n}$ as a $k\times k$ determinant of Chebyshev polynomials modulo $U_k-xU_{k-1}$. Using a linear map found by Yu, we show that the recurrence is a reduction of the Hirota-Miwa equation for Casorati determinants. This gives a second proof, and the recurrence holds for $n\ge2k+2+\max(0,N-\lfloor k/2\rfloor)$ for the Hankel determinants of $n\mapsto L(X^n(U_k-xU_{k-1}))$ whenever the moment functional $L$ has the recurrence coefficients of the Chebyshev polynomials above height $N$. For any monic polynomial in place of $U_k-xU_{k-1}$ the Hirota-Miwa equation gives an identity with a free parameter between symplectic characters, and Yu's identity for rectangular characters follows from it by fixing the parameter and restricting to a line. On the curve $xc+x^2+1=0$ we express the Hankel determinants of the sequences shifted by $2$ and $-1$ through the $D_{k,n}$. There the recurrence becomes the Desnanot-Jacobi identity, which gives a third proof, and a recurrence for the Hankel determinants of odd convolution powers of Narayana polynomials, shifted backward by $k$. We also prove identities that Cigler stated as observations, an analogue of odd orthogonal type, and a factorization for paths with a weighted return step.</summary>
    <category term="math.CO" scheme="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom"/>
    <published>2026-11-20T15:44:20Z</published>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27685v1</id>
    <title>Proximity and Remoteness in Trees with given Segment Sequence</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T14:54:28Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27685v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27685v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>The average distance of a vertex $v$ of a connected graph $G$ is the arithmetic mean of the distances from $v$ to all other vertices of $G$. The proximity $π(G)$ and the remoteness $ρ(G)$ of $G$ are the minimum and the maximum of the average distances of the vertices of $G$, respectively. A segment $S$ of a tree is a path-subtree whose terminal vertices are either branching or pendant vertices, and all internal vertices have degree $2$. The segment sequence $(\ell_{S_1}, \ell_{S_2},\ldots,\ell_{S_m})$ of T is the non-increasing sequence of the lengths of all segments of T.
  In this paper, we characterise trees with a given segment sequence that minimise proximity and those that maximise remoteness. For trees that minimise remoteness, we establish sufficient conditions under which the tree is starlike and conjecture that a remoteness-minimising tree is always either starlike or a ($Δ,2$)-tree. For trees that maximise proximity, we derive a collection of necessary conditions that any tree maximising proximity must satisfy.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27657v1</id>
    <title>The categorical graph minor conjecture and matching complexes</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T14:24:14Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27657v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27657v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>In the graph minor category $\mathcal G$ of Miyata, Proudfoot and Ramos, the morphisms are the ways of obtaining one connected graph from another by deleting and contracting edges. The categorical graph minor conjecture asserts that every submodule of a finitely generated $\mathcal G^{\mathrm{op}}$-module is finitely generated; it is known for graphs of bounded first Betti number. We disprove this conjecture: it fails for the module assigning to each graph the free module on its spanning trees, which is generated by one element. A quotient of this module has unbounded torsion. We prove, however, that the conjecture holds for all modules depending on a minor morphism only through the induced injection of edge sets. This applies to matching complexes. Let $M_d(G)$ be the complex of edge sets of $G$ spanning subgraphs of maximum degree at most $d$. We prove that the $\mathcal G^{\mathrm{op}}$-module $G\mapsto H_i(M_d(G);\mathbb Z)$ is finitely generated for all $i$ and $d$, which for $d=1$ confirms a conjecture recorded by Ramos, and that a positive integer depending only on $i$ annihilates the torsion of all these groups. The proofs combine Robertson and Seymour's labelled graph minor theorem with a new criterion: if a category has a faithful functor to finite sets and injections and, for every finite set of colours, its objects with coloured underlying sets are well-quasi-ordered by colour-preserving morphisms, then its representations over a left-Noetherian ring form a locally Noetherian category. Unlike the Gröbner method of Sam and Snowden, this criterion requires no ordering compatible with the morphisms.</summary>
    <category term="math.CO" scheme="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom"/>
    <published>2026-11-20T14:24:14Z</published>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27575v1</id>
    <title>A proof of Cigler's quadratic recurrence for Hankel determinants of Motzkin path generating functions</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T13:11:42Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27575v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27575v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>For an integer $k\ge0$ let $a_{n,k}(x,c)$ be the generating polynomial of the Motzkin paths from $(0,0)$ to $(n,k)$ that never go below height $0$, where level steps have weight $c+x$ at height $0$ and weight $c$ at positive height, and let $D_{k,n}(x,c)=\det(a_{i+j,k}(x,c))_{0\le i,j\le n-1}$. We prove that for all $k\ge0$ and $n\ge2k+2$ $$D_{k,n}D_{k,n-2k-2}-x^2D_{k,n-1}D_{k,n-2k-1}=(1-x^2)D_{k,n-k-1}^2,$$ a quadratic recurrence conjectured by J. Cigler in 2023 (eq. (18) of arXiv:2309.15557 and MathOverflow question 456683). As a by-product we obtain an expression of $D_{k,n}$ as a $k\times k$ determinant built from Chebyshev polynomials reduced modulo $U_k-xU_{k-1}$, together with a bilinear identity for these $k\times k$ determinants that holds for all integer shifts. We also give a proof of Cigler's companion conjecture that $D_{k,n}(x,c)$ equals the determinant of an explicit matrix $H_{k,n}(x)$ with entries $0$, $1$ and powers of $x$, and in particular does not depend on $c$; this statement has recently been proved by V. Jandhyala, and our proof was found independently. The proofs use Chebyshev polynomials, a model of $\mathbb{Q}(x)[X]/(U_k-xU_{k-1})$ by antisymmetric Laurent polynomials, a lemma on complementary minors, and a three-term Plücker relation.</summary>
    <category term="math.CO" scheme="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom"/>
    <published>2026-11-20T13:11:42Z</published>

    </author>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27562v1</id>
    <title>Counting cliques in optimal $1$-planar graphs</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T12:58:39Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27562v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27562v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Extremal problems concerning the maximum number of cliques in $n$-vertex graphs from a given graph class have been widely investigated. In this contribution, we present several results on counting cliques that extend beyond the existing framework. Firstly, we address this problem for the class of optimal 1-planar graphs where we determine the maximum numbers of copies of $K_3$, $K_4$, and $K_5$ in an $n$-vertex optimal 1-planar graphs and characterize all extremal graphs. This resolves Question {\b 8.1} of Gollin-Hendrey-Methuku-Tompkins-Zhang. Secondly, we prove that every 3-connected plane quadrangulation on $n\geq14$ vertices has at most $2n-14$ 3-separators and characterize the corresponding extremal graphs. This confirms Conjecture {\b 8.2} posed by Gollin-Hendrey-Methuku-Tompkins-Zhang. Lastly, we construct, for every integer $r\geq1$, a simple 2-planar graph with $5r+3$ vertices and $44r+1$ triangles, thus disproving Conjecture {\b 8.3} of theirs. Our proofs use radial graphs, tree decomposition and SPQR trees.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27519v1</id>
    <title>Additive cubes are avoidable by a non-uniform morphism of length $6$ over $\{0,a,b\}$ (with $b \ge 4$ and $\gcd(a,b) = 1$)</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T12:09:53Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27519v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27519v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We prove that additive cubes are avoidable over every ternary alphabet $\{0, a, b\}$ with $1 \le a < b$, $\gcd(a, b) = 1$, and $b \ge 4$, thereby solving and extending Rao's~(2015) conjecture from $b \ge 6$ down to $b \ge 4$. Our construction applies a single dual pair of parameterized non-uniform morphisms of image length at most~$6$ to the additive-cube-free word $\mathbf{w}$ of Cassaigne et al.~(2014). For $b \ge 10$, we prove that every additive square in the image is an abelian square, reducing additive cubes to abelian cubes; the absence of abelian cubes and the $24$ finite cases with $4 \le b \le 9$ are then certified via the finite-graph method of Jamet and Rosenfeld~(2026).</summary>

    <title>The Optimal Sample Complexity of Agnostic PAC Learning for Partial Concept Classes</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T18:18:09Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27946v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27946v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Let $\mathcal H\subseteq\{-1,+1,\star\}^{\mathcal X}$ be a partial concept class of finite VC dimension $d$. We construct a deterministic agnostic PAC learner that, for every $\varepsilon,δ\in(0,1)$, uses $O((d+\log(1/δ))/\varepsilon^2)$ i.i.d. examples from an arbitrary distribution $\mathcal D$ over $\mathcal X\times\{-1,+1\}$ and returns a total concept $\hat h:\mathcal X\to\{-1,+1\}$ satisfying $\text{er}_{\mathcal D}(\hat h)\leq \min_{h\in\mathcal H}\text{er}_{\mathcal D}(h)+\varepsilon$ with probability at least $1-δ$, where $\text{er}_{\mathcal D}(h)=\mathbb P_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal D}[h(x)\neq y]$. This establishes the optimal sample complexity, matching the lower bound of Alon et al. (FOCS 2021).</summary>
    <category term="cs.LG" scheme="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom"/>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27700v1</id>
    <title>Geometrically Constrained Learning II: Agnostic Proper Learning of Lipschitz Functions</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T15:07:03Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27700v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27700v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We give a proper learner for Lipschitz functions over the Gaussian distribution on $\mathbb{R}^d$. Given random Gaussian examples labeled by a $λ$-Lipschitz function, $λ\ge 1$, the learner returns a function $h:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$ that is globally $λ$-Lipschitz and has loss (absolute or squared) at most $\varepsilon$. The sample complexity, running time, and representation size are \[
  (d+1)^{\mathsf{poly}(λ/\varepsilon)}. \] The learning algorithm can be made \emph{agnostic}, given a known bound on the variance of the label marginal distribution. Some known control of label scale is information-theoretically necessary. For arbitrary labels with variance at most $V^2 \ge 1$, the complexity is \[
  (d+1)^{\mathsf{poly}(Vλ/\varepsilon)}, \] and the error is $\mathsf{opt} + \varepsilon$, where $\mathsf{opt}$ is the minimal error among Lipschitz approximators.
  Our approach combines $L_1$ polynomial regression under a convex gradient constraint with local correction of the Lipschitz property. The learner finds a polynomial that, after smoothing and clipping its range, is very close to a canonical Lipschitz correction of itself, the lower Lipschitz envelope. Our local corrector modifies the lower envelope by replacing distances to sublevel sets with a Gaussian sampling proxy, allowing the construction to be locally and stably estimated from samples.</summary>

    <title>Time Series Structure Learning with Local Causal Parent Discovery</title>
    <updated>2026-11-19T15:06:06Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26232v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.26232v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Learning and inference on time series can pose significant statistical challenges, including autocorrelated observations, distribution shift over time, and the curse of dimensionality. These challenges complicate the practical application of causal discovery algorithms, which already suffer from high computational and sample complexity in the general case. To mitigate these issues, this work introduces Iterative Temporal Parent Discovery (ITPD): a sound and complete constraint-based procedure for causal structure learning on multivariate time series with causal nonstationarity. ITPD takes a local-to-global learning approach that discovers the global graph by sequentially discovering the parent set for each variable. ITPD exploits temporal structural priors, graph partitioning, and the local Markov condition to swap higher-order conditional independence tests for lower-order alternatives. With an exact oracle, ITPD performed the least number of tests and used the smallest average conditioning set sizes relative to baselines. In benchmarking simulations, ITPD sat on the Pareto frontier with respect to F1 and wall-clock time and was faster than baselines on large graphs ($\geq$ 1000 nodes). For graphs with 2000 nodes, ITPD ran $2.3\times$, $9.1\times$, and $40.9\times$ faster than iterative IAMB, DF-PC, and PCMCI, respectively.</summary>

    <title>Attention Head Specialization: Phase Transitions in Sample Complexity</title>
    <updated>2026-11-19T15:02:51Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26228v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.26228v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Attention heads specialize into distinct functions during training, often emerging in stages together with sharp changes in model behavior. While this phenomenon has mostly been studied as a function of training time, we ask how head specialization depends on the amount of available training data. Empirically, we find that heads specialized to syntactic relations in BERT emerge as the dataset size increases. We then study this phenomenon in a solvable high-dimensional model of multi-head attention and establish that, in this model, head specialization is a genuine phase transition in sample complexity, corresponding to a non-analyticity in the test error and other observables. Depending on data structure and regularization, specialization can follow uninformative head differentiation or occur through a cascade of phase transitions that progressively recover weaker latent features, providing a statistical form of simplicity bias. Finally, we relate these statistical transitions to the stagewise emergence of specialized heads during online learning, disentangling statistical from dynamical origins of head specialization.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.25372v1</id>
    <title>Fundamentals for Binary Classification Under Label Noise</title>
    <updated>2026-11-19T02:11:34Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.25372v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.25372v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>This chapter surveys fundamental results for binary classification under label noise. Binary classification under label noise involves training models on datasets where class labels are partially incorrect, leading to degraded performance and misclassification. We distinguish poisoning attacks from noise processes and formalize random classification noise, Massart noise, and malicious classification noise within the probably approximately correct (PAC) framework. These models capture different adversarial strengths and data-generation realities. We then highlight some core ideas and representative results. In particular, we explain why random classification noise preserves the expected ordering of hypotheses and thus supports learning using the empirical risk minimization (ERM) principle, how sample complexity depends on the noise rate, and why learning algorithms often require an upper bound on the corruption level, as well as how such a bound may be estimated from data in the case of random classification noise. We also discuss computational aspects of ERM under noise and present a canonical negative result technique -- the method of induced distributions -- within the malicious noise model where the adversary has more power and may affect not only the label of an example but also the instance. We conclude with pointers to related work and a taxonomy that organizes classical label-noise models using the NCAR/NAR/NNAR lens.</summary>

    <title>Diffusion Models are Provably Efficient Priors for Sparse Recovery</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T15:27:29Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24602v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24602v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Diffusion models have transformed generative modeling through their ability to capture and generate samples from complex data distributions. This success has spurred substantial interest in using pretrained diffusion models as expressive priors for highly ill-posed inverse problems in imaging and sensing. Despite strong empirical performance, theoretical understanding of this approach remains limited: existing guarantees are often asymptotic or entail prohibitive computational costs in the worst case. In this paper, we address this gap by studying sparse recovery from a small number of linear measurements, a classical problem in compressed sensing. We show that, given an accurate diffusion model capturing a sparsity-promoting Bernoulli-Gaussian prior, a likelihood-guided annealed Langevin sampler provably recovers the sparse signal in polynomial time with near-optimal sample complexity for a broad family of random and deterministic sensing matrices. When the signal is indeed drawn from the postulated prior, we further establish total variation guarantees for posterior sampling after a final denoising step. These results lay a theoretical foundation for statistically and computationally efficient inverse solvers with diffusion priors.</summary>
