    <title>Temporal Contrastive Alignment of EEG and Naturalistic Video Only Beats Linear Decoding On In-Sample Stimuli</title>
    <updated>2026-11-19T15:31:27Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26258v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.26258v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Neural tracking, the temporal alignment between a continuous stimulus and the elicited brain response, enables decoding of attention from electroencephalography (EEG), yet its application to naturalistic video remains largely unexplored and mainly relies on linear canonical correlation analysis (CCA). We investigate whether a temporal contrastive model, pairing pretrained VideoMAE features with a lightweight EEG encoder trained on a correlation-based InfoNCE objective, can strengthen EEG-video alignment. Benchmarked against CCA under three generalization regimes, the model outperforms CCA across subjects (leave-one-subject-out), matches it within the stimulus manifold (leave-video-segment-out), and falls behind CCA when extrapolating to entirely novel videos (leave-one-video-out). Because this advantage appears only for seen stimuli, we probe its basis: a sham control shows that a high accuracy does not certify genuine alignment, as a synthesized correspondence fit to the seen stimuli can reproduce it without genuine temporal alignment in the training pairs. This does not preclude practical use: on a downstream attention-decoding task with seen stimuli, the model remains better than CCA since the decoding only requires a strong statistical coupling, regardless of whether that coupling is physiologically meaningful. Using a group-averaged EEG reference, we further show that genuine, generalizable coupling is nonetheless learned, only buried in the noise of single-subject EEG. These results indicate that progress hinges on data scale, diversity, and single-subject denoising.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26101v1</id>
    <title>Revealing Pathway Interactions in Network Computations with Complete Path Contribution</title>
    <updated>2026-11-19T13:34:00Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26101v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.26101v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Networks pass signals through many layers of interconnected units, so explaining what they compute means tracing how information travels from input to output and how pathways interact. Most existing approaches analyze only pairwise interactions between components such as units, layers or attention heads. Even when these measurements are combined post hoc into a circuit, they do not capture higher-order interactions along full causal chains (paths) from input to output, and so cannot address how exponentially many paths interact to construct network computation. This leaves a large set of mechanistic questions unanswerable, for example whether inhibitory pathways veto excitatory ones, and how the two combine to yield network decisions. To address this gap, we introduce Complete Path Contribution, a method to decompose the network output into mathematically complete contributions of individual paths to study path-level interactions directly and at scale. Partial summation then induces definitions of contributions for any circuit at any granularity level, with completeness guaranteed at every level. We further present an efficient algorithm that identifies the $k$ strongest paths without examining all of them, with runtime empirically linear in $k$ rather than exponential in depth. By applying Path Contribution to benchmark image classification networks, we quantify excitatory-inhibitory interactions and show how they collectively construct network decisions at a level of detail previously unmeasurable. Furthermore, in an interpretable model of the mouse retina, it reveals how dynamic receptive fields emerge from excitatory-inhibitory interaction motifs among pathways between different cell types in response to time-varying natural stimuli. Overall, Path Contribution reveals how a network's causal pathways interact at scale to transform input to output.</summary>

    <title>Déjà View: A Shared Working-Memory Model for Visual Tasks</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T18:23:14Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23177v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.23177v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>A working-memory model must remember stimuli and use its memory flexibly to perform different tasks. Here we introduce a model of working memory for images that combines dynamic activity with temporary associations between image features. We train the model on five tasks, including remembering a sample while other images are presented, categorizing distractor images while remembering the sample, and determining whether an image is new or has been presented before. The same trained model performs all tasks, guided by explicit cues about which response is required. We use this flexible memory model to ask how delay, distraction, and image history affect performance. Delays have little effect on sample-memory performance for the delays we tested, while seeing more images leads to more false alarms even when the target image appeared equally recently in all cases. On the sample-memory-plus-categorization task, the probability of correct responses on all questions decreases as more questions are asked, despite robust sample-memory performance. Finally, the model maintains stable performance across 40 brief trials of each task under the tested conditions. Together, these results demonstrate how a single working-memory system can be flexibly used to perform different tasks, and how its errors depend on both previous images and task demands.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22054v1</id>
    <title>A single inference process underlies the behavior and neural circuits of working memory</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T01:29:43Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22054v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.22054v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Working memory holds past inputs online for future behavior. Despite decades of research, accounts of working memory remain divided across levels of analysis, with long-standing debates on whether its capacity reflects discrete slots or continuous resources, how attention improves recall, and whether its representations rely on persistent neural firing or activity-silent states. Here we show that MemGP, a theory that is specified at the computational, algorithmic, and circuit levels of analysis simultaneously, can explain diverse behavioral and neural phenomena in working memory. At the computational level, MemGP casts working memory as probabilistic inference over a continuous function on feature space, with a variational objective that balances memory strength against a Gaussian-process prior. At the algorithmic level, writing, storing, and reading of memories correspond to approximating this posterior with a finite set of inducing points, the resource that all items share. In simulations, MemGP reproduces load-dependent precision loss, attentional benefits during maintenance, and inter-item attraction and repulsion, in each case revealing multiple complex computational dependencies. At the circuit level, the algorithm analytically (without training) maps onto a recurrent circuit, including its architecture and dynamics. Beyond reproducing neural phenomena such as delay-dependent drift, this analytical map deduces center--surround connectivity, a property long assumed in attractor models, and a structured combination of persistent activity and synaptic weights to hold memories. Thus, a single inference objective not only jointly predicts the behavioral and neural signatures of working memory, but also addresses, across several instances and different levels of analysis, existing competing explanations.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26590v1</id>
    <title>Probing the "Conscious" Mind: Selective Access and Global Workspace in Vision-Language Models</title>
    <updated>2026-11-19T18:46:50Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26590v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.26590v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Vision-language models (VLMs) integrate visual and textual information, but their outputs do not reveal internal concept representations. Global workspace theory (GWT) proposes that information is selected from parallel brain processes, integrated in a shared workspace, and made available to specialised processes. We introduce the Multimodal Concept Lens (MC-Lens), a multimodal Jacobian lens, to study these functions in VLM concept processing. Its vision encoder and language decoder lenses map intermediate states to a shared semantic space defined by the decoder's output vocabulary to compare concept accessibility across modalities. MC-Lens supports internal concept interventions to examine the role of accessed concepts in downstream computation. (i) Accessibility and selective access. Multimodal concept information is readable in intermediate states and selectively accessible as tasks require. We extend "readout carriers" from one name token to a token set to better capture and express concept information and support counterfactual experiments. (ii) Concepts in downstream computation. Counterfactual experiments show that accessed concept information participates in downstream computation and reasoning. (iii) Development of cross-modal alignment and selective access. We develop two J-space metrics tracking the development of cross-modal concept alignment more clearly than hidden state cosine in controlled VLM training. The experiment also shows that reliable selective access develops later than concept accessibility. (iv) Shared functions across models. Across VLM families and sizes, we find shared patterns of concept accessibility, query-dependent selectivity and cross-task intervention effects despite differences in internal organisation. These findings offer an experimental basis to study GWT in multimodal artificial systems and how it can guide cross-modal alignment improvements.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26018v1</id>
    <title>Does the Workspace Do the Work? A Causal Protocol for Verifying Global-Workspace Computation in a Language Model</title>
    <updated>2026-11-19T12:33:35Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26018v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.26018v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Global Workspace Theory (GWT), a leading theory of consciousness, holds that information becomes conscious when it is broadcast to specialized processes that use it. Building a workspace into a network does not reveal what the trained network computes with it: a module that reports an answer may have combined a broadcast message with its own knowledge, or merely forwarded an answer computed elsewhere, and task accuracy and ablation cannot tell these apart. We introduce a causal protocol that identifies who computes when modules communicate. Its central test transplants a message from another input, chosen so that ignoring, relaying and recombining it predict three different answers. On networks built to relay or to recombine, the test assigns the right computation in every case. Among trained workspace models it finds all three outcomes: one leaves its broadcast nearly unused, and of two models that differ only in their training data, one relays and the other recombines. In AFGW, a language model whose modules communicate only through a learned workspace, a transplanted message yields the answer that recombination predicts in 97% of cases, and its content acts by redirecting what the receiver retrieves from its own memory. The tests carry over to other communication designs and to a known interface of a pretrained Transformer, turning GWT's central claim into a testable property of trained models.</summary>

    <title>Knowing What You Know: A Trait Theory of Reviewer Value in Human-AI Cognitive Systems</title>
    <updated>2026-11-18T18:55:07Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.24932v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.24932v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>When a capable model and a human reviewer cooperate on the same decision, which human still adds value? We argue this is a question about a single cognitive trait, metacognitive calibration: the alignment between a reviewer's behavioral confidence and the actual correctness of their judgments. We develop a trait theory of reviewer value to make it precise. The theory makes five claims: value is governed by calibration rather than by activity, speed, agreement, or tenure; calibration leaves observable traces in behavioral telemetry; those traces are non-diagnostic on their own, because the fast, low-revision signature of a calibrated expert is indistinguishable from that of a confident novice until it is gated by outcomes; human calibration and a model's self-knowledge are the same construct, so the joint system should defer to whichever agent is better calibrated on each item; and individual calibration is causally identifiable only above the level of the single judgment. We ground each claim in a six-month production window of an AI-assisted accounting system (541621 reviewer events, 483 reviewers), and find that a purely behavioral expertise profile inverts the ground truth, scoring an overconfident cohort (5.2 percent correction survival) higher than genuine experts (99.2 percent); that reviewer quality is flat across tenure, so the trait is not learned on the job; and that the same calibration logic that separates good from bad reviewers, applied to the model, concentrates 92.5 percent of human effort on genuine errors. We close with the boundary the theory must respect: under majority-vote aggregation, individual causal value is unidentifiable.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23106v1</id>
    <title>Natural Language Programming: Rethinking Language, Memory, and Cognition in the Era of Generative AI</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T17:27:01Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.23106v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.23106v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Generative Artificial Intelligence is transforming the role of natural language in computational systems. In classical Natural Language Processing (NLP), language was treated as an object of computation: something to analyse, classify, translate, or generate. Large Language Models (LLMs) challenge this perspective, enabling natural language to function increasingly as an executable cognitive medium through which humans structure reasoning, orchestrate problem solving, and regulate hybrid human/AI workflows.
  This paper introduces Natural Language Programming (NLPg) as a theoretical and epistemological extension of traditional NLP. Rather than focusing on language understanding alone, NLPg conceptualises prompts as dynamic cognitive artefacts that externalise goals, constraints, assumptions, validation criteria, and intermediate reasoning states. Prompting is thus not merely a technical interaction technique, but a form of dialogic cognitive programming operating within distributed human/AI memory architectures.
  Building on theories of distributed cognition, extended mind, metacognition, and dialogic learning, the paper proposes the notion of Dialogic Working Memory, describing how prompts and conversational states function as temporary external memory structures supporting reasoning continuity and reflective regulation. We further map existing memory architectures (BTMA, SKGE, RMR) onto this framework, illustrating how episodic, semantic, and metacognitive layers support long-horizon conversational coherence.
  Finally, implications for computational linguistics and AI/mediated knowledge systems are discussed, suggesting a post symbolic and post interface paradigm in which natural language operates simultaneously as communication medium, executable specification, cognitive scaffold, and distributed memory architecture.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20826v1</id>
    <title>Conversing with a Conversational Agent: A Real Conversation, Not a Simulated One</title>
    <updated>2026-11-16T10:09:08Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20826v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.20826v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>The claim that interactions with artificial conversational agents merely simulate human conversation rests on a philosophical distinction between reproducing the observable features of an activity and actually performing it. Although this distinction is appropriate for certain physical phenomena, its application to linguistic and symbolic activities is far less straightforward. This article argues that conversations with large language model (LLM)-based agents are genuine conversational activities rather than mere simulations, without thereby attributing consciousness, subjective understanding, or human intentionality to artificial systems. Drawing on the distinction between subjective and objective simulation, the article first examines the limitations of defining conversation exclusively through the intrinsic properties of its participants. It then develops a relational and semiotic account of conversational activity, informed by linguistic pragmatics, Lacan's Conversing with a Conversational Agent theory of the mirror, Baudrillard's concept of the simulacrum, Simondon's philosophy of individuation, and Peirce's semiotics. These perspectives make it possible to distinguish the reality of conversational interaction from the appearance of artificial subjectivity and from the epistemic validity of the meanings produced. The argument culminates in the concept of Hybrid Semiotic Fabrication, which characterizes meaning-making as a distributed process involving human participants, artificial intelligence, corpora, and technical arrangements. Recognizing the reality of human-AI conversation therefore entails neither anthropomorphizing artificial agents nor granting their outputs epistemic authority. Rather, it requires a more precise account of the relational, semiotic, and normative conditions under which conversational meaning is produced and justified.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.12809v1</id>
    <title>Qualiaphobic artificial neural networks (and why to build them)</title>
    <updated>2026-11-09T18:14:43Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.12809v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.12809v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>This paper introduces qualiaphobic AI: artificial neural network architectures that are hostile to theories of consciousness. I show that qualiaphobia can be well-justified by knowledge about theories of consciousness, like when such theories are trivial or unfalsifiable or contradicted by overwhelming scientific evidence. It can also be justified by how theories of consciousness must be grounded in phenomenology, as well as how current popular theories of consciousness are applied to AI. I identify and explore three convergent ways of engineering qualiaphobia that would minimize the potential for artificial consciousness. These include making AI architectures as close as possible to "anchor points" of systems with minimal potential for consciousness, fragmenting any potential phenomenology AI might have, and designing artificial neural networks in a way adversarial to popular theories of consciousness. In particular, I develop one "anchor point" of minimal potential for consciousness: systems where only behaviorist theories of consciousness can apply, and I propose qualiaphobic transformations that move existing artificial neural networks toward such systems. Additionally, I develop an account of how AIs can form justified beliefs about their own non-consciousness (or minimal potential for consciousness) and expand on how this knowledge would change their behavior. Most critically, I begin with why this research is important: qualiaphobic AI has epistemic properties that make it far better aligned with human civilization. Since consciousness is central to moral value, a world in which AIs are non-conscious ensures it is always morally correct for AI to assist and serve humanity, rather than pursue its own ends.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.12762v2</id>
    <title>Sage-Taiyi: A Metacognitive Architecture for Scientific Discovery</title>
    <updated>2026-11-13T08:33:13Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.12762v2" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.12762v2" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We introduce Sage-Taiyi, a metacognition-inspired architecture that uses accumulated scientific understanding to guide what to investigate next and how to investigate it. Through explicit monitoring and control, the system revises its understanding of evidence, assumptions, and unresolved questions, then uses these assessments to adapt research targets and select reusable reasoning methods. On Taiyi-Bench, an AI co-scientist ideation benchmark comprising 265 tasks from 50 papers across ten disciplines, Sage-Taiyi ranks first on all eight metrics of historical rediscovery and open-ended ideation, achieving an Overall score of 54.0 compared with 47.9 for the strongest baseline, AI Scientist-v2. It also performs well on two external scientific ideation benchmarks. Five expert-guided collaborations further connect its proposals to experimental and computational validation across chemistry, materials science, and engineering. In chemistry, reaction-condition optimization raises the yield of cobalt-catalyzed carbonylation from trace amounts to 84% and photocatalytic allylic amination from 13% to 69%. These results support metacognitive regulation as an approach to scientific ideation and its progression toward practical validation.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08469v1</id>
    <title>Same Behavior, Different Mechanism: What Finite Experiments Can Certify About Integrated Information</title>
    <updated>2026-11-05T18:55:31Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08469v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08469v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Interpretability, AI auditing and assessments of machine consciousness increasingly rest on mechanism-level quantities: functionals of a system's causal transition law that describe how it computes, not what it outputs. Experiments see that law only through finite, partial and noisy interventions. We ask when such a quantity is identifiable from an experiment's access, continuous in the mechanism and certifiable from finite data, and answer exactly for a deliberately demanding case - the integrated information $\varphi$ of integrated information theory - in stochastic networks of four and five units with known ground truth. Behavior can be silent: a recurrent and a feed-forward network with identical input-output laws at their response delay carry 0.28 and 0 bits, yet internal recordings separate them within 4-53 trials. Partial access can be just as blind: in our examples, units left out of a one-step recording impose precision floors of 0.30-1.02 bits that no sample size lowers, and in all-but-self parity networks, recordings of any length see several hidden units only through the product of their fidelities - a symmetry that one intervention broke in exact checks. The measure has sharp edges: because $\varphi$ selects a partition, and the cause and effect it specifies, by one criterion and reports another, infinitesimal changes of mechanism that cross an edge change it by 25-100% at 99% of the edges we found in random networks, and about 1% of surrogate models that fit interventional data almost perfectly misreport it by more than 20%. One-sided claims survive: the same data certify a lower bound on both sides of an edge, and we prove $\varphi>1.004$ bits throughout a 64-dimensional region of mechanisms and certify it from about $10^7$ controlled transitions with false-certificate probability at most $α$. Measurability is thus a design question with computable answers.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30030v1</id>
    <title>Evidence Toward a Conjecture in List Recoverability of Folded Reed--Solomon Codes</title>
    <updated>2026-11-23T04:33:02Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30030v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.30030v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>This paper investigates the list-recoverability of folded Reed--Solomon codes and provides new evidence toward a recent conjecture. Chen--Zhang (STOC 2025) established that for any $\ell,a \ge 2$ and $L = \ell^a - 1$, if a folded Reed--Solomon code of rate $R$ is $(ρ,\ell,L)$-list-recoverable, then $ρ\leq \frac{L+1-\ell}{L+1}(1-\frac{aR}{a-1}).$ It is conjectured that this upper bound is tight. We provide two pieces of evidence concerning this conjecture. First, we prove that explicit folded Reed--Solomon codes of rate arbitrarily close to $\tfrac{a-1}{a+\ell-2}$ are $(0,\ell,L)$-list-recoverable, which confirms the conjecture in the special case $ρ=0$ and $\ell=2$. Second, we show that for any $R\in(0,\tfrac{a-1}{a})$, there are rates arbitrarily close to $R$ at which attaining the conjectured bound requires exponentially large alphabets. This mirrors the phenomenon observed by Alrabiah--Guruswami--Li (SODA 2024), where achieving the generalized Singleton bound in the list-decoding setting also necessitates exponential alphabet size.</summary>

    <title>Cylindrical dimers and monomial immanants</title>
    <updated>2026-11-23T00:40:51Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.29860v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.29860v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>For a bipartite graph on a cylinder, group its perfect matchings by homological height and sum their weights in each group. We prove that every minor of the resulting Toeplitz matrix has nonnegative coefficients in the edge weights, settling a question recorded by Lai. We first prove conjectures of Galashin and the author concerning directed cycles in cylindrical networks, and then deduce the dimer theorem from them. A related, stronger positivity property for superpositions of cylindrical matchings turns out to be equivalent to Stembridge's interval-product conjecture on monomial immanants. Using annular webs, we prove this conjecture for partitions with at most four columns. A stretching argument extends this to all partitions with parts in $\{n,2n,3n,4n\}$.</summary>

    <title>The dimensions of curly and dipolar Besicovitch-Kakeya sets</title>
    <updated>2026-11-22T22:06:56Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.29803v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.29803v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>In this paper, we establish sharp Hausdorff dimension and box-counting dimension bounds for sets containing meridian circles and for sets whose difference sets contain a sphere.
  Fix two antipodal points N, S on S^{n-1}, n\ge 3, and consider the family of great circles passing through them. Assuming the Besicovitch-Kakeya overlapping conjecture in R^{n-1}, we prove that every bounded set K\subset R^n containing a translated and dilated copy of each circle in this family satisfies \dim_H K\ge n-1. In particular, the same conclusion holds for bounded sets containing a circle in every orientation. This bound is sharp, as shown by the unit sphere. We also prove unconditionally that every bounded set K\subset R^n, n\ge2, satisfying S^{n-1}\subset K-K has lower box counting dimension greater than or equal to n(n-1)/(2n-1), and the bound is also sharp.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.29786v1</id>
    <title>Parity-safe digraphs with countably many ends are kernel-perfect</title>
    <updated>2026-11-22T21:41:53Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.29786v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.29786v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>A kernel of a digraph is an independent set that every other vertex points into, and a digraph is kernel-perfect if every induced subgraph has a kernel. A digraph without odd cycles in which no ray contains infinitely many vertices that each send an infinite fan of disjoint paths to that ray is safe. The conjecture that every safe digraph is kernel-perfect was proved earlier for digraphs with finitely many ends.
  We prove a stronger statement for at most countably many ends. Number the vertices of a ray, and let the type of a path that ends on the ray be the parity of the sum of its length and the number of its last vertex. A fan is mixed if it has infinitely many paths of each type, and a digraph is parity-safe if it has no odd cycle and no ray containing infinitely many vertices with a mixed fan to it. Yablo's graph (omega,<) is not parity-safe. Its variant with edges only between vertices of different parity has a kernel - it is parity-safe but not safe. Our main result is that a parity-safe digraph with at most countably many ends is kernel-perfect, and the claim for safe digraphs follows since safety implies parity-safety. The digraph may have any cardinality, and nothing is assumed about the structure of the ends, but the case of uncountably many ends remains open.</summary>

    <updated>2026-11-22T21:31:05Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.29782v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.29782v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>This paper introduces the notion of a commutative bishuffle algebra, that linearizes classical pattern avoidance. The free commutative bishuffle algebra on one generator has a basis of permutations, divisibility of monomials is pattern containment, and the classes of permutations avoiding given patterns are the monomial bases of its quotients by monomial ideals. This free algebra is not Noetherian, but we show that its quotient by the antisymmetrizer $e_k$ is Noetherian for every $k$, and we conjecture that the same holds for its quotient by any nonzero ideal stable under the symmetric groups, in analogy with the Specht problem. We develop Gröbner bases for ideals of the free algebra and prove that the elements $e_k\oplusτ$, with $τ$ ranging over any set of permutations, form a Gröbner basis for the lexicographic ordering and for its opposite. This gives an algebraic form of the theorem of Backelin, West and Xin: the permutations avoiding all $k\cdots21\oplusτ$ and those avoiding all $12\cdots k\oplusτ$ are two monomial bases of one and the same quotient.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.29726v1</id>
    <title>Counting Eulerian Orientations in Regular Graphs</title>
    <updated>2026-11-22T19:45:25Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.29726v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.29726v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Let $G$ be a pseudograph, and let $\varepsilon(G)$ denote the number of Eulerian orientations of $G$. Lieb and Wu, and later Schrijver, showed that if $G$ has degree sequence $(d_1,d_2,\dots,d_n)$, where each $d_i$ is a positive even integer, then \[ \varepsilon(G) \geq \prod_{i = 1}^n 2^{-d_i/2} \binom{d_i}{d_i/2}.\] Schrijver conjectured that for simple $d$-regular graphs, $\varepsilon(G)\leq\varepsilon(K_{d+1})^{n/(d+1)}$, with equality attained by disjoint unions of cliques of order $d+1$. In this paper, we prove a multigraph bound that implies the known case $d=4$, and we also improve Schrijver's lower bound for $d$-regular graphs, using an inductive relation between $\varepsilon(G)$ and the number $\ell_i(G)$ of cycles of each possible length $i \geq 1$ in $G$. We define \[ \ell(G) = \sum_{i = 1}^n \frac{\ell_i(G)}{(d - 1)^i}\] and we prove with $λ= (d - 1)\log(1 + 1/(d - 1))$ that for all $d \geq 2$, \[ \varepsilon(G) \geq \exp(λ\ell(G)) \cdot S_d(n),\] where $S_d(n)$ denotes $2^{-dn/2}\binom{d}{d/2}^n$. The bound sharply improves the lower bound of Lieb, Wu and Schrijver, and gives good estimates for $\varepsilon(G)$ for various graphs, such as integer lattices. The bound is almost tight for random regular graphs, and we conjecture for each even $d \geq 4$ that there exists a constant $c_d > 0$ such that $\varepsilon(G) \leq \exp(c_dλ\ell(G)) \cdot S_d(n)$ for every $n$-vertex $d$-regular pseudograph.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.29669v1</id>
    <title>Universal Implications Among $k$-Prime Graph Labelings</title>
    <updated>2026-11-22T18:22:36Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.29669v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.29669v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>For $k\ge1$, let $\mathcal P_k$ be the class of graphs admitting a bijective labeling by consecutive integers beginning at $k$, with coprime labels at adjacent vertices. We determine all universal inclusions between distinct such classes: $\mathcal P_i\subseteq\mathcal P_j$ holds for $i\ne j$ if and only if $(i,j)=(2,1)$ or $(3,1)$. In particular, the classes are pairwise distinct. The proof translates universal inclusion into a spanning-embedding question for coprimality graphs on consecutive integer intervals. Edge-count identities, arithmetic-progression estimates, and prime-residue switching exclude all other inclusions; a prime-gap argument reduces the remaining finite range to fifteen explicit rational inequalities. We further show that, for each nonexceptional ordered pair, the graph orders at which edge counts obstruct inclusion have a positive natural density. This density is described through a limiting distribution of correlated Euler products, for which we give an atomlessness argument. The classification resolves the distinct-index formulation of the universal-implication conjecture.</summary>

    <title>The Eulerian transformation preserves log-convexity</title>
    <updated>2026-11-22T14:34:05Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.29517v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.29517v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>In their 2007 paper on the log-convexity of combinatorial sequences, Liu and Wang conjectured that the Eulerian transformation preserves log-convexity. We completely solve their conjecture by showing that this transformation preserves strong $q$-log-convexity. More generally, we provide a sufficient condition for a linear transformation, defined by a triangular array satisfying a certain three-term recurrence relation, to preserve strong $q$-log-convexity. As applications, we show that both the $r$-colored Eulerian transformation and the $m$-Stirling Eulerian transformation preserve strong $q$-log-convexity. In particular, we confirm a conjecture due to Liu and Zhu, which states that the Eulerian transformation of type $B$ preserves log-convexity.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30146v1</id>
    <title>Optimal Private Gaussian Multi-sampling</title>
    <updated>2026-11-23T06:49:38Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30146v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.30146v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We give polynomial-time algorithms for Gaussian multi-sampling under approximate $(\varepsilon,δ)$-differential privacy, with optimal sample complexity up to logarithmic factors. Our main construction uses $\widetilde{O}(m+d\sqrt{m}/\varepsilon)$ independent input samples from a $d$-dimensional Gaussian $P$ with unknown mean and covariance to generate $m$ exactly independent outputs. Their joint distribution is $α$-close in total variation to $P^{\otimes m}$. Our lower bounds hold even for dependent outputs under the same joint accuracy guarantee, showing that exact independence incurs no additional sample cost beyond logarithmic factors.
  The single-sampler of Iverson, Kamath, and Mouzakis [COLT 2025] uses $\widetilde{O}(d/\varepsilon)$ input samples. Running it on a separate input dataset for each of $m$ outputs therefore costs $\widetilde{O}(md/\varepsilon)$ in total. Our construction reduces this dimension-dependent sample cost from linear to square-root dependence on the number of outputs.
  Our approach builds on the stable weighted statistics of Brown, Hopkins, and Smith [COLT 2023], also used for Gaussian single-sampling by Iverson, Kamath, and Mouzakis. To control privacy loss when the entire batch shares these statistics, we compare the joint output densities and obtain a privacy bound that scales with the square root of the batch size. The stability step downweights influential records and can reject the entire batch. Both actions can make the outputs dependent. Our correction restores exact independence while preserving differential privacy and joint accuracy.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30038v1</id>
    <title>Super-Multiplicativity of the Noncommutative Minimum and Applications to Quantum Privacy and Hypothesis Testing</title>
    <updated>2026-11-23T04:46:01Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30038v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.30038v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>The hockey-stick divergence is a fundamental distinguishability measure in quantum information theory. It characterizes quantum differential privacy and determines the optimal error probability of binary quantum hypothesis testing with arbitrary priors. We study how it behaves on tensor-product states. To this end, we consider the noncommutative minimum $m(A,B):=(\mathrm{Tr}[A]+\mathrm{Tr}[B]-\|A-B\|_1)/2$ of positive semidefinite operators, which reduces to $\sum_x\min\{a_x,b_x\}$ when $A$ and $B$ commute, and we prove that it is super-multiplicative, i.e., $m(A\otimes C,B\otimes D)\ge m(A,B)\,m(C,D)$. As a consequence, we establish a sub-additivity property of the hockey-stick divergence on product states, in which the parameters of the individual systems are multiplied, and no additional prefactor appears. We show that this bound is tight, also for noncommuting states, and that it is strict for faithful states whenever at least two of the divergences are positive. Using this, we obtain sub-additivity of the Datta-Leditzky divergences, a parallel composition theorem for quantum differentially private channels under product neighboring inputs with at most linear degradation of the privacy parameters, and a sharp sub-additivity property of the hypothesis-testing relative entropy normalized by the acceptance probability. Finally, we apply the same tools to symmetric binary quantum hypothesis testing. We determine the exact prefactor of the quantum Chernoff bound for every pair of noncommuting states satisfying mild conditions including a nonlattice condition and, under a quantitative version of this condition, the full asymptotic expansion to every fixed order in $1/n$, with explicitly computable coefficients. As a consequence, we determine the sample complexity of symmetric binary quantum hypothesis testing up to one sample, as the error probability tends to zero.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30003v1</id>
    <title>Statistically Optimal and Near Linear Time Hypothesis Selection</title>
    <updated>2026-11-23T04:08:34Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30003v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.30003v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>In hypothesis selection we are given $n$ distributions $q_1,\dots,q_n$ on a countable domain $\mathcal{X}$ and samples from an unknown distribution $p$. The goal is a distribution $q$ with $\mathrm{TV}(p,q)\leα\min_i\mathrm{TV}(p,q_i)+ε$. The factor $α=2$ is optimal for algorithms using a number of samples from $p$ that is independent of $|\mathcal{X}|$, and in general only improper learners achieve it. We give a learner that achieves $α=2$ with $O(\log(n/δ)/ε^2)$ samples of $p$, with probability at least $1-δ$. This matches the sample complexity of Yatracos's factor-$3$ estimator, and it removes the logarithmic factors in the factor-$2$ bound of Bousquet et al. (FOCS 2021). The learner accesses the $q_i$ only through sampling and pointwise comparisons. We measure its running time by its oracle complexity, the number of oracle calls. In expectation it makes $O((nε^{-2}+ε^{-4}\log(1/ε))\log(n/δ))$ oracle calls, independent of $\mathcal{X}$. It runs multiplicative weights over the constraints $\mathrm{TV}(q,q_i)\le\mathrm{TV}(p,q_i)$ and uses at most one sample of $p$ per round.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.29720v1</id>
    <title>Randomized Weighted Distance Nearest Neighbor Classification</title>
    <updated>2026-11-22T19:40:22Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.29720v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.29720v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>The nearest neighbor classifier is known to be memory-inefficient, and a popular solution is to compress its training data. Recently, a compression algorithm based on weighted distance nearest neighbor (WNN) was proposed, which has elegant theoretical properties and effective classification performance. However, its compression process is computationally expensive, for it performs a greedy search of the densest homogeneous balls in data space. In this paper, we propose a randomized variant RWNN. It simply randomizes the ball search process, and results in substantially reduced compression time (often 0.1%--1% of WNN's) and similar classification accuracy. RWNN also inherits several theoretical properties of WNN including consistency and a generalization bound. Experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate its efficacy.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28628v1</id>
    <title>Nearly Minimax-Optimal Sample Complexity of Natural Policy Gradient with a Matching Information-Theoretic Lower Bound</title>
    <updated>2026-11-21T07:31:10Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28628v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.28628v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>A fundamental question in reinforcement learning is how many sampled transitions are needed to learn a near-optimal policy, and whether direct policy optimization can attain this statistical limit. To answer this question, we consider natural policy gradient (NPG), a widely used policy optimization method. We study tabular finite-horizon Markov decision processes (MDPs) with known rewards and unknown horizon-dependent transition kernels, accessed through a generative model. Our sample-based NPG algorithms update the policy by backward sweeps and do not estimate transition probabilities. Under three different batch-size and step size schedules, we establish last-iterate guarantees with sample complexity $\widetilde O(SAH^4/\varepsilon^2)$, where $S$, $A$, and $H$ denote the number of states, the number of actions, and the horizon length, respectively. In this setting, horizon-dependent transition kernels contribute a factor of $H$ to our transition-query bound. Our information-theoretic lower bound of $Ω(SAH^4/\varepsilon^2)$ shows that the resulting $H^4$ dependence is unavoidable in the worst case, even for agents that select their queries adaptively. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first last-iterate guarantees for NPG whose sample complexity matches an information-theoretic lower bound up to logarithmic factors. Consequently, our results demonstrate that direct policy-space optimization through NPG can achieve the fundamental statistical limits of reinforcement learning while guaranteeing the performance of the final policy. Furthermore, for known kernels, we prove that exact NPG with a constant step size $η=1/H$ requires $Ω(H^2/\varepsilon)$ iterations in the worst case, matching the known upper bound for that step size.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28460v1</id>
    <title>Optimal User-Level Private Stochastic Convex Optimization and Mean Estimation with Heavy Tails</title>
    <updated>2026-11-21T01:26:29Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28460v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.28460v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We study stochastic convex optimization with heavy-tailed stochastic gradients under $(\varepsilon, δ)$-user-level differential privacy, which protects each user's entire collection of samples. Instead of assuming a uniformly bounded Lipschitz constant, we only assume bounds on the second- and $k$-th moments of the random sample Lipschitz parameters. This allows for unbounded, heavy-tailed stochastic gradient distributions and can lead to sharper excess risk bounds. We characterize the minimax optimal excess population risk up to logarithmic factors. Our algorithm achieves the optimal rate with only $\widetilde{O}(1/\varepsilon)$ users. As a byproduct of our algorithmic developments, we obtain tight bounds for user-level private mean estimation under norm-moment assumptions, improving over the guarantees of Esfandiari et al. (2022) and Zhao et al. (2024). Finally, for mean estimation under the directional-moment assumption of Agarwal et al. (2025), we close their remaining approximate-DP gap by removing the additional $d/\varepsilon$ user requirement and attaining the optimal sample complexity up to logarithmic factors.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28399v1</id>
    <title>Data-Dependent Probability Estimation via Sample Amplification</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T23:06:04Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28399v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.28399v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Can we estimate the probability of an event chosen after seeing the data, without using any fresh samples? Its empirical probability can be arbitrarily misleading, while learning the entire distribution to constant accuracy requires $Θ(d)$ samples on a domain of size $d$. We show that $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{d})$ samples suffice for constant mean squared error, provided the rule choosing the event is known. More generally, our estimator handles arbitrary $[0,1]$-valued queries and runs in polynomial time given evaluation access to the rule. This sample complexity matches the known lower bound up to logarithmic factors and resolves the open question posed by Feldman, Kale, Raman, Talwar, and Tewari (arXiv:2610.41244).
  Our estimation framework relies on a new combination of sample amplification (arXiv:1904.12053 and arXiv:2201.04315) with distribution learning via online optimization. Our estimator achieves mean squared error $O(d^{3/4}/n)$ when $d\leq n$ and $\widetilde{O}(d^{1/4}/\sqrt{n})$ when $d>n$. We complement this with a lower bound of $Ω(\min\{1,\sqrt{d}/n\})$ on the mean squared error. Using our framework, we also design an efficient estimator for data-dependent queries on Gaussian distributions with unknown mean and identity covariance. Finally, we show that a smoothed variant of the problem is much (exponentially) easier. For discrete distributions, if the sample size is chosen uniformly from $\{n,\ldots,2n-1\}$, then $n=O(\log d)$ suffices for constant mean squared error.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28234v1</id>
    <title>Learning the Projection onto the Data Support: Distribution Learning that Avoids Memorization</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T19:07:27Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28234v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.28234v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We introduce a framework for learning distributions supported on manifolds based on estimating the nearest-point projection onto the data support. Specifically, we define an objective functional over a class of functions whose minimizer recovers this projection. The proposed framework automatically adapts to the intrinsic dimension and allows for data supported on unions of manifolds with varying dimensions. The resulting objective can be optimized using standard neural network architectures. We present population-level results establishing recovery of the manifold projection and prove finite-sample Wasserstein generalization bounds. Furthermore, we validate the approach empirically across a range of settings. In contrast to widely used generative models such as diffusion models, whose objectives can be minimized by memorizing training samples, our formulation excludes such behavior. We also introduce a direct memorization metric to verify that the learned projection generates new samples rather than reproducing the training set.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30521v1</id>
    <title>Collective order from language models without communication, memory or shared context</title>
    <updated>2026-11-23T11:38:18Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30521v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.30521v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Physical matter orders without a centre: units interact only with neighbours, and fluctuations carry them over energy barriers from a locally stable arrangement to the ordered state. We ask whether language-model agents can do the same, treating each memoryless query as a particle that sees its neighbours but cannot communicate, has no identifier or shared context and receives the same question as all others. Such a particle behaves as if at zero temperature: told a rule or a temperature, it returns the most probable state, and a collective can freeze in a local minimum. We therefore give each particle only a goal and a die whose weights it sets itself, and test several models. Some of them use the die as a noise source even at a local optimum, with weights that fall with the energy cost of the move; on a lattice the energy of one of them climbs over barriers and reaches the ground state, where the noise stops by itself. Particles in three-lane counterflow also order, from mixed traffic into one-way lanes: a spontaneous symmetry breaking. Decentralized collective order can thus arise from disorder without communication, memory or shared context, with noise that the particles choose themselves.</summary>
    <category term="cond-mat.stat-mech" scheme="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom"/>

    <title>Metastable states are precursors of Turing patterns in Adaptive Networks</title>
    <updated>2026-11-21T14:27:36Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28828v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.28828v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>In networked reaction-diffusion systems, emergence of patterns from a homogeneous equilibrium can be described by Turing instability. Recently, Turing theory has been developed to include adaptive networks where, i.e., link weights change as a function of the states of the nodes. In this work we show that metastable states, defined as long living transient epochs with unique dynamical properties, could be observed in a range of parameters between Turing patterns and absence of any spatial pattern. Stated differently in the metastable regime the system ''switches'' between the homogeneous solution and the Turing pattern, never settling in any of those states, i.e., alternating silent and spiking regimes. By using phase diagrams and recurrence plots, we have numerically shown the existence of metastable states for the Brusselator model. Moreover, the dependence of the emergence of the metastable states on the adaptive control parameter has been characterized. The applicability of methods and ideas proposed in this work go beyond the considered case, they can help us in understanding conditions under which metastable states arise and could thus be informative to predict and control the latter.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27766v1</id>
    <title>Critical slowing down in hive temperature does not provide actionable early warnings of honey bee colony collapse</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T15:56:59Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27766v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27766v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Early warning signals (EWS) based on critical slowing down (CSD) have been proposed as model-independent indicators of approaching ecological regime shifts and may help anticipate honeybee colony collapse. However, whether theoretically expected signals can be reliably observed and provide useful prediction in real-world systems remains uncertain. Here, we combine structural analysis, mechanistic modeling and longitudinal observations to assess the dynamical plausibility, detectability and predictive accuracy of CSD-based EWS for honeybee colony collapse. Our results show that the presence of EWS is not equivalent to successful prediction of the transition. The analyzed models exhibit regime shifts accompanied by CSD, but detecting these signals in finite and noisy observations requires longer and more densely sampled time series than typically available for practical monitoring. Moreover, in empirical temperature records, CSD-like trends were detectable but provided limited discrimination between colonies that subsequently collapsed and those that survived. Declining mean temperature provided slightly greater discrimination than conventional CSD indicators, although its predictive value remained modest. Non-Gaussian correlated noise and the imperfect correspondence between hive temperature and colony strength further constrained EWS performance. These findings show that EWS can exist at the dynamical level without becoming useful predictors at the observational level, at least for our case study, thus cautioning against treating CSD-based indicators as generic predictors of ecological collapse.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27647v1</id>
    <title>Cyclic perturbations encode memories in trained neural networks without loss of performance</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T14:11:43Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27647v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27647v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Many disordered materials exhibit a remarkable form of memory: they retain information about the history of cyclic perturbations. Whether this phenomenon also occurs in artificial neural networks, whose mathematical structure and dynamics share many similarities with disordered physical systems, is unknown. Here we show that cyclically perturbing a trained, overparameterized deep neural network encodes information in the structure of the weights that can subsequently be retrieved, thus retaining memory of the perturbation history. During each write cycle, all weights are displaced, after which the network relaxes through gradient descent. Repeated cycles organise the neural network into a state that is reversible for perturbations up to the write amplitude, allowing the encoded value to be read from the onset of irreversible weight motion. Multiple memories can also be encoded, although under deterministic writing only the largest persists at long times. Inspired by cyclically sheared suspensions, we introduce a novel noisy-write protocol that preserves all encoded memories at long times. Remarkably, neither deterministic nor noisy memory writing measurably affects the network's performance on unseen data from its original learning task. Our results establish cyclic memory as a phenomenon shared by disordered physical systems and deep neural networks, and show that networks can exploit as yet unexplored memory capabilities without compromising their original function.</summary>

    <title>Potential emergence in LLM agents: a statistical physics perspective</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T13:46:24Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27618v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27618v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>There has been significant recent interest in understanding the behaviour of LLM agents from the perspective of human preferences or corpus statistics. In this paper we propose agent states as intermediate variables through which post-training can be measured and predicted. From a statistical physics perspective, we study the emergence of a global potential which governs the transition of state in LLM agent reasoning. We introduce a partition function to model the ideal KL-regularised transition distribution and track potential structure, mean reward and state entropy. We demonstrate our approach in two Qwen3.5-9B tasks: safety-test selection and physics-reasoning auditing. We observe that the potential structure strengthens during post-training as predicted from our framework, while joint changes in reward and state entropy provide consistency evidence. States thus provide a quantitative description of how post-training organises agent behaviour.</summary>

    <title>Saddle Buckling of a Multicellular Alga Driven by Differential Growth</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T13:00:17Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27563v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27563v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>During development of many simple multicellular organisms there is a complex interplay between cell growth and generation of an extracellular matrix that confers structure. We study this problem quantitatively using $Gonium~pectorale$, a 16-cell alga that transforms from a flat to a buckled shape during growth without cell division or rearrangement. Cell-level measurements and 3D reconstructions show that the $12$ peripheral cells grow faster than the central $4$, producing hoop stress that selects the saddle mode, whose amplitude displays a continuous bifurcation with classical square root singularity. These results are consistent with a continuum model of differential growth within Föppl--von Kármán theory, which yields information on the mechanical properties of the ECM. Implications of this transformation in evolutionary transitions to multicellularity are discussed.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27258v1</id>
    <title>A preference for local interaction between layers emerges during training</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T08:01:07Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27258v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27258v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>A deep neural network is a stack of layers, and all layers are trained to lower one shared error. A change in one layer can therefore reach every other layer. Because the error is shared by all layers, one would expect the other layers to respond alike, whether they are next to the changed layer or far from it. We find that early in training the response is weak and its order by distance is not stable. As training proceeds, the response grows, and neighboring layers come to respond to changes in each other more strongly than layers further apart, in almost every network. This locality forms during training, although training links every layer to every other. We show this by pushing one layer of a copy of the network at many stages of training and measuring how much of the push reaches each of the other layers. The experiments use 512 five-layer networks trained on modular addition with each of two optimizers, AdamW and stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26587v2</id>
    <title>High-Accuracy Neural-Network Quantum States via Randomized Real-Time Dynamics</title>
    <updated>2026-11-23T02:56:24Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.26587v2" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.26587v2" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Neural-network quantum states (NQSs) exhibit a disparity in converging to the ground state during energy minimization: while the energy converges quadratically with the error in the variational wave function, other observables converge only linearly, which limits the accuracy of physical predictions. Here we show how to close this gap by introducing a new algorithm that improves the accuracy of NQSs. Our method, termed dynamical averaging, estimates expectation values by averaging over a state (or observable) evolved in real-time. Using insights from quantum information, we prove an up-to-quadratic suppression of error in arbitrary ground state observables, thus matching the fast convergence of the energy. Importantly, this improved accuracy requires neither further energy minimization nor increased model complexity, but rather exploits the effect of randomization on quantum states. We demonstrate dynamical averaging on non-integrable spin models, where it accelerates convergence and substantially reduces errors in observables.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30657v1</id>
    <title>Computational Complexity and Energy Landscapes of Coulomb Crystals</title>
    <updated>2026-11-23T13:20:46Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30657v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.30657v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Simulated annealing is widely used to search for ground states of trapped-ion Coulomb crystals and of charges on a sphere (the Thomson problem). Elementary nonuniform bounds clarify the role of the input encoding. For identical ions in a fixed trap, unary ion count and a binary energy threshold define a decision problem in P/poly; NP-hardness would imply a collapse of the polynomial hierarchy. The same holds on the unit sphere. With unary ion count and logarithmic precision parameter, approximate configuration search on the sphere and in a fixed positive-definite harmonic trap admits a solution function in FP/poly. These advice bounds provide no uniform search algorithm. In simulations of up to 100 ions, the number of distinct minima found and the time to reach the best-known minimum both grow approximately exponentially. When ions are pinned to prescribed candidate sites, choosing which sites to occupy to minimize the Coulomb energy is NP-hard in two and three dimensions; a finite-precision promise version is NP-complete. All ions are identical, the interaction is bare Coulomb repulsion, and the hardness is carried by the site positions alone. We extend a previous inverse-square reduction to the Coulomb interaction by deriving its angular law, including the quartic field term, and sharpening two estimates. The construction is an array of quadrupoles whose common monopole term cancels from energy differences between legal configurations. Its energy landscapes exhibit large barriers between nearly degenerate minima. Barrier trees resolve this structure, and simulated annealing becomes trapped above the ground state in the cube example. At laboratory parameters, with individually tunable well depths, the encoding survives numerically on a half-filled square lattice. For Doppler-cooled strontium ions, this requires stiff wells a few to tens of micrometers apart, as in electrode trap arrays.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30405v1</id>
    <title>Optimistic Online Learning for Coding Agents with Aggregate Feedback</title>
    <updated>2026-11-23T10:05:39Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30405v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.30405v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Large language model (LLM) coding agents operating on Web development platforms can interact with repositories, issue trackers, and continuous integration services to carry out long-horizon software engineering tasks. However, behavioral drift remains a major bottleneck in such multi-turn reasoning and action trajectories. To mitigate this, activation steering has emerged as a promising approach for regularizing agent behaviors by intervening on the LLM's transformer residual streams. Nonetheless, existing methods typically apply a static steering policy across all tasks, overlooking the fact that a single policy is rarely effective across heterogeneous tasks and varying execution turns. This limitation motivates dynamic online selection among candidate steering policies. Yet, doing so in long-horizon agentic settings is challenging: verifiable task-level feedback is only revealed upon task completion, leaving the contributions of individual steering turns unobserved. To address this challenge, we formulate online steering-policy selection as a multi-armed bandit problem with delayed task-level feedback and turn-level predictive hints derived from residual-stream activations. Within this formulation, we introduce Online Optimistic Activation Steering, a meta-framework that uses hints to guide within-task steering policy selection and leverages terminal task-level feedback to correct cumulative reward estimates. Theoretically, against the best fixed policy in hindsight, we prove regret bounds that tighten with increasing hint accuracy and establish a matching lower bound with respect to prediction error and candidate policy count. Empirical evaluations on realistic coding benchmarks demonstrate that our framework outperforms both static steering policies and naive online adaptive baselines.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30104v1</id>
    <title>A Polynomial-Time Best-of-Both-Worlds Algorithm for Matroid Semi-Bandit Problems</title>
    <updated>2026-11-23T06:02:01Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30104v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.30104v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Follow-the-Perturbed-Leader (FTPL) offers a computationally attractive framework for online learning, with recent advances establishing Best-of-Both-Worlds (BOBW) guarantees for various bandit settings. For matroid semi-bandits, existing methods offering such guarantees primarily rely on Follow-the-Regularized-Leader (FTRL), which requires solving an optimization problem at each round. We establish BOBW guarantees for FTPL with Fréchet and Pareto distributions with a certain parameter with geometric resampling in the matroid semi-bandit problem, showing that FTPL can simultaneously achieve the minimax-optimal $O(\sqrt{mdT})$ regret in adversarial setting and a logarithmic regret in stochastic setting. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first polynomial-time algorithm for matroid semi-bandits that achieves BOBW guarantees.</summary>

    <title>Safe Quantum Stochastic Linear Bandits</title>
    <updated>2026-11-23T01:59:42Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.29904v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.29904v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We initiate the study of safe quantum stochastic linear bandits, in which a learner maximizes an unknown linear reward while satisfying unknown linear mean constraints at every interaction. Under coherent unitary access to the joint reward-and-constraint distribution, we develop QRS-COLTS, a staged quantum resampled-scaling analog of constrained linear Thompson sampling (COLTS). With high probability, QRS-COLTS plays only feasible actions and achieves regret that is polylogarithmic in the query horizon and scales only with the square root of the number of constraints. We also study a model in which the learner queries superpositions of actions while an unsafe-action flag, a "bomb" that terminates the interaction upon violation, is measured after every query. In this setting, the bomb provides exact membership access to the safe set, and query regret is evaluated over the action superposition. For this model, we propose BCO-QLinTS, which selects feasible actions via bomb-certified quantum convex optimization without estimating the constraint matrix. Its query-weighted regret remains polylogarithmic in the horizon, with the constraints entering the bound only through the geometry of the safe set.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.29808v1</id>
    <title>Information-Theoretic Analysis of Multi-Objective Bandits: Pareto Violations & Gap-Based Regret</title>
    <updated>2026-11-22T22:21:02Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.29808v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.29808v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We study Bayesian multi-objective bandits and ask an information-theoretic question: what aspects of an unknown environment must be resolved to achieve low regret? We show that the answer depends on the regret criterion and the information needed to represent its loss. For Pareto-violation regret, which incurs unit loss whenever a dominated action is selected, the Pareto-optimal set is a natural information target. We introduce a predictive separation measure for competing candidate Pareto sets, connect it to information gain about the unknown set, and use this connection to analyze Thompson Sampling and develop an Information-Directed Sampling strategy. We establish sublinear Bayesian regret under uniform and polynomially decaying separation and prove a lower bound showing that weak separation can impose an unavoidable statistical cost. We then study gap-based Pareto regret, which quantifies the magnitude of Pareto suboptimality. Here, Pareto-set information is generally too coarse: distinct environments can share the same Pareto set while inducing different reward geometries and Pareto gaps, and averaging environments consistent with one Pareto set need not preserve Pareto dominance. This motivates retaining finer information about the environment. We develop parameter-level information-theoretic analyses of Thompson Sampling and Information-Directed Sampling to derive gap-based regret guarantees. Under sublinear information budgets, Pareto Thompson Sampling also achieves sublinear gap regret while recovering the full Pareto set on the same run, with a related guarantee for a fixed mixture with gap-based IDS. Together, our results reveal a hierarchy of information requirements: binary Pareto membership can be controlled through set-level information, whereas quantitative Pareto-gap suboptimality can require finer knowledge of reward geometry.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.29795v1</id>
    <title>Dimension Is Free, Horizon Is Not: When Evolution Strategies Rival Policy Gradients for LLM Fine-Tuning</title>
    <updated>2026-11-22T21:54:42Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.29795v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.29795v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Policy gradient (PG) methods such as GRPO dominate LLM fine-tuning, yet recent work showed that Evolution Strategies (ES) also scale to fine-tuning models with billions of parameters. Which method needs fewer samples, and on which tasks, remains unclear. We view the two methods as estimators of the same gradient that differ in where they explore. Because ES perturbs parameters, its noise grows with the number of parameters, and because PG samples actions, its noise grows with the number of generated tokens. Only noise along the directions that change the reward slows learning. The cost of ES then depends on the effective dimension, the number of independent skills a task requires rather than its parameter count, while the cost of PG depends on the effective horizon, which counts only the tokens that share both credit and weights with the reward-carrying ones. We train both methods on a synthetic task where the number of skills and the effective horizon can be varied separately. PG is cheaper when the horizon is short, ES becomes cheaper once it is long enough, and this crossover moves to longer horizons as the number of skills grows. We then measure the effective horizons of 20 NLP, math reasoning, and agentic tasks and compare the two methods with Qwen2.5-7B. PG leads on short-horizon tasks, the two tie on the moderate-horizon math ones, and no task has a horizon in the regime where the theory predicts an ES advantage. Terminal-Bench has a far longer horizon. There, in a preliminary comparison with Qwen3.5-4B, ES without any credit assignment reaches a higher success rate than the PG checkpoint released with Tmax, as the theory predicts. ES should thus have the advantage on long-horizon tasks with few independent skills and a nonvanishing reward signal. Current benchmarks are only at the onset of this regime, so ES should become more competitive as agentic tasks grow longer.</summary>

    <title>Quantum-Annealing-Assisted Search-Space Reduction for Large-Scale Shortest-Path Computation</title>
    <updated>2026-11-22T19:43:11Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.29724v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.29724v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Computing point-to-point shortest paths in large weighted graphs can require classical algorithms to explore a substantial portion of the graph. We ask whether quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) can reduce the work required to return a verified shortest path. For a known set of queries, we select paths that share arcs. For new queries, we select a corridor and test whether any path leaving it could improve the distance found by Dijkstra's algorithm. We also partition the graph into blocks and reuse local paths between their boundaries. We compare path encodings on identical inputs using simulated annealing on classical processors.
  The comparison of exact block overlays with direct Dijkstra search covered 45 synthetic graphs and the New York road network with 264,346 vertices. The overlay reduced the number of arc inspections in the final search in 97 of 200 graph and block-size combinations. Once endpoint attachment, assembly, and reconstruction were included, every combination took longer per query than direct Dijkstra search. On a separate set of 168 synthetic graphs, tightening the flow penalty increased the fraction of trials returning a verified local optimum within 20,ms from 35.8% to 84.1% under the same annealing schedule and update policy. A cost model for a prepared graph of 16,384 vertices predicts a 1.072x query speedup over a parallel classical overlay if five local problems can be solved accurately in one batch at the assumed service cost. The practical benefit of reduction thus depends on whether savings in the final search cover the cost of obtaining and verifying the local paths.</summary>

    <title>Subsurface Model Programming: Frontier Large Language Models Natively Interpret and Edit Dynamic Reservoir Models</title>
    <updated>2026-11-22T17:11:16Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.29612v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.29612v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Multiphase flow simulation in heterogeneous porous media supports decisions in hydrocarbon recovery, geological carbon sequestration, and geothermal extraction. We introduce Subsurface Model Programming, a workflow in which large language models (LLMs) read and edit reservoir simulation decks directly without numerical gradients or external optimization algorithms. We evaluate four benchmarks using geometric checks for connectivity and open-source simulators for dynamic tasks. In one text-only response, the LLM correctly classified all six reservoir-layer well-pair labels and all three flow-path labels between open completions. On PUNQ-S3, a single proposal modified 54 of 1,761 active cells (3.1%) and reduced well-balanced water-cut RMSE by 71.9%. On the SPE10 sector model, the best of five LLM proposals yielded 1.795 million standard cubic meters of cumulative oil over ten years, 8.9% more than the best plan from 25 particle swarm optimization evaluations. On the 533,403-cell UNISIM-IV-2026 compositional model, five rounds of script-based editing reduced combined field-and-well NRMSE from 37.98% to 11.62% (a 69.4% reduction) and field production error by 73.9%. Replacing exhaustive stochastic search with physically auditable causal interventions in just one to five runs provides a generalizable foundation for autonomous reservoir development, rapid history matching, legacy model diagnosis, and coupled multiphysics engineering.</summary>
