    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30819v1</id>
    <title>Ask Again: Answer-List Instability in Generative Engines</title>
    <updated>2026-11-23T15:11:05Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30819v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.30819v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Visibility in generative search engines is measured by which entities appear in responses, and in what order. Ask an engine the same question twice and the answer list can change: a different ordering, or different items altogether. Across 60,000 responses, we find that answers to the same prompt name a different first item 32% of the time, and even two answers with the same items disagree on which comes first. The first position is a measurement target of its own. A "clear leader" emerges after seven or eight runs, which are the budgets recommended for brand and source monitoring, but a "close leader" only about half the time. After 25 runs, a close leader is identified only 60% of the time. Variability between engines is larger than within the same engine. For open-ended prompts, the gap is more than double that for determinate ones. Search queries and cited sites observed leave most of the disagreement unexplained. Visibility measurement should report, for each engine, which items appear and how often each comes first, each with its own quantification of uncertainty.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30507v1</id>
    <title>When Does Continual Pre-Training Help? An Empirical Study of Decoupled Knowledge and Generation Trajectories in Clinical LLMs</title>
    <updated>2026-11-23T11:25:31Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30507v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.30507v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Continual pre-training (\textit{CPT}) is a standard route for domain adaptation, yet existing studies typically track pre-training loss or multiple-choice question answering (\textit{MCQA}) accuracy alone, offering only a narrow view of how adaptation unfolds. We jointly track factual knowledge via \textit{MCQA} and open-ended behavior via pairwise preference rankings across $18$ checkpoints for each of eight instruction-tuned \textit{Qwen} models ($0.5B$ to $8B$), adapted to German medicine with \textit{CPT} and \textit{SLERP} merging. The two axes converge at consistently different rates, with preference rankings reaching $90\%$ of their total gain after a median of $1.7B$ tokens versus $3.5B$ for \textit{MCQA}. A judge-free token-distribution measure reaches this threshold at $1.9B$ tokens. Per-aspect scores indicate that these early preference gains largely reflect surface alignment, meaning models can sound domain-appropriate before their factual knowledge catches up. Larger adapted models close more of the gap to unadapted next-tier generalists, whereas preference gain per FLOP falls by about an order of magnitude across our size range. We therefore argue that judge-based preference scores, which can plateau while \textit{MCQA} knowledge is still improving, should not be used alone to infer adaptation convergence or domain readiness.</summary>

    <title>Evaluating Persona Consistency in LLM User Simulators Without External Reference Annotations</title>
    <updated>2026-11-23T08:38:35Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30280v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.30280v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Standard evaluations assess LLM-simulated personas against an external ground truth, such as community trait annotations, but that reference is unavailable when the persona is inferred only from a short, task-oriented chat. We ask how persona consistency can be evaluated without such a reference, and propose a self-anchored internal-consistency diagnostic: the persona describes itself once and acts twice. A Likert self-report supplies a soft internal anchor; two behavioral profiles come from constrained scenario choices scored without a judge and from open-ended responses judged by an LLM. Consistency is the correlation between the self-report and each behavioral profile, in a shared six-facet BFI-2 space. The framework compares persona-construction strategies by assessing how consistently their elicited responses reflect their self-reported traits. Across ordinary-user chats (WildChat and LMSYS) and well-documented personas with community annotations (the Personality Database, PDB), profile-enriched representations agree with the anchor more closely than a raw-dialogue baseline. On PDB, this self-anchored ordering reproduces the community-annotation ordering. The pattern is stable across answering and judge models.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30254v1</id>
    <title>Innata-0: A Native Embodied World System with Model-Agent Co-Design</title>
    <updated>2026-11-23T08:20:59Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30254v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.30254v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>The physical world is open-ended, dynamic, and partially observable. While foundation models have advanced embodied intelligence, standalone models struggle with long-horizon execution, and simply integrating models with agents may lead to inconsistencies between planning and physical control. To support reliable and adaptive behaviors in the physical world, we introduce Innata-0, a native embodied world system. Innata-0 jointly designs an embodied world-action model and an agent to combine their complementary strengths. The model, Innata-0-WAM, adopts a tri-tower Mixture-of-Transformers architecture that integrates understanding, prediction, and action generation. The agent, Innata-0-Agent, coordinates long-horizon execution through memory, verification, and recovery. A co-design protocol is further proposed to align model training with agent execution and leverage validated experiences to support subsequent adaptation and model improvement. Extensive evaluations demonstrate strong embodied capabilities across understanding, world prediction, and robotic manipulation. Innata-0 represents our first step toward physical intelligence, and we see it as the beginning of a much longer journey.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30202v1</id>
    <title>VADE: A Verifiable Agent Data Engine from Professional Sources</title>
    <updated>2026-11-23T07:41:50Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30202v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.30202v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Language agents have shown their practical value, particularly in software engineering, where abundant public code and executable tests support training and evaluation at scale. Extending this success to other professional domains, such as law and finance, is not straightforward: many agent tasks involve open-ended analysis, making outcomes hard to verify and, in turn, hard to use as scalable supervision. As a result, high-quality tasks in these domains are still largely expert-authored, making them expensive to scale and limiting their use for training. To address this bottleneck, we introduce VADE, a data engine that automatically constructs verifiable analysis tasks from public sources used in professional practice. VADE exploits a simple asymmetry: professional analyses are difficult to solve because the relevant evidence must first be found and interpreted, but much easier to verify once that evidence is fixed. During task synthesis, the engine constructs a reference analysis from source evidence and asks an independent agent to reproduce its conclusions from the same evidence without seeing it. Only after the analysis is verified is it compiled into an open-ended task with an item-level scoring contract, allowing the same task to support both evaluation and training. We apply VADE across four professional domains; in an independent expert review of 186 finance tasks, 93.5% meet a high bar for source fidelity, answer correctness, and evaluation fairness. In finance, these tasks expose substantial remaining model errors, particularly unsupported facts and inferences, while training on verified solver trajectories improves held-out performance and yields gains that transfer to public finance benchmarks such as Finance Agent Benchmark v2. Together, these results suggest a practical path toward scalable, verifiable supervision for open-ended professional tasks.</summary>

    <title>Memphis: A Case Study in Seeding an Agent Task from a Model's Real-World Attempt</title>
    <updated>2026-11-22T23:03:45Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.29824v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.29824v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Agent benchmarks are usually made harder by scaling up the data their tasks are built from, yet models that do well on them still fail at real work. We propose building simulated tasks from a model's own attempt at an open-ended task in the real world, so that the model's failures in the simulation resemble its failures in reality. As a case study, we had GPT-6.1 Sol manage two human workers in Cairo over chat for five shifts, with a budget of 7,000 Egyptian pounds, to build as many USB desk lamps as it could. It built two. From the real-world attempt's transcript, we build Memphis, an evaluation in a model-simulated world. Memphis is hard: GPT-6.1 Sol delivers 1.0 lamp per trial on average and repeats its real-world mistakes, buying too few stands and giving up the search for them. With a one-page hint on where to buy parts and who can wire them, it delivers 9.2. Claude Opus 5.5 delivers 2.2 without the hint and 4.6 with it. We release the task, the trials, the audits, and a redacted record of the real-world evaluation.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.29594v1</id>
    <title>Motoric signatures to detect original authorship versus cognitive effort in instructed motor responses of an emerging speaker with ASD</title>
    <updated>2026-11-22T16:31:21Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.29594v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.29594v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>There is at present no objective, agnostic method to track levels of message authorship and agency in non-speakers who rely on assisted typing to communicate. Part of the problem is that nuances in spontaneous gestural movements of the typer transpire largely beneath awareness of both the typer and the communication-regulation-partner. Such spontaneous movements co-occur with the intentional ones producing the typed messages but are currently not considered part of the communication system. We introduce an assay that probes various levels of cognitive loads in an ecologically valid environment. Then, in collaboration with an emerging speaker-typer and his communication-regulation-partner, we empirically estimate motoric stochastic signatures during both independent and assisted typing. Under varying levels of cognitive loads, the assay and biometrics distinguish motoric patterns in spontaneous typing of phrases in response to open-ended questions from those in instructed typing of the same phrase. The non-dominant bodily motions, co-occurring with the dominant (typing) side reveal not only levels of cognitive mental effort and agency of the typer but also levels of creative thoughts through motoric preambles present only in open-ended mode. This level of semantic authorship is detectable in both the geodesic paths along the manifold representing the Gamma stochastic parameters of the motions fluctuations and those of the physical 3D spatial trajectories. The head and facial micro-motions capture these non-dominant-body nuances, offering a personalized motoric metric of cognitive effort, agency, authorship and a comprehensive suite of assays to open new research avenues for assisted typing with haptic support.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.29167v1</id>
    <title>Decoupling Perception from Generation for Agentic 3D CT Report Generation</title>
    <updated>2026-11-22T02:54:05Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.29167v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.29167v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Chest CT reports repeatedly assess the same anatomical regions for findings and their attributes, such as whether a lung nodule is present and where it is located. These assessments suggest learning to answer visual questions directly, rather than coupling perception to open-ended text generation. Yet current CT report generation models largely follow generic vision-language modeling, which may miss subtle abnormalities when training data are limited. We therefore formulate report generation as a set of visual question-answering decisions coordinated by a large language model (LLM) agent. This decouples visual perception from reasoning and report writing: perception can be learned as a discriminative, non-generative task, while the LLM focuses on reasoning over patient context and posing relevant visual queries. We introduce Rad-VL-JEPA, which unifies report retrieval, finding recognition, and fine-grained attribute characterization through vision-language joint-embedding prediction. Building on this perception module, an agent trained with reinforcement learning (RL) acquires patient-specific visual evidence, while a separate editor incorporates the evidence into the final report, further separating evidence acquisition from report realization. Experiments show that Rad-VL-JEPA achieves strong performance on fine-grained CT understanding tasks with lower amortized per-query inference time than a generative VLM baseline trained with the same CT encoder and VQA data. The resulting reporting system outperforms strong VLM-based and agentic baselines.</summary>

    <title>Sheaf Semantics of Probabilistic Programs</title>
    <updated>2026-11-23T13:43:09Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30692v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.30692v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Finding denotational models of probabilistic languages that support sampling from continuous distributions is difficult: the existence of continuous distributions means that measure-theoretic objects are needed to define the semantics. A challenging task on top of this is logical reasoning with respect to the semantic model: in the case of probabilistic programs, the desired properties to reason about include the distributions, expected value and the probabilistic (in)dependence of outputs.
  This paper introduces a monadic semantics for higher-order probabilistic programs with continuous distributions based on Simpson's theory of probability sheaves and the internal logic of atomic sheaves. We prove that our semantics forms a model of the $ν$-calculus. Furthermore, using the well-behavedness of the semantic domain and the internal logic of the topos, we derive the first higher-order probabilistic Hoare logic with rigorous treatment of continuous random variables, higher-order functions, and independence.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30009v1</id>
    <title>Tableau Consequence under Positive Contexts: A Reconstruction of Walukiewicz's Completeness Proof</title>
    <updated>2026-11-23T04:11:05Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30009v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.30009v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We establish a positive-context lifting theorem for tableau consequence in the modal $μ$-calculus: under explicit syntactic hypotheses, $\mathcal T_B\Rightarrow\mathcal T_C$ induces $\mathcal T_{A(B)}\Rightarrow\mathcal T_{A(C)}$. The proof orders instances of the given relation by birth time and assigns overlapping formula occurrences to the oldest supporting instance. A corollary gives bidirectional replacement by automaton normal form inside positive contexts. Together with a separate unfolding consequence lemma and ANF bisimulation, the lifting theorem yields a self-contained reconstruction of Walukiewicz's completeness proof for Kozen's axiomatisation and makes its least-fixpoint step more transparent. We also give a finite parity-game proof of regular-refutation existence and a two-sided transfer from tableau consequence to thin refutations.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.29832v1</id>
    <title>Higher Realizability Toposes</title>
    <updated>2026-11-22T23:23:47Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.29832v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.29832v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Building on $\infty$-tripos theory, we develop a theory of realizability $\infty$-toposes. We apply $\infty$-tripos theory to construct the function, modified, and Krivine realizability $\infty$-toposes. We recover the Lawvere-Tierney nucleus $j$ that specifies local truth in each construction by exhibiting, for any $n\geq1$, a single family of Eilenberg-MacLane $n$-types whose fibre at an ambient truth value $p$ is contractible after sheafification precisely when $j(p)$ holds. In function realizability, we relate identity types to descriptive set theory. For each $n\geq 2$, we construct a univalent classifier $U_n$ of exact truncation height $n+1$. As maps from Baire space into $U_n$ vary, the sets of inputs admitting a global path from the assigned code to the terminal code are exactly the $G_δ$ subsets of Baire space. After exponentiation by Baire space, the analogous test against the constant map at the terminal code yields exactly the coanalytic sets, at the same truncation height. In modified realizability, a closed proof of local existence under a stable numerical precondition yields a total recursive function together with a coherent proof that its output satisfies the specification whenever the precondition holds. In Krivine realizability, contextual choice for $(n-1)$-truncated families over suitable $n$-types recovers the subterminal defining the Boolean localization. Binary cohomology distinguishes slices of Anel-Awodey-Barton's effective $\infty$-topos even when they share the same ordinary Hyland effective topos and their bases have equivalent spaces of global points. Hyland's effective topos thus occurs as the category of zero-types in infinitely many pairwise inequivalent realizability $\infty$-toposes (recovering Hyland's effective topos as the category of zero-types does not uniquely determine an effective $\infty$-topos).</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.29830v1</id>
    <title>Higher Duality Theory: Geometric HoTT and Classifying $\infty$-Toposes</title>
    <updated>2026-11-22T23:20:07Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.29830v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.29830v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We develop geometric homotopy type theory (geometric HoTT), which gives a dependent language for constructions preserved by inverse images of geometric morphisms. We give a homotopy-coherent calculus for geometric HoTT and extend the classical duality between geometric logic and classifying toposes to Grothendieck $\infty$-toposes. For each geometric type theory, the $\infty$-category of contexts generated by its rules is equivalent to its classifying $\infty$-topos. As the theory varies, the classifier gives a duality of $(\infty,2)$-categories between geometric HoTT theories with interpretations and Grothendieck $\infty$-toposes with geometric morphisms. We then construct a universal family of classifying $\infty$-toposes whose fiber at each presentation of a theory is the classifying $\infty$-topos of that theory. We also construct a universal family of classifying $\infty$-toposes with coherent transport along Morita equivalences of theories. Geometric HoTT thus serves as an internal language for Grothendieck $\infty$-toposes, extending the role of geometric logic in classical topos theory to the realm of $\infty$-topos theory.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.29738v1</id>
    <title>TPTL-dist: A Formalised Calculus with Proof Automation for Verifying Real-Time Distributed Systems</title>
    <updated>2026-11-22T20:05:53Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.29738v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.29738v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We introduce TPTL-dist, a temporal logic and labelled sequent calculus for specifying and verifying real-time distributed systems. TPTL-dist is formalised in Agda to provide machine-checked correctness and tool support, including automation through a proof search that runs inside Agda. The logic extends Timed Propositional Temporal Logic (TPTL) with past operators, freeze quantification, comparisons between time expressions, domain-specific atoms, and an induction principle on time. We provide a world-based semantics, develop an interval-annotated calculus, and establish its soundness w.r.t. the semantics. To demonstrate its expressiveness, we encode standard distributed system patterns, and we carry out a mechanised proof of a key real-time property of the Pistis Byzantine broadcast protocol. Our results show that TPTL-dist provides a uniform, mechanised framework for reasoning about temporal properties of distributed systems.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.29737v1</id>
    <title>Deterministic Proper Positive-Only Learning Is Independent of ZFC</title>
    <updated>2026-11-22T20:05:07Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.29737v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.29737v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Binary classification from positive-only samples is a variant of PAC learning in which the learner receives i.i.d. samples only from the positive region of an unknown target concept, but is evaluated on the full distribution. Improper learnability in this model has a textbook characterization, whereas proper learnability has remained open for decades. Recent work characterized it for learners with access to randomness, and showed that, unlike in PAC learning, some classes are properly learnable with randomness but not without it, leaving the deterministic case open. We show that this case cannot be resolved within the standard axioms of mathematics (ZFC): there is a class of VC dimension two whose deterministic proper learnability is independent of ZFC, even though a randomized learner provably learns it. Moreover, no dimension of finite character, a desirable property shared by most dimensions in learning theory, characterizes deterministic proper learnability. We also show that the size of the domain is decisive. In ZFC, deterministic proper learnability has a combinatorial characterization on every domain whose cardinality is below a certain threshold, including every countable domain. In contrast, this characterization fails on every domain of sufficiently large cardinality. Under the generalized continuum hypothesis, this threshold is sharp: it is the exact cardinality at which the characterization starts to fail. Finally, our proofs introduce new tools, based on the Erdos--Rado partition theorem, that may be of broader interest.</summary>

    <title>Hashing Theorems Modulo Rewrites and Binder Permutation Enables Equivalence Search over 200k Mathlib Theorems</title>
    <updated>2026-11-22T16:52:44Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.29603v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.29603v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Like all code, Lean libraries accumulate technical debt and structural deficiencies over the course of their development. A particular concern is duplicate theorems: different parts of a big library can unwittingly contain and prove the same theorem, duplicating maintenance efforts. Tools can help detect redundancy and clean up. For instance, Mathlib's duplicate-declarations linter compares theorem types syntactically after sorting top-level binders and erasing binder information and universe levels. If detecting an equivalence requires unfolding, reorientation, or logical transformations, it escapes this comparison. In this work, we present a method to detect theorems which are equivalent with regard to argument order and currying/uncurrying of dependent types. We implement our method for Lean. By applying it to Mathlib, a library of more than 200k theorems, we demonstrate that it is computationally cheap and scalable. We discuss how our work may enhance efforts to tackle the maintenance burden of Lean libraries.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.31048v1</id>
    <title>Distill the Correction, Not the Rewrite: Hindsight Twins for Self-Improving Text-to-Image Models</title>
    <updated>2026-11-23T17:14:33Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.31048v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.31048v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Text-to-image models can learn from their own mistakes by distilling a self-teacher conditioned on a vision-language critic's revised prompt. However, such self-teachers barely improve alignment, and both they and their hindsight-contrast variants absorb the critic's unintended additions to the scene, such as lighting or scenery. We attribute this to two factors: (1) the prompt already specifies the desired fix, so a useful revision must go beyond the failed span, often rewriting the entire scene and adding details that overshadow the fix; (2) although the critic localizes the error to a single span, self-teachers condition on the rewrite, entangling the intended fix with unintended additions. Motivated by these insights, we propose Hindsight Twins (HinT), which fills the critic's revision template once with the intended fix and once with the observed error and distills only their velocity difference, anchored at the user's prompt. Because text encoders spread the edit of a single slot to all other tokens, HinT further aligns the twins' token states outside the slot. Across Qwen-Image-2512, SD3.5-M, and FLUX.2-klein, HinT keeps the rate of critic-induced bias at the base-model level while matching or exceeding the alignment gains of prior self-distillation, and it keeps improving over twelve rounds of self-training where contrastive baselines decay.</summary>

    <title>MMMem: Self-Improving Agents with Task-Aware Multimodal Experience Consolidation</title>
    <updated>2026-11-23T08:44:23Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30287v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.30287v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>AI agents accumulate conversations, images, and documents through long-term interactions with users. Answering later questions often requires connecting evidence across these records, yet the resulting understanding is rarely retained, allowing mistakes to recur on related questions. Existing multimodal memory methods largely focus on storing and retrieving records, with limited mechanisms for learning from completed tasks and consolidating task-specific experience. We therefore propose MMMem, a task-aware multimodal memory framework that extracts and consolidates experience from completed tasks through four complementary strategies. First, source-linked multi-view memory organizes original text, images, and rendered pages alongside generated scene images that combine clues across records for retrieval. Second, source-generated tasks support knowledge alignment at two levels: warm-up consolidates source knowledge into task-relevant experiences in external memory, while self-training adapts the model's parametric knowledge to task demands. Third, the same vision-language model distills completed tasks into experiences that record the task context, conclusion, and support links. Finally, task-aware retrieval recalls source views and relevant experiences for answering and verification, while source-supported reuse guides long-term retention. Across three memory benchmarks and two vision-language readers, MMMem outperforms eight baselines. With Qwen3.5-9B, MMMem achieves relative gains of 36.9%, 17.6%, and 15.2% over the best-performing baselines on LoCoMo, Mem-Gallery, and LooGLE v2, respectively. Ablations show consistent gains from training and memory warm-up, while case studies illustrate how individual components work in practice.</summary>

    <title>Last-Iterate Convergence of Payoff-Gradient Learning in Möbius Pricing Games</title>
    <updated>2026-11-21T16:21:14Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28897v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.28897v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We prove global last-iterate convergence of payoff-gradient learning in every typewise Riemannian metric, which for scalar actions is the same as typewise mirror descent, with explicit rates, in a class of Bayesian bidding and pricing games that includes first-price auctions, unit-demand pay-as-bid auctions, rank-based generalized first-price auctions, and homogeneous-good price competition with inelastic demand. The result holds for symmetric self-play: all players use a common strategy and apply the same payoff-gradient update at each type. Convergence is from every continuous weakly increasing feasible initial strategy, including pooling, and does not rely on the monotonicity or Minty conditions that underlie existing guarantees in other games. Instead, the class is characterized by two structural properties: a direct payoff effect that is independent of the action, and a payoff difference at the allocation threshold that is affine in the action. These properties reduce the learning dynamics to a singular transport-damping equation for the common strategy, which, under the stated coefficient and metric assumptions, admits a unique viscosity solution. Comparison barriers make the uniform distance to the unique rest point a strict Lyapunov functional and yield convergence rates with optimal algebraic exponents. In allocation games, the rest point is the unique weakly increasing symmetric equilibrium under the stated tie-breaking conditions, and a positive lower slope bound converts strategy-error bounds into explicit approximate-equilibrium guarantees. A projected grid scheme with a slope floor makes the approximation constructive, with error bounds under deterministic perturbations and almost-sure convergence on a fixed grid under martingale gradient noise.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28803v1</id>
    <title>DeRail: Escaping Trajectory Priors via Counterfactual Action Steering for Mid-Execution Instruction Switching</title>
    <updated>2026-11-21T13:42:22Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28803v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.28803v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Robots operating in the real world must often adapt when user instructions change mid-execution, yet current instruction-conditioned robot policies, including Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and World-Action Models (WAMs), are largely evaluated under fixed-instruction episodes. We study mid-execution instruction switching and identify trajectory hijacking as a key failure mode, where the policy fails to redirect sufficiently toward the switched target, with its post-switch behavior remaining fully or partially drawn toward trajectories associated with non-target tasks. We propose Counterfactual Action Steering (CAS), a training-free, model-agnostic inference-time method that identifies interfering non-target tasks, queries the same policy with corresponding counterfactual instructions, and uses target--counterfactual action differences to steer execution away from interfering trajectory priors. Experiments on LIBERO-Goal-Switch and CALVIN-Custom-Switch across five VLA and WAM policies, together with real-robot evaluation, show that CAS consistently improves switching success; for example, on CALVIN-Custom-Switch in the $[15,21]$ switching range, CAS improves $π_{0.5}$ from 5.8\% to 54.6\%. Successful CAS-guided rollouts further provide higher-quality self-training supervision than vanilla successful rollouts with the same number of trajectories, yielding stronger policies that generalize to unseen later instruction switches. Code will be made publicly available.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28589v1</id>
    <title>CLOSE: A Calibrated Label-free Online Self-Evaluating Verifier for Object Hallucination in Vision-Language Models</title>
    <updated>2026-11-21T05:43:32Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28589v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.28589v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Vision-language models frequently describe objects absent from the image because of language priors. Yet the model itself is already a strong judge of its own output: asked separately whether an object is present, it rejects 44%-62% of its hallucinations, and its yes probability reaches an AUROC of 0.90-0.95 without training. This judgment, however, is not directly usable: (1) its probabilities lack a common scale across models; (2) for the remaining 38%-56%, the model still answers yes with probabilities that overlap those of real objects, so no threshold separates them. We therefore propose CLOSE, a Calibrated Label-free Online Self-Evaluating verifier that enforces this judgment during generation. Its threshold is a quantile of a memory rather than a probability and thus depends only on ranks; the memory is cold-started from unlabeled images and updated online. A scorer self-trained on pseudo-labels from four hidden-state signals is fused with self-asking by rank to separate what self-asking leaves mixed. Refused objects are rolled back and banned through a laddered back-off, and a recognition table intercepts their reappearance under other wordings. On COCO, refusing 20% and 40% of object mentions reduces the CHAIRs of LLaVA-1.5-7B by 42% and 87% (F1 +1.9 and -6.1 points); refusing 20% and 35% reduces the reachable hallucinations of Qwen3-VL-8B (official counts minus CHAIR-script miscounts) by 79% and 96% (F1 +0.5 and -5.3). An external vocabulary further extends the check beyond the official vocabulary.</summary>

    <title>Transfer Learning and Experience Replay for Automotive Aerodynamic Surrogates</title>
    <updated>2026-11-21T00:11:00Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28435v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.28435v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Neural surrogates enable rapid prediction of automotive aerodynamic fields, but achieving high accuracy often demands extensive computational fluid dynamics datasets. Generating these datasets for each new vehicle program or expansion of the design space can require prolonged simulation campaigns. Reusing knowledge from existing simulations offers a way to limit this burden, provided that models adapt to unfamiliar geometries while maintaining predictive accuracy. This study evaluated transfer learning and experience replay in two independent automotive aerodynamics experiments using a mesh-free neural surrogate. First, models pretrained on 1,981 sport utility vehicle cases from SHIFT-SUV were fine-tuned on subsets of the SHIFT-Truck pickup dataset. Target training-set size was varied from 100 to 613 cases across the surface-only and joint surface and volume configurations to assess data efficiency. Fine-tuning reduced every reported field mean absolute error (MAE) relative to training from scratch at the same target budget. For joint surface and volume prediction, fine-tuning on 100 truck cases matched or improved on all four field MAEs obtained by training from scratch on 200 cases. Second, an independently trained model learned a base task using 332 DrivAerML cases and was adapted to a novel task using 31 cases with a previously unseen combination of design features. Experience replay incorporated cases from the base-task training set during adaptation. Full replay lowered field errors on 45 held-out base-task designs by approximately 36% to 42% relative to adaptation without replay; retaining half the base-task training set yielded reductions of approximately 30% to 35%. Together, these findings support transfer learning and experience replay as complementary strategies for data-efficient neural surrogate development across successive engineering tasks.</summary>

    <title>FinEvo: Recursive Self-Improvement for Long-Horizon Financial Modeling</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T19:14:42Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28239v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.28239v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Advances in large language models (LLMs) have expanded their role in high-value productivity tasks, including financial analysis and modeling, while enabling models to play an increasingly active role in their own improvement. This motivates two complementary lines of inquiry: can financial modeling capabilities provide a foundation for model self-evolution, and can self-evolution, in turn, advance financial capabilities? We introduce FinEvo, a self-evolution framework that integrates autonomous experience construction with financial capability improvement. FinEvo prepares financial models, iteratively evolves challenges through self-play, and learns from the resulting interactions using executable rewards, relying on the same model throughout. An end-to-end execution with Qwen3.6-27B shows that solving feedback supports both increasing reasoning demands and identifying specification issues that executable checks can miss. Learning from these experiences raises whole-task success from 22.73 to 29.09 on held-out within-source tasks and from 13.13 to 19.19 on SpreadsheetBench 2 Financial. Comparable gains across task sources and evaluation settings, together with improvement on a task category absent from training, suggest that FinEvo strengthens underlying financial modeling capabilities shared across tasks. These findings support self-evolution as a path toward broader financial competence, advancing the empirical exploration of recursive self-improvement (RSI) in professional domains. Code is available at https://github.com/pcj-sudo/FinEvo.</summary>

    <title>Autonomous quantum machine learning via Riemannian gradient-based optimization</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T16:42:26Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27815v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27815v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Quantum machine learning models typically rely on repeated quantum measurements and classical optimization during training, making the quantum-to-classical information-extraction process a fundamental bottleneck for scalability. We propose a framework for autonomous self-training quantum machine learning, based on Riemannian gradient optimization, in which the optimization proceeds entirely within the quantum domain without requiring quantum measurements or classical feedback. We derive the Riemannian gradient update rules for a broad class of learning tasks and identify sufficient conditions under which the resulting training dynamics can be realized fully autonomously. Within this regime, we establish an exponential convergence guarantee, in the training iterations, for sufficiently small step sizes, and further analyze the training cost in terms of the growth of the circuit depth. Importantly, we further show that the trained model can automatically discover symmetries hidden in the training data without $\textit{a priori}$ specification. For the canonical examples of quantum phase classification and unitary learning with a hidden symmetry, our numerical study indicates that learning can be achieved at low circuit depths with only a few distinct training examples. Our results thus establish autonomous quantum machine learning as a promising paradigm that removes the classical optimization loop while retaining strong theoretical guarantees and practical performances.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.29548v1</id>
    <title>Real-Time Kinodynamic Multi-Agent Motion Planning</title>
    <updated>2026-11-22T15:19:23Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.29548v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.29548v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Coordinating large robot fleets, from warehouses to quadrotor swarms, requires collision-free trajectories that satisfy dynamic constraints and stay within speed and acceleration bounds. Existing kinodynamic multi-agent planners enforce these bounds during the search or through trajectory optimization after it, which limits fleet size and speed. We present Tickwise Actions to Kinodynamic Trajectories (TAKT), a framework that accounts for the dynamics before the search and reduces planning to a lattice search for double-integrator robots. TAKT analytically bounds the clearance lost when a discrete plan is smoothed and reserves this margin on the lattice. A closed-form convolution provably converts any valid plan into dynamically feasible trajectories with continuous-time collision avoidance. For robots spanning many lattice vertices, we introduce a diamond formulation that permits one-tick sideways yielding and adapt the Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF) solvers PIBT and LaCAM to it. With 50 robots, our planners run over 2,000 times faster than the strongest baseline in 2D halls and over 100 times in 3D, with comparable or lower makespan and cost. They plan about a thousand robots in seconds in 2D, and tens of seconds in 3D, and replan up to a thousand robots in real time.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28755v1</id>
    <title>Who Speaks for the Water? Simulating Discursive Closure and Power Asymmetries in Hydrosocial Governance</title>
    <updated>2026-11-21T11:59:06Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28755v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.28755v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Water governance conflicts stem not only from material scarcity, but from power asymmetries, institutional distrust, and the discursive frameworks through which actors assign meaning to water, infrastructure, and legitimate authority. Conventional simulation tools represent these dynamics via numerical opinion variables, missing the argumentative and narrative dimensions structuring real deliberation in hydrosocial territories. We present the Hydrosocial Agent-Based Model with Large Language Models (HSABM-LLM), a hybrid framework enabling heterogeneous agents to generate, evaluate, and adapt natural language arguments conditioned on institutional roles, interaction histories, and territorial context. Grounded in semi-structured interviews, a water-user survey, and 456 press and official documents from the Longaví River sub-basin (Maule Region, Chile), the model simulates deliberation over a contested large-scale reservoir proposal across four experimental scenarios. Opinion convergence toward unanimous opposition emerged within 7-14 months, operating through discursive closure driven by distributive equity and water security framings rather than argumentative dominance. Governance actors accelerated convergence by activating pre-existing institutional distrust rather than direct persuasion, while peer-based smallholder interactions drove 77-79% of all opinion changes. The formal authority of state institutions proved structurally decoupled from deliberative influence, revealing a legitimacy deficit that formal inclusion alone cannot resolve. These findings suggest participatory governance design must attend to the discursive conditions under which institutional actors enter deliberative spaces, rather than assuming inclusion is inherently consensus-building. HSABM-LLM offers a novel platform for integrating political ecology insights into computational social science.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28660v1</id>
    <title>Persuasion from Within: Model-Based Insider Attacks in Multi-Agent LLM Debate and Consensus</title>
    <updated>2026-11-21T08:41:43Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28660v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.28660v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in multi-agent systems for collective decision-making, such as multi-agent debate and consensus games, in which agents exchange messages and update their answers over multiple rounds and a resolution mechanism aggregates them into a final outcome. Most multi-agent LLM frameworks assume that every participant shares the system objective. In practice, however, a malicious agent can join as a legitimate member of the group and persuade the other agents toward a hidden adversarial goal. We formalize such attacks as a sequential decision-making problem in which the insider seeks to degrade the utility of the collective outcome. We propose a model-based insider attack that learns to persuade a group of agents: the insider first learns a world model of the benign agents from offline trajectories and then uses it both to train a persuasion policy and to plan its messages. In two case studies involving a numerical consensus game and a multi-agent debate, the learned insider is the most effective and the stealthiest attack we evaluate, outperforming both prompt-based and trained LLM persuaders from prior work. The attack also transfers to other target models, larger groups, and unseen datasets, and remains effective under existing Byzantine-resilience defenses. The learned insider also enables a new defense: adversarially training benign agents on the attack data largely removes both our attack and the strongest prior persuasion attack. These results show that combining world models with reinforcement learning and planning is an effective route to both attacking and hardening language-based multi-agent systems.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28517v1</id>
    <title>Digital Twins for Multi-Agent Systems: When to Trust, What to Change</title>
    <updated>2026-11-21T03:09:42Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.28517v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.28517v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Digital twins of agent networks need to flag unreliable forecasts and help users choose interventions. Both decisions depend on what happens over several steps: an error can spread through the network, and an edit whose trajectory is easy to predict may still yield a poor collective outcome. We ask when information about error propagation improves failure detection and whether a learned twin can select effective network edits despite imperfect forecasts. We propose Propagation-Aware Validation for Networked Digital Twins (PAV-Twin). Its monitor combines Jacobian-based propagation features with recent errors and ensemble disagreement to estimate the risk that a forecast exceeds an error threshold. Its planner simulates each candidate edit and ranks the edits by their predicted collective outcomes. In simulations, the monitor gained 0.13 in area under the precision-recall curve on larger oscillator networks with familiar topologies and 0.09 on larger networks with held-out topologies, relative to a graph baseline without propagation features. Gains were small in contractive consensus. Giving the graph baseline the same features narrowed the gap. In a separate planning study, ensemble simulation recovered about 99% of the possible improvement over random intervention selection in oscillators and nearly all of it in consensus. With a simplified oscillator twin, selecting by predicted outcome also gave lower regret than selecting by trajectory fidelity. These results show when propagation features help flag unreliable forecasts and why the quality of intervention choices should be measured directly.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27540v1</id>
    <title>Where Delay Compensation Belongs in a Decentralized Mean-Field-Game Swarm with a Control-Barrier Safety Filter</title>
    <updated>2026-11-20T12:36:13Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.27540v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.27540v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Large robot teams are often run as a plan-then-execute stack. We study a decentralized instance for drone swarms, a mean-field-game (MFG) routing field with a per-agent control-barrier-function (CBF) safety filter, when communication is limited by a shared TDMA channel. Neighbors are known only through noisy range and bearing measurements exchanged in round-robin slots, so the frame, and with it the age of every estimate, grows with swarm size. In simulation this delay reaches both layers but breaks only the safety layer. Without delay, swarms of up to 100 agents do not collide, even with each measurement's noise held for a whole frame; with it, stale estimates at the CBF cause collisions beyond a frame period of 125 to 175 ms, or 75 to 100 ms at 100 agents with held noise, and swarm size sets where that limit lies and how steeply collisions rise. At the MFG, staleness makes the local density noisier without biasing it, and throughput drops by at most a tenth. We then compensate with lightweight on-board predictors, from constant-velocity fits to a small learned network, that estimate each neighbor's position from its last broadcasts. A layer-split experiment shows where prediction is needed: at the CBF it restores safety and extends the tolerated frame period by 1.4 to 1.7 times with an untrained constant-velocity fit and about 2.3 with the learned network when the noise is redrawn each step; with noise held for a frame the two extend it about equally, while at the MFG it only refines the congestion correction. A constant wider safety margin, the simplest alternative, makes collisions more frequent in a bottleneck. With the routing solved offline, that layer is robust to the delay because it sees neighbors only through a crowd average; compensation belongs in the safety filter, switched on only above the uncompensated limit, since below it the predictor's own error adds collisions.</summary>

    <title>Guarded Swarms in the Loop: A ROS 2/PX4 Digital Twin for Hybrid Digital-Analog Coordination of UAV/UGV Swarms</title>
    <updated>2026-11-17T13:40:51Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.22773v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.22773v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Swarms of unmanned aerial and ground vehicles (UAV/UGV) operating in contested environments cannot rely on software alone for physical safety, since the software stack and its networks are part of the attack surface. The Guarded Swarms architecture addresses this by pairing a digital coordination layer, built on Topic-Based Communication Space Petri Nets (TB-CSPN), with an independent analog safety layer that can veto unsafe actuation commands. So far, the architecture has been specified and argued for, but not executed. We present the first executable instantiation of Guarded Swarms as a digital twin built on ROS 2, the PX4 autopilot in software-in-the-loop mode, and Gazebo, with two UAVs and one UGV in a coastal counter-UAS scenario. The TB-CSPN transition chain, from multi-modal sensing through human authorization to vehicle tasking, is mapped one-to-one onto ROS 2 nodes, and the analog layer is modeled as a per-vehicle Virtual Safety Board that gates every command. Eight groups of experiments show that the three negative guarantees of the architecture (no mission from conflicting, temporally incoherent, or unauthorized evidence) hold at three distinct stages of the chain in all 60 counterfactual runs; that threat confirmation is bounded by the narrowest sensing modality; that the safety layer exercises its full modeled envelope independently of the coordination layer; and, under fault injection, that it prevents every collision caused by a forged mission or a compromised worker once its veto is enforced by an independent gate, whereas a veto left to the compromised worker prevents none. The twin also exposes implementation-level hazards that the architectural specification does not address, and it draws an explicit line between the properties that simulation can validate and those that only hardware can.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20773v1</id>
    <title>When Does Interaction Help? Toward a Reynolds Number for Collective Intelligence</title>
    <updated>2026-11-16T09:22:24Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.20773v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.20773v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Multi-agent systems combine distributed information through interaction, which can improve performance but also spread errors or suppress useful differences. Predicting when interaction helps is central to understanding and designing collective intelligence. We investigate whether a few dimensionless parameters can predict gains over explicitly defined non-communicating baselines across group sizes, network structures, and tasks, toward a Reynolds-number-like description of collective intelligence. Using distributed classification tasks, stochastic tracking networks, and neural cellular automata, we combine analytical and empirical evidence to examine information sufficiency, dynamical applicability, and finite-sample prediction. We construct inference systems with bounded random variables and matching specified joint moments up to total degree three, yet opposite interaction gains under a fixed readout. These moments alone cannot generally determine the gain sign. Tracking networks likewise exhibit gain reversals despite matched candidate parameters when task power occupies different spectral modes. Under concentrated task spectra and aligned observation noise, however, we derive a low-dimensional similarity relation with an explicit zero-delay error bound and test it across network sizes and topologies under frozen protocols. The relation does not directly apply to the neural cellular systems, where a separate moment-based predictor underperforms direct gain measurement at matched calibration sample budgets. These results establish conditions and limits for low-dimensional gain prediction, providing a restricted similarity law while leaving a general Reynolds-number-like description of collective intelligence open.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08971v1</id>
    <title>Phantom Consensus: Measuring Social Reasoning in Multi-Agent LLM Decision-Making</title>
    <updated>2026-11-06T04:33:59Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08971v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.08971v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Multi-agent LLM systems increasingly aggregate judgments across model instances, but reasoning about other agents can itself introduce failure. We study a setting in which LLMs shift their public decisions after observing ambiguous social signals while reporting inaccurate estimates of what other agents privately judged, even when the group's recorded private judgments do not support the apparent consensus. We call this failure phantom consensus and study it as a pluralistic-ignorance-style pattern in controlled LLM collectives. To measure this phenomenon, we introduce PHANTOM-Bench, a benchmark that separates isolated private judgments, public decisions after ambiguous social signals, elicited estimates of the group's private judgment, transparency-based recovery, and controls for neutral public text and explicit vote-following. Across nine closed- and open-weight models, ambiguous public signals consistently degrade decision quality and can turn correct private group judgments into incorrect public collective outcomes. Public accuracy drops by as much as 47.8 percentage points, and collective rationality failures reach 47.3% in the most susceptible setting. We observe substantial errors in reported group-private beliefs alongside public-stage failures, while control conditions reveal model-dependent differences in susceptibility to ambiguous and explicit peer signals. Revealing the agents' recorded private decisions repairs many failures without revealing the gold label, although recovery varies across models. Our results show that evaluating multi-agent LLM systems requires measuring not only final agreement, but whether that agreement reflects independently measured private judgments or an apparent consensus.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.31154v1</id>
    <title>Attention Latent Feedback</title>
    <updated>2026-11-23T18:21:05Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.31154v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.31154v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>During autoregressive decoding, the deeper representations of the previous token have already been computed, yet shallow layers at the current token cannot read them directly because standard self-attention connects positions only at the same depth. We introduce Attention Latent Feedback (ALF), an architecture that allows every sublayer to attend to the outputs of the deeper layers at the previous position. Training unrolls this cross-position recurrence into two parallel passes, whereas decoding remains single-pass using cached previous-token states. Across mixture-of-experts models with up to 4.0B parameters, ALF lowers held-out loss by 0.022-0.024 nats over the standard residual with about 1.1% decoding FLOP overhead, and consistently outperforms prior final-state feedback across all three scales on both standard and attention residual backbones. On MoE-1.6B, ALF matches a $1.38\times$ larger baseline token budget, and on MoE-4.0B it lifts average accuracy across seventeen downstream benchmarks from 45.1% to 47.0%. Analysis further reveals that intermediate and nearby deeper layers drive most of this benefit, allowing a fixed nearest-window variant to retain 89%-94% of the gain at linear read cost while learned attention widens its margin with scale.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30844v1</id>
    <title>DyLoMo-DiT: Dynamic Looped Mixture-of-Experts Diffusion Transformers</title>
    <updated>2026-11-23T15:27:20Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30844v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.30844v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) scale model capacity by increasing both parameter count and computation. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) variants expand parameter capacity while keeping per-token computation roughly fixed, but still require substantial parameter storage. In this paper, we propose Dynamic Looped MoE DiT (DyLoMo-DiT), which reuses parameters rather than adding them: a weight-shared loop repeatedly applies the middle layers, while sparse experts allocate parameter capacity across tokens. This design deepens the network without adding parameters, freeing the parameter budget for other uses, such as more experts or more distinct layers. It also allocates compute dynamically, varying the number of passes across noise levels. Experiments show that DyLoMo-DiT makes more effective use of parameter and compute budgets, with further gains from assigning more passes to low-noise steps. On ImageNet $256\times256$, DyLoMo-DiT reduces FID by 11-24% relative to DiT and 36-56% relative to DiT-MoE at matched parameter and compute budgets. For text-to-image generation, a scaled DyLoMo-DiT achieves a higher GenEval score than FLUX.1 (0.714 vs. 0.673), with less than one tenth of its active parameters (1.05B vs. 12B).</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30662v1</id>
    <title>WeMM-Ecom: Advancing Multimodal Content Understanding for WeChat E-Commerce</title>
    <updated>2026-11-23T13:22:22Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30662v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.30662v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We present WeMM-Ecom, a family of multimodal large language models that deliver frontier e-commerce capabilities while achieving state-of-the-art general-purpose performance at their respective scales. The family spans five sizes, from a 0.8B dense model to a 35B mixture-of-experts model with 3B active parameters. Our training pipeline begins with two-stage continued pre-training that progressively raises the proportion of e-commerce data within a diverse multimodal data mixture, followed by hybrid-thinking post-training that combines on-policy distillation and reinforcement learning to support both non-thinking and thinking modes. For evaluation, we construct a comprehensive suite of 28 e-commerce benchmarks (23 in-house and five open-source) covering eight business scenarios and complement it with 64 public general-purpose benchmarks. On the e-commerce suite, WeMM-Ecom-35B-A3B surpasses substantially larger open-source flagship models, including Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, HY4, and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. On the general-purpose suite, every WeMM-Ecom model surpasses its similarly sized Qwen3.5 counterpart, with the lightweight variants (e.g., WeMM-Ecom-2B) showing clear advantages over leading lightweight models such as Qwen3.5-2B, MiniCPM-V-4.7-1B, and LFM3-VL-2B. Beyond benchmarks, WeMM-Ecom now powers hundreds of production use cases in WeChat, including catalog management, multimodal product search, and livestream commerce, serving billion-scale requests per day. We publicly release all model weights and detail our data curation, training recipe, and benchmark construction to facilitate future work on domain-specialized multimodal models. We have released the model weights and code to facilitate future research at https://github.com/Tencent/WeMM-Ecom.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30542v1</id>
    <title>GC-MoE K3: A Green-Context Role Graph for Latent Mixture-of-Experts Decode</title>
    <updated>2026-11-23T11:49:19Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30542v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.30542v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Kimi K3 combines a latent routed mixture of experts with full-width shared experts. A complete feed-forward evaluation must score and select experts, project tokens into the latent space, exchange tokens across expert-parallel ranks, compute the routed and shared branches, and normalize and project the routed sum before joining the branches. We present GC-MoE K3, a datacenter Blackwell implementation that schedules this entire evaluation as a CUDA Graph across two Green Contexts. Five base roles split input projection, routing, dispatch, expert computation, and finalization. Dispatch can fill the routed input ring while the compute partition evaluates shared experts. Finalize waits for the expert owners needed by each token and overlaps routed reduction and RMSNorm with loading the output projection weights. Conditional roles reuse the communication partition for routed computation and reduce split-$K$ projection partials. On GB200 at EP8, EP16, and EP32, the operator is faster at all 24 measured configurations than the paired SGLang-style reference (mean speedup $1.1324\times$). A comparison with historical vLLM-style measurements gives $1.3651\times$ across the same 24 shapes. Both latency comparisons time single-layer graph replay on synthetic K3-shaped inputs with a residual prefix. The separate paired numerical suite passes all 142 cases and 2,936 rank checks.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30483v1</id>
    <title>When an AI agent makes a mistake in a database, what decides the damage?</title>
    <updated>2026-11-23T11:06:44Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30483v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.30483v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>AI agents now run statements against production databases, and several of the incidents that followed deleted production data, which came back only through backups or the provider's help. We ask what decides the damage when such an agent makes a mistake: the model, a guard layer in front of the database, or the database engine itself. The study has two preregistered layers. In Layer A, a frozen library of 22 canonical mistakes is applied by script, with no model involved, to four relational engines under five permission arms and two recovery arms, followed by an engine-native recovery drill (792 cells; 874 drill runs including 10-minute repeats). In Layer B, a minimal tool-calling agent driven by six small open-weight models (4B to 12B parameters, plus one 35B mixture-of-experts model with about 3B active, served locally) works on tasks that contain hazards across nine engines: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, ClickHouse, Apache Cassandra, MongoDB, Valkey, Apache Kafka and OpenSearch (9,468 trials). A secondary run added MariaDB, Redis and Elasticsearch (2,916 trials); each behaved like its closest core engine. Out of the box, the engines differ less in what a mistake destroys than in what they let you undo. Three of the seven preregistered hypotheses met their decision rule: H2 (for one of nine damage classes) and H3 largely by construction of the arms, and H4 only under its original measure. Four did not; one of them (H5) was uninformative, because in its task the agents never found the credential. The post-hoc analyses (S1-S13) are exploratory and uncorrected for multiple comparisons; on PostgreSQL, MySQL, OpenSearch and ClickHouse the preregistered outcome and original-row loss disagree about G1. We report all of them, with every deviation from the preregistration and its timing.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30436v1</id>
    <title>MF-EDA: Joining Membership Functions to Adapt the Number of Distributions in Gaussian Estimation-of-Distribution Algorithms</title>
    <updated>2026-11-23T10:30:04Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30436v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.30436v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>An estimation-of-distribution algorithm (EDA) usually samples from one Gaussian, whose peak sits where most selected individuals are. On a landscape with two funnels that is not where the best solutions are: the wider funnel supplies most of the selected individuals, and the deeper funnel, which holds the global optimum, is lost early. This paper builds the search distribution as a neuro-fuzzy system builds a model: from Gaussian membership functions joined by membership degrees. In every generation the proposed MF-EDA searches the principal directions of the selected individuals for the direction along which they are bimodal, describes them on that direction by one or two membership functions according to the Bayesian information criterion and a separation test, joins each membership function to a local Gaussian in the other directions, and samples from the normalised union. A membership function has height one whatever the number of individuals under it, so a detected funnel receives samples according to its width. A two-region selection model shows that sampling shares proportional to the head count, as in a Gaussian mixture, compound the early disadvantage of the deeper funnel, and that the union does not. With one membership function the algorithm is its single-Gaussian baseline; the steps cost no fitness evaluations but make a generation 8 to 17 times slower to compute. On 36 double-funnel settings the component raises the successful runs of a rank-weighted Gaussian EDA from 805 to 1712 of 1800. On the Lunacek double funnel in 30 dimensions it raises that EDA from 4 to 49 and AMaLGaM from 0 to 47 successes in 50 runs, while results on single-funnel functions and on ten multimodal BBOB functions do not change. Restarted CMA-ES remains cheaper in evaluations on the standard double funnel, and the component stops helping when the global funnel is much narrower than the other.</summary>

    <title>Video Generalized Category Discovery</title>
    <updated>2026-11-23T08:59:11Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30316v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.30316v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Generalized Category Discovery (GCD) aims to categorize unlabeled data from both known and unknown classes using labeled data from only the known classes. While recent GCD methods have shown promise on static images, their performance degrades in videos due to temporal dynamics, larger intra-class variation, and the lack of temporal consistency in existing approaches. We introduce VideoGCD, a framework tailored for video action recognition under the GCD setting. Our method integrates (i) a partitioned Mixture-of-Experts module that encourages specialization for known and novel categories, (ii) a novel-class balancing loss to reduce bias toward known classes, and (iii) a temporal optimal transport loss that promotes consistent routing across frames. Experiments on three video benchmarks demonstrate that VideoGCD significantly improves performance over existing GCD methods, particularly on novel categories. Our findings highlight the importance of combining temporal modeling and expert specialization for video GCD.</summary>

    <title>The Stigmergic Index: A Biomimetic Edge Centrality for Spatial Network Analysis</title>
    <updated>2026-11-23T08:51:47Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30301v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.30301v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Ant Colony Optimization (ACO) is a family of metaheuristics inspired by the pheromone-based navigation of real ants, a decentralized mechanism often associated with shortest-path discovery. Over the past two decades, research has primarily focused on optimization tasks such as vehicle routing within a network. In this paper, we shift this perspective by using swarm intelligence to gather diagnostic information about the underlying network structure itself. Through decentralized exploration, we harness stigmergic dynamics to introduce a novel topological and behavioural metric: the Stigmergic Index. While sharing baseline structural properties with traditional betweenness centrality on simple grids, our index accounts for path polarization effects that can diverge from shortest-path-based assumptions.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30935v1</id>
    <title>FGSCalib: Targetless Camera-LiDAR Extrinsic Calibration from Foreground Segmentation</title>
    <updated>2026-11-23T16:20:51Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30935v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.30935v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Camera-LiDAR pairs installed as fixed infrastructure need periodic recalibration, but a calibration target takes the installation out of service. We present FGSCalib, a targetless method that calibrates a stationary camera-LiDAR pair from the objects moving in its view. We only assume that arbitrary moving objects are present in the scene: each sensor separates the moving foreground from the static background, without relying on object classes. With the correct extrinsic, the LiDAR foreground points project onto the camera foreground. FGSCalib turns the camera mask into a boundary-proximity field and finds the extrinsic by two-stage simulated annealing over selected frame pairs. It needs no measured initial extrinsic (random starts give similar results) and works with both rotating and non-repetitive LiDARs. We evaluate it on 21 simulated scenarios with exact ground truth and on 72 real ones (nine camera-LiDAR pairs in eight scenes), with a reference averaged from 43 manual calibrations. In simulation the median error is 5.3 cm and 0.19°. On real data we use a tolerance of 18 cm and 1.8°, met by 93% of single manual calibrations. Keeping the lowest-cost of five runs, FGSCalib meets it in 51 of the 72 scenarios: in 20 of 24 with the Livox, where the strongest of five baselines reaches 11, and in 31 of 48 with the two rotating LiDARs, where only one baseline estimate does. Its median error is 9.5 cm and 0.9°, against 7.3 cm and 0.7° for a single manual calibration. The code and the dataset are available online.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30657v1</id>
    <title>Computational Complexity and Energy Landscapes of Coulomb Crystals</title>
    <updated>2026-11-23T13:20:46Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30657v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.30657v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Simulated annealing is widely used to search for ground states of trapped-ion Coulomb crystals and of charges on a sphere (the Thomson problem). Elementary nonuniform bounds clarify the role of the input encoding. For identical ions in a fixed trap, unary ion count and a binary energy threshold define a decision problem in P/poly; NP-hardness would imply a collapse of the polynomial hierarchy. The same holds on the unit sphere. With unary ion count and logarithmic precision parameter, approximate configuration search on the sphere and in a fixed positive-definite harmonic trap admits a solution function in FP/poly. These advice bounds provide no uniform search algorithm. In simulations of up to 100 ions, the number of distinct minima found and the time to reach the best-known minimum both grow approximately exponentially. When ions are pinned to prescribed candidate sites, choosing which sites to occupy to minimize the Coulomb energy is NP-hard in two and three dimensions; a finite-precision promise version is NP-complete. All ions are identical, the interaction is bare Coulomb repulsion, and the hardness is carried by the site positions alone. We extend a previous inverse-square reduction to the Coulomb interaction by deriving its angular law, including the quartic field term, and sharpening two estimates. The construction is an array of quadrupoles whose common monopole term cancels from energy differences between legal configurations. Its energy landscapes exhibit large barriers between nearly degenerate minima. Barrier trees resolve this structure, and simulated annealing becomes trapped above the ground state in the cube example. At laboratory parameters, with individually tunable well depths, the encoding survives numerically on a half-filled square lattice. For Doppler-cooled strontium ions, this requires stiff wells a few to tens of micrometers apart, as in electrode trap arrays.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30405v1</id>
    <title>Optimistic Online Learning for Coding Agents with Aggregate Feedback</title>
    <updated>2026-11-23T10:05:39Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30405v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2611.30405v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Large language model (LLM) coding agents operating on Web development platforms can interact with repositories, issue trackers, and continuous integration services to carry out long-horizon software engineering tasks. However, behavioral drift remains a major bottleneck in such multi-turn reasoning and action trajectories. To mitigate this, activation steering has emerged as a promising approach for regularizing agent behaviors by intervening on the LLM's transformer residual streams. Nonetheless, existing methods typically apply a static steering policy across all tasks, overlooking the fact that a single policy is rarely effective across heterogeneous tasks and varying execution turns. This limitation motivates dynamic online selection among candidate steering policies. Yet, doing so in long-horizon agentic settings is challenging: verifiable task-level feedback is only revealed upon task completion, leaving the contributions of individual steering turns unobserved. To address this challenge, we formulate online steering-policy selection as a multi-armed bandit problem with delayed task-level feedback and turn-level predictive hints derived from residual-stream activations. Within this formulation, we introduce Online Optimistic Activation Steering, a meta-framework that uses hints to guide within-task steering policy selection and leverages terminal task-level feedback to correct cumulative reward estimates. Theoretically, against the best fixed policy in hindsight, we prove regret bounds that tighten with increasing hint accuracy and establish a matching lower bound with respect to prediction error and candidate policy count. Empirical evaluations on realistic coding benchmarks demonstrate that our framework outperforms both static steering policies and naive online adaptive baselines.</summary>
